Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 1:

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear signs, that you may remember.﴾

It is permissible that (sūrah) be a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada' muqaddar) indicated by the opening of the surah, so that the sense is: "This is a surah." The omitted demonstrative (ism al-ishārah al-muqaddar) refers to what is present to the hearing, namely the continuous speech, so everything that is sent down of this surah and joined to it of verses is among what is pointed to by the omitted demonstrative.

This demonstrative is used very frequently in speech.

Page 142
It is also permissible that (sūrah) be a subject (mubtada'), and that His saying: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ [al-Nur: 2] to the end of the surah be a predicate (khabar) about (sūrah), the beginning being with the word (sūrah), and then descriptions were attached to it to create anticipation for what comes after it, like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two words are beloved to the Most Merciful, light on the tongue, heavy in the Scale: Glory be to Allah and praise Him, Glory be to Allah the Mighty."

The best of the ways of estimating (the omitted element) is that which the listener's mind is led to without effort, so set aside the other estimations which they permitted here.

The meaning of (sūrah) is a part of the Qur'an defined by a beginning, an end, and a number of verses. Its explanation has already been given in the eighth introduction (muqaddimah) of this commentary.

The clause (We sent it down) and what is conjoined to it are in the position of a description (sifah) of (sūrah). The purpose of those descriptions is to draw attention to this surah, so that the Muslims may turn wholeheartedly to receiving what is in it. In this there is also a favour upon the community, for determining the rules of its way of life in its affairs.

So in His saying (We sent it down) there is an honouring of the surah through what (anzalnā) indicates of the attribution to the Name of Majesty (Allah), which indicates care for it and its exaltation. He expressed the sending down of its verses with (anzalnā) after He had decreed them by His knowledge through His inner speech. The purpose of attributing its sending down to God Most High is to honour it. He expressed its sending down in the past tense, though it actually occurs in the present, considering the intention to send it down; it is as if it were said: "We intended its sending down and its conveyance," and this care was treated as though it were past, out of eagerness for it. This is from the use of the verb to mean the intention of its occurrence, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and the verse continues.

The indication is His saying (and We made it obligatory). The meaning of (faradnāhā) according to the exegetes is: "We made obligatory acting upon what is in it." This interpretation fits only with regard to most of this surah, not all of it, for some of it has no action connected to it, like His saying: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35] and the verses, and His saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

Page 143
What I choose is that obligation (fard) here means specification and determination, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a portion ordained﴾ [al-Nisa': 7], and His saying: (﴿There is no fault in the Prophet regarding what Allah has ordained for him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 38]). The attribution of the verb (faradnā) to the pronoun of the surah is of the kind that in the discussions of the principles of jurisprudence is expressed as ascribing rulings to entities while meaning their states, like ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], that is, its eating. So the meaning is: "and We made its verses obligatory." We will mention shortly what clarifies this further at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses﴾ [al-Nur: 34], and how the three attributes mentioned here are paired with the three attributes mentioned there.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-faradnāhā﴾ with a light (unshaddaded) rā' in the bare verb form. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (wa-farraḍnāhā) with a shaddah on the rā' for intensification, like (nazzala) with the shaddah. In the margins of the Kashshaf, a verse of al-Zamakhshari is quoted:

"As if he were a worker in the religion of his nobility, with a surah sent down concerning him and made obligatory."

These two rulings, namely the sending down and the obligation, apply to the whole surah.

As for His saying: ﴿and in which We have sent down clear signs﴾, it is another honouring of this surah, honouring every verse that the surah contains: from guidance to monotheism, the truth of Islam, and proofs and parables, and what is in the signs of Allah's craftsmanship indicating the vastness of His power, knowledge and wisdom. These are what His saying indicates: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and an example from those who passed before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Nur: 34], and His saying: ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds﴾ [al-Nur: 43] to His saying: ﴿a straight path﴾ [al-Nur: 46].

Among the clear signs sent down in it is Allah's informing His Messenger of the innermost secrets of the hypocrites, of what they concealed in their souls, from His saying: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾ [al-Nur: 48] to His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ Thus the honouring occurred first through the whole surah together, and secondly through each part of it.

The word (āyāt) is the plural of (āyah), which is a portion of Qur'anic speech indicating an independent meaning. Its explanation has already been given in the eighth introduction of this commentary.

Page 144
The intended meaning of the verses sent down in this surah is all that the surah contains of verses, not specific verses from among them. The purpose is to honour its verses by applying the description (bayyināt) to them.

Since the verses that the surah contains in their entirety are themselves the surah, not a part of it, as there is nothing other than those verses that actually contains those verses, nor anything likened to what contains them, the particle (fī), which is designated for the sense of location, is used in other than its proper sense, neither literally nor as an explicit metaphor.

Therefore it is determined that the word (fīhā) indicates an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), by likening the verses of this surah to mental treasures that are stored up and kept carefully from being wasted or lost, as though they were things placed in a chest or the like. The likened-to is alluded to by one of its attributes, namely the particle of location, so the particle (fī) is an imaginative indication (takhyīl) alone and not an imaginative metaphor (isti'arah takhyīliyyah), since there is nothing that is likened to a chest or the like. The position of this imaginative indication is like the position of the claws of death in the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

"When death sinks its claws, you find that no amulet avails."

This locative sense is similar to the explanatory genitive (iḍāfah bayāniyyah), like His saying: ﴿Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], and His saying: ﴿Are your disbelievers better?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43], for the disbelievers are the very referent of the plural pronoun addressed, and they are the polytheists.

So His saying (and We sent down in it) means: "and We sent it down, verses that are clear." The description (verses) as (clear), that is, evident, is a metaphor in the attribution to the mind (majāz 'aqlī), because (al-bayn) is in fact its meanings. The verb of sending down is repeated, with the conjunction particle dispensing with it, to show further care for them.

The point is that the clause ﴿that you may remember﴾ is connected to the clause ﴿and We sent down in it clear verses﴾, because verses in this sense are a likely cause of remembrance; that is, they are proofs that are likely to bring about your remembrance. Thus by this hope a further description of the surah is obtained: that it is a source of remembrance and admonition. Remembrance (al-tadhakkur) is the arising in the mind of what was forgotten, and here it is used metaphorically for acquiring knowledge from its certain proofs, by treating it as knowledge that was already present before and then forgotten by the mind; that is, knowledge that by its nature should be known, so its ignorance is likened to forgetting and its knowledge is likened to remembering.

Al-Jumhur read (tadhdhakkarūn) with a shaddah on the dhal, its original form being (tatadhakkarūn), which was assimilated. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read (tadhakkarūn) with a light dhal, one of the two tā's being deleted for brevity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The adulteress and the adulterer: flog each one of them with a hundred lashes.﴾

This is the beginning of a statement, and it serves as a heading and a chapter title in the arrangement of the text. For this reason the particle *fa* (فـ), which signals that what follows it has the force of an answer and what precedes it has the force of a condition, comes after it. The sense is: "The adulteress and the adulterer are among those for whom this surah was revealed and prescribed." Since this calls for the listener's attention, the statement carries the force of: "If you want their ruling, then flog each one of them with a hundred lashes." This is the function of this *fa* whenever it comes after something that has the form of a subject (*mubtada'*): that subject has some sense in which the listener is eager to learn its condition. An example is the line of poetry, one of the verses cited in Sibawayh's *Kitab* whose speaker is unknown:

*"Someone said: 'Marry the women of Khawlan, and the nobility of the two tribes is as it is.'"*

The implied sense is: "This is Khawlan, or Khawlan is of those whose in-law relationship is desired; so marry their young women if you desire it." Those who turned their minds away from these subtleties of usage said: "The *fa* is superfluous in the predicate." The superfluity of *fa* was discussed earlier in His words, ﴿And the thief, male and female: cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], in the surah of al-'Uqud.

The two forms, *al-zaniyah* and *al-zani* (الزانِيَةُ والزّانِي), are the form of the active participle, and here it is used in its basic meaning, which is that its bearer is characterized by the sense of its root. For this reason it is treated as equivalent to the present tense in indicating the characterization by the act in the present time. It is as if it were said: "The one who commits adultery (*allati tazni*) and the one who commits adultery (*alladhi yazni*), flog each one of them," and so on. The command to flog each one of them supports this, since flogging is consequent upon being engaged in the act that causes it.

[p. 146]

Then it is possible that the story of Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, in which His words were revealed, ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3], and so on, is the occasion of revelation of the beginning of this surah. In that case the verse ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3] is the primary purpose of this surah, and His words, ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer: flog each one of them with a hundred lashes﴾, serve as a preface and introduction to His words, ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. This is because condemning the condition of prostitutes deserves to be preceded by what is more deserving of legislation, namely the punishment of one who commits fornication. Marthad was not moved to desire marrying 'Anaq except that she proposed to him that he commit fornication with her.

The mention of *al-zaniyah* is placed before *al-zani* because of the concern with the ruling, since the woman is the one who prompts a man to commit fornication, and through her encouraging the man fornication occurs. If the woman refused herself, the man would find no way to fornicate, so mentioning the woman first is more effective in warning her. His words, *kulla wahidin minhuma* (كُلَّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما, "each one of them"), indicate that neither of them is more deserving of the punishment than the other.

The definiteness of *al-zaniyah* and *al-zani* is definiteness of the genus, which generally conveys totality, and the context of legislation requires it. When the genus *alif-lam* (ال) enters on the active participle, it removes the description from resemblance to the verb, so the participle is not literally in the present or in any other time; rather, it indicates that the characteristic is realized in its bearer. By this generality it includes female slaves and male slaves. Thus *al-zaniyah* and *al-zani* refer to whoever is characterized by fornication.

*Al-zina* (الزِّنى) is the verbal noun of *zana*, and it means sexual intercourse between a man and a woman who are not lawful to each other. One says: *zana al-rajulu* (the man fornicated) and *zanat al-mar'ah* (the woman fornicated). One also says *zana* in the form of *mufa'alah* (زانى), because the act arises from two agents, and for this reason its verbal noun is *al-zina'* (الزِّناءُ) with a long vowel, in the pattern *fi'al*, and its hamza may be lightened so that it becomes a shortened noun. Most of what happened in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyyah) was done out of desire for love and mutual agreement between the man and the woman without any compensation. If it was for compensation, it was *al-bigha'* (البِغاءُ, prostitution). It occurred among free women but was more common among slave women, and they would openly display it. Prostitutes would place banners on their houses, like the banner of the veterinarian, so that they would be known by it. All of this is included in the term *al-zina* in the usage of the Qur'an and in the legal ruling. The mention of *al-zina* was discussed earlier in His words, ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ [al-Isra': 32], in the surah of al-Isra'.

*Al-jald* (الجَلْدُ) is striking with a strip of hide. It is derived from *al-jild* (الجِلْد, with a kasra on the jim), because it is striking the skin, that is, the surface of the body, just as *jabahahu* (he struck his forehead), *batanahu* (he struck his stomach), and *ra'asahu* (he struck his head) are derived from the body parts: *jabahahu* means he struck his forehead, *batanahu* means he struck his stomach, and *ra'asahu* means he struck his head. In *al-Kashshaf* he said: "In the word *al-jald* there is an indication that the pain should not go beyond the flesh." That is, the blow should not tear the skin so that the flesh shows. So the choice of this word rather than *al-darb* (striking) is intended to indicate this meaning by way of *idmaj* (إدماج, embedding a figure of speech within another).

The jurists of the major cities agreed that the flogging is done with a whip, that is, with a strip of hide. The *sawt* (سَوْط, whip) is that with which the rider strikes the horse, and it is a braided hide. The whip should be moderately flexible, and the striker should raise his hand moderately. The place of the flogging, according to Malik, is the back. Al-Shafi'i said that all limbs except the face and the genitals are struck. They agreed on avoiding striking vital parts, among which is the head in a punishment. Al-Tabari reported that 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar punished a slave girl who had committed a offense, and he said to the one doing the flogging: "Strike her legs and her lower body." His son 'Abdullah said to him: "Then where is the word of God, ﴿Let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of God﴾?" He said: "She has been punished." His words, *kulla wahidin minhuma* (كُلَّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما), are an emphasis of the generality derived from the definiteness, so He did not suffice with saying *fa-jliduhuma* (flog them both), as He said, ﴿And the thief, male and female: cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. The masculine form of *kull wahid* is a predominance of the masculine, like ﴿And she was among the obedient﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12].

The address of the command to flog is directed to the Muslims, so it is carried out by whoever is in charge of the affairs of the Muslims, from among the rulers and judges, and is not carried out by the guardians. Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad said: the master punishes his male slave and female slave for fornication. Abu Hanifa said: only the Imam punishes. Malik also said: the master does not punish fornication on his female slave if she is married to a free man or a slave, and only the authority (*wali al-amr*) punishes her.

[p. 147]

The people of the pre-Islamic period did not punish fornication, because it was by mutual consent between the man and the woman, except when the woman had a husband or a guardian who defended his honor by himself, as indicated by the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I passed through guards to reach her, and a band who were eager to kill me, if they could conceal it."*

And the words of 'Abd Bani al-Hasḥas:

*"And they are the daughters of the people; if they perceive us, one of the daughters of the people will become one of the calamities."*

*Al-dahāris* (الدَّهارِسُ) are the calamities. There was no fixed punishment in this, but rather the ruling of the sword or reconciliation on what the two parties agree upon. In the *Muwatta'* (the book of Malik) from Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani: "Two men disputed before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). One of them said: 'O Messenger of God, judge between us by the Book of God.' The other, who was the more learned of the two, said: 'Yes, O Messenger of God, judge between us by the Book of God, and permit me to speak.' He said: 'Speak.' He said: 'My son was a laborer (*'asīf*, a hired worker) for this man, and he committed adultery with his wife. They informed me that upon my son is stoning, so I ransomed him with a hundred sheep and a slave girl of mine. Then I asked the people of knowledge, and they informed me that upon my son is only a hundred lashes and exile for a year, and they informed me that stoning is upon his wife.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will judge between you both by the Book of God. As for your sheep and your slave girl, they are returned to you.' He flogged his son a hundred lashes and exiled him for a year, and he ordered Unays al-Aslami to go to the wife of the other man: if she confesses, stone her. She confessed, and he stoned her." Malik said: *al-'asīf* is the hired worker.

This ransoming was a remnant of what they had been doing in the pre-Islamic period. Then the punishment for fornication was prescribed in Islam by what is in the surah of al-Nisa', which is harm to the male fornicator, that is, a painful punishment, and confinement for the female fornicator for the duration of her life. The verse indicated that this ruling was general with regard to the man, since harm is suitable to be specified by flogging or stoning, and it was temporary with regard to the woman by His words, ﴿Or God makes for them a way﴾ [al-Nisa': 15]. Then the punishment for fornication was prescribed by what is in this surah.

So the prescription of the punishment for fornication by this verse is a hundred lashes, which covered the married and the unmarried. The Sunnah specified it for the unmarried men and women. As for one who is married (*ahsana*) from among them, that is, who has married by a valid contract and the consummation has occurred, the punishment for the married fornicator is stoning with stones until he dies. This was a mutawatir Sunnah (a practice transmitted by so many chains that it is certain) in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ma'iz ibn Malik was stoned. The scholars agreed upon this, and this consensus was a trace of its being mutawatir.

It has been reported from 'Umar that stoning was in the Qur'an: "The married man and the married woman, if they commit fornication, stone them absolutely." In another narration: "The elderly man and the elderly woman." And that it was recited, and its recitation was abrogated. In *Ahkam* of Ibn al-Faras on the surah of al-Nisa' there is: "Some people denied this." I have not seen anyone who identified those who denied it. It was mentioned in the surah of al-Nur that all of the Kharijites hold that this verse applies generally to the married and the unmarried, and they do not hold stoning, and they say: "There is no stoning in the Book of God, so there is no stoning."

There is no doubt that the judgment of stoning occurred after the revelation of the surah of al-Nur. 'Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa was asked about stoning: "Was it before the surah of al-Nur or after it?" The questioner intended by this that the verse of the surah of al-Nur would be abrogated by the hadith of stoning, or the reverse, that is, that stoning is abrogated by flogging. Ibn Abi Awfa said: "I do not know." In the narration of Abu Hurayrah, he witnessed the stoning. This implies that it was acted upon after the surah of al-Nur, because Abu Hurayrah embraced Islam in the seventh year (AH), and the surah of al-Nur was revealed in the fourth or fifth year, as you know. The scholars agreed that the punishment of the married fornicator is stoning.

It has also been established by the Sunnah that the fornicator is exiled after being flogged, for a full year, and there is no exile for a woman. Exile is not fixed according to Abu Hanifa, but is left to the discretion of the Imam, if he sees exile as appropriate because of his corruption.

[p. 148]

The manner of stoning and flogging and their instruments are explained in the books of jurisprudence, and the meaning of the verse does not depend on mentioning them.

* * *

﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of God, if you believe in God and the Last Day.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause *fa-jlidu* (so flog). Since flogging is painful, and the one who carries it out may feel tender toward the one being flogged because of his pain, the Muslims were forbidden to let pity for the adulteress and the adulterer take hold of them, so that they would abandon the punishment or reduce it.

*Al-akhdh* (الأخْذ), its literal meaning is seizure. Here it is used figuratively for the strong effect of pity on the addressees and its taking possession of their will, to the point that they become too weak to carry out the punishment. It is like His words, ﴿Pride took hold of him in sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206]. So it is used in the sense of the strong attachment of the attribute to the thing described.

*Bihima* (بِهِما) may be connected with *ra'fah* (pity), so the *ba'* indicates accompaniment, because the sense of seizure here is the arising of the attribute at the sight of them. It may also be connected to *ta'khudhukum* (take hold of you), in which case the *ba'* indicates cause: the seizing of pity because of them, that is, because of their flogging.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb is for emphasis on mentioning the adulterer and the adulteress, as an alert to attention to carrying out the punishment. The prohibition against pity taking hold of them is a metonymy for the prohibition of its effect, which is abandoning the punishment or reducing it. As for pity itself, it occurs in the soul without choice, so the prohibition does not apply to it. Rather, the Muslim must train himself to repel pity in the situations where pity is blameworthy.

Ar-ra'fah (tenderness): a special mercy that arises upon seeing harm befall the one who is pitied. Its discussion has already been given at His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is to mankind Kind (ra'uf), Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is permissible to pronounce the hamzah with sukun, and Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited it thus. It is also permissible to vocalize it with fatha, and Ibn Kathir recited it with fatha.

His saying ﴿in the religion of Allah﴾ is attached to ar-ra'fah to indicate that this tenderness is not praiseworthy, because it nullifies the religion of Allah, i.e., His rulings. Allah legislated the hadd (prescribed punishment) for the sake of public welfare, so tenderness in establishing it becomes corruption. There is in this an allusion that Allah, who legislated the hadd, is more tender toward His servants than some of them are toward others. In the Musnad of Abu Ya'la, from Hudhayfah, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ): "The one who struck beyond the hadd is brought forward, and Allah says to him: 'My servant, why did you strike beyond the hadd?' He says: 'I became angry for Your sake.' Allah says: 'Was your anger greater than My anger?' And the one who fell short is brought forward, and He says: 'My servant, why did you fall short?' He says: 'I had mercy on him.' He says: 'Was your mercy greater than My mercy?' And both are ordered to the Fire."

The clause ﴿if you believe in Allah﴾ is a conditional whose answer is omitted, its meaning being indicated by what precedes it: i.e., if you are believers, then let not tenderness toward them take hold of you, meaning let not tenderness toward them affect you. The purpose is intense warning against being so affected by tenderness toward them that it is presupposed that they do not believe. This is delivered in the manner of stirring and incitement, until the listener says: how could I not believe in Allah and the Last Day?

The belief in the Last Day is conjoined with the belief in Allah to remind that tenderness toward them in suspending or diminishing the hadd is forgetfulness of the Last Day, for such tenderness leads to their being taken to account for punishment on the Day of Resurrection. It is thus a harmful tenderness, like the tenderness of withholding medicine from the sick, for the hudud are expiations for what the indications of the Shari'ah point to.

* * *

﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾: He commanded that a group of Muslims attend the establishment of the hadd for fornication, to ensure the hadd is carried out and as a safeguard against leniency in it. Concealment is a means to forgetfulness; if the believers do not witness it, they may ask why it was not carried out, and when its neglect becomes evident to them, there will not be lacking among them one who changes the wrong by reversing the suspension of the hudud.

There is another benefit: among the aims of the hudud, along with punishing the offender, is that others be deterred, and by the presence of a group of believers those present are admonished and restrained, and the report of it spreads by the present conveying it to the absent.

Al-ta'ifah (the group): a company of people. Its mention has already been made at His saying ﴿Let a group (ta'ifah) of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying ﴿that you might say: The Book was only sent down to two groups before us﴾ [al-An'am: 156] at the end of al-An'am. Its number here has been disputed. The apparent meaning is that it is a number by whose report widespread transmission is achieved, and this varies with differences of places. The well-known view of Malik is two or more; Ibn Abi Zayd said four, by analogy with the testimony for fornication. It was also said: ten.

The apparent sense of the command requires the obligation of a group's attendance at the hadd. The Hanafis took it to mean recommendation, and likewise the Shafi'is; I have not found an explicit statement of its ruling in the Maliki school. It appears from the unrestricted statements of the exegetes and the jurists of the Malikis, and from their disagreement over the minimum number that suffices for a group, that it is understood as obligation, since that is the default reading of a command according to Malik. Whatever its ruling, it is a collective obligation (fard kifayah), and it is not demanded of one who has a special close relation to the convicted person which would grieve him to witness the establishment of the hadd upon him.

[p. 153]

This verse was revealed as a self-contained unit, both at its beginning and at its end, as will be mentioned shortly in the account of its occasion of revelation, whether it was revealed before the verses with which the surah opens or after them. Thus this sentence is an independent statement, and the connection of its placement after the preceding sentence is clear.

Its meaning has been difficult, so the exegetes (mufassirun) sought out aspects of interpretation (ta'wil), and some of these aspects branch into several possibilities. The occasion of revelation of this verse is what Abu Dawud narrated, and what al-Tirmidhi narrated and graded as sound and good (hasan): "There was a man called Martad ibn Abi Martad al-Ghanawi, from among the Muslims, [p. 153] who used to go out from Madinah to Makkah carrying prisoners and bring them to Madinah. There was a prostitute in Makkah called 'Anaq, who was his female companion (khalilah). He had promised a man among the prisoners of Makkah that he would carry him off. He said: I came until I reached a garden wall of Makkah on a moonlit night. He said: 'Anaq came and said: 'Martad?' I said: 'Martad.' She said: 'Welcome and well come! Come, spend the night with us.' He said: I said: 'God has forbidden fornication (zina).' 'Anaq said: 'O people of the tents! This man is carrying off your prisoners!' Eight of the polytheists followed me... until he said: Then they turned back and I returned to my companion, carried him, and unfastened his shackles until I came to Madinah. I came to the Messenger of God and said: 'O Messenger of God, may I marry 'Anaq?' The Messenger of God remained silent and did not answer me at all, until this verse was revealed: ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is married by none but a fornicator or an idolater; and that has been forbidden to the believers.﴾ The Messenger of God said: 'O Martad, do not marry her.'"

It thus becomes clear that this verse was revealed in answer to the question of Martad ibn Abi Martad, whether he might marry 'Anaq. The source of what is obscure and difficult in its meaning is this: that marriage (nikah) here means the contract of marriage (aqd al-tazwij), as the scholarly exegetes such as al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and others definitively affirmed. I hold that the word nikah was not coined for, nor used in any sense other than, the marriage contract and what follows from it. The claim that it is applied to sexual intercourse (wati') arises only from some exegetes' interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], on the basis of the jurists' agreement that a mere contract with a woman to a husband does not make her lawful to her former husband who has divorced her irrevocably (batta), unless the second husband has consummated the marriage with her. There is a lengthy discussion on this, but this is not its place.

There is no doubt that this verse was revealed after the prohibition of fornication, since the prohibition of fornication was among the first rulings legislated in Islam, as in the many verses revealed in Makkah. And it suffices that al-A'sha counted the prohibition of fornication among what the Prophet ﷺ brought of legislation, when he said in his qasidah, when he came to Makkah intending to embrace Islam and praised the Prophet ﷺ, and Abu Jahl hindered him so that he turned back to al-Yamamah and died there:

"Did you not, by your fortune, heed the injunction of Muhammad, the Prophet of God, when he enjoined and called to witness,
...
And do not approach a neighbouring woman, for her secret is forbidden to you; so marry, or remain celibate."

We have mentioned this in our exegesis of the surah of al-Isra'.

At first glance, it appears from the apparent meaning of the verse, up to His words "or an idolater," that its opening is a report about the situation of marrying a fornicating woman, and that it is not a legislation of the ruling on marriage among Muslim fornicators, nor is there marriage among polytheists. If it is a report, the meaning of the verse does not hold, since a fornicator may marry a chaste woman, and a polytheist may marry a chaste woman, and this is the more common case; so the words ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ have no sound meaning. Also, a chaste Muslim may marry a fornicating woman out of desire for her beauty, or in order to rescue her from the vice of fornication, and he is neither a fornicator nor a polytheist; so the words ﴿and the fornicatress is married by none but a fornicator or an idolater﴾ have no sound meaning. And if we concede that it is for legislating a ruling, the problem is greater, since there is no sense in legislating a ruling on the marriage of a fornicator and a fornicatress, or a polytheist and a polytheistress. Therefore, the interpretation of the verse must be one that yields a meaningful sense.

The correct interpretation is that the whole verse is intended as legislation and not as report, because God the Exalted said at its end: ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers.﴾ And because it was revealed in answer to Martad's question about marrying 'Anaq, who was a fornicatress and an idolatress, while Martad was a Muslim and pious. However, the beginning of the verse is not what is intended by the legislation; rather, it is a preface (tamhid) for its end, pointing to the reason for what was legislated at its end. In it there is what clarifies the referent of the demonstrative noun in the words "that" [p. 155] and that its ruling is general for Martad and other Muslims, by virtue of the generality of the word "believers."

It follows from this foundation that His words ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ are a preface to the intended ruling in His words ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾, and that it is delivered in the manner of a report and not of legislation. Therefore it is necessary that the word "fornicator" (al-zani) means the nominal sense of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), which is the sense of being characterized by its verbal noun (masdar), and not the sense of occurrence (huduth). For one must not overlook that the active participle has two aspects: the aspect of being derived from the verbal noun, whereby it is like the imperfect verb, so that "darib" resembles "yadrib" in indicating the occurrence of the action from an agent; and the aspect of its signifying an entity characterized by an action, whereby the aspect of nouns that signify entities becomes stronger in it. Interpreting it in this verse in the nominal sense is required by the contextual indication, since it is not understood that the meaning is that one who commits fornication does not marry except a fornicatress, because there would be no benefit in legislating a prohibition of one form of marriage on the one who committed fornication. This is the reverse of the sense of His words ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2], for there it is in the descriptive sense, i.e., being characterized by the commission of fornication, as we have interpreted it just above, by a contextual indication that makes the flogging follow from the description, since flogging is a punishment which follows only from the commission of a crime that requires it.

Thus it becomes evident that what is meant by His words ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress﴾ etc. is: one for whom fornication has been a habit before Islam, and who was accustomed to it, then embraced Islam and wished to marry a woman who is constant in fornication, such as prostitutes and women who take lovers (mutakhidhat al-akhdan), (and who are not, in any case, except non-Muslim women). So God forbade the Muslims to marry such women with His words ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾. And before it was mentioned what gives it a disgraceful character, namely that it does not suit the state of a Muslim and is only the practice of the people of fornication, i.e., non-believers; for a believer does not make fornication his habit, and if it proceeded from him, it would be a lapse, as happened with Ma'iz ibn Malik.

Thus His words ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ are a preface and not a legislation, because the fornicator, in the sense of one for whom fornication is a habit, is not a believer, so the rulings of Islam are not legislated for him.

[p. 156] This is of the same kind as the words of the Exalted: ﴿Evil women are for evil men, and evil men for evil women﴾ [al-Nur: 26]. This implies that a Muslim who marries a fornicatress has placed himself in the ranks of the fornicators, that is, the polytheists.

His words "or an idolatress" are coordinated with "a fornicatress" to intensify the reproach, since a non-Muslim fornicatress may not be an idolatress, such as the fornicating women of the Jews and Christians and their prostitutes. Likewise "or an idolater" is coordinated with "a fornicator" because it is evident that the context is not concerned with legislating for idolatresses and idolaters the rulings of marriage among themselves, since they are not addressed by the branches of the Shari'ah.

From this it becomes clear that the righteous believer does not marry a fornicatress. That is because habituation to fornication produces a character that suits the states of fornicators, men and women, so he does not desire to associate with a fornicatress except one whose kind of character pleases him. The Muslims at that time were recent converts from polytheism and ignorance, so it was among the important policies of the Shari'ah for the Muslims to keep them far from anything that might remind them of what they used to be accustomed to, with the aim that the morals of Islam would become firm dispositions (malakat) in them. God therefore wanted to keep them away from what might renew in them morals they were on the verge of forgetting.

Thus the position of this verse is the position of the intended purpose of the speech after the introduction, and for this reason it came as a new sentence (mustanifah), just as conclusions come after their proofs. The ruling on the punishment for fornication was mentioned before it, to establish its ruling and what that requires of condemning the act. Therefore, the meaning of "the fornicator" is: one for whom the characteristic of fornication is a habit.

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, from 'Amr ibn al-'As and Mujahid: this verse is specific to a man among the Muslims who asked the Messenger of God ﷺ for permission to marry a woman called Umm Mahzul, who was among the prostitutes (baghaya) who fornicated, and she stipulated that she would spend on him. Perhaps Umm Mahzul is the kunya of 'Anaq, and perhaps the story is one, since no other account has been transmitted. Al-Khattabi said: this is specific to this woman, since she was an unbeliever; as for a Muslim fornicatress, the contract with her is not annulled.

[p. 157] In this verse the mention of the fornicator is placed before the mention of the fornicatress, in contrast with what preceded in His words ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. The reason for placing the fornicatress first in the previous verse is what you have come to know. Here, however, the occasion of revelation of this verse was the desire of a man to marry a woman who had become accustomed to fornication, so the context required attention to what follows from this question by way of censure of the man who marries such a woman.

The sentence ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾ completes the intended meaning of the two sentences before it, and it is an explicit statement of what was meant to be a condemnation of marrying a fornicatress, and a clarification of the legal ruling in the matter.

The demonstrative "that" refers to the meaning contained in the two preceding sentences, namely the marriage of a fornicatress, i.e., "the marriage of a fornicatress has been forbidden to the believers." Therefore the sentence ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾ is conjoined, because it provides a completion of what came before it, and the nature of completion is that it is conjoined by means of coordination (ʿatf). Some scholars took the verse according to its apparent sense of prohibition and said: this is an abrogated (mansukh) ruling, abrogated by the verse after it, ﴿And marry the unmarried (al-ayama) among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32], so the fornicatress entered among the unmarried, that is, after Islam became established and the fear for the Muslims that the morals of the people of ignorance would return to them had gone.

This is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and Ibn 'Umar, and Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i adopted it. It is not reported that anyone married a fornicatress in the period between the revelation of this verse and the revelation of its abrogator, nor that the marriage of a Muslim to a fornicatress was annulled. The requirement of prohibition is invalidity (fasad), and that requires annulment (faskh). Al-Khattabi said: this is specific to this woman, since she was an unbeliever; as for a Muslim fornicatress, the contract with her is not annulled. Others held that its ruling remains in force. Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] attributed the view that the ruling of prohibition remains in force to Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with them all, and others attributed it to the Successors (tabi'un), but the jurists of the regions did not adopt it after them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verses 4–5:

Page 158
﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses — lash them eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after. And those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun).﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

It was widespread in the Jahiliyyah that some of them accused others of fornication when they saw acquaintance or conversation between men and women. And it was widespread among them to impugn lineages baselessly when they saw little resemblance between a father and his son. So it was customary that the ruling on the punishment for fornication (hadd al-zina) be followed by the ruling concerning those who accuse chaste women of fornication when they are not their husbands, and this is the hadd of qadhf (slander). The reason for the connection with the particle fa' (then) was previously discussed in His saying: ﴿The fornicatrix and the fornicator — flog each of them﴾ [al-Nur: 2], and so on.

The basic meaning of ramy (accusing) is throwing something from the hand. Its usage became common for attributing an act or a quality to a person. It was discussed previously in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and then throws it at an innocent person﴾ [al-Nisa: 112], in Surat al-Nisa. The object of ramy is omitted in this verse because the intended meaning is clear from the context and the mention of "chaste women" (al-muhsanat).

Al-muhsanat are the married free women. Ihsan (chastity/protection through marriage) is entering into a marriage by a valid contract. The muhsan is a passive participle from ahsana al-shay' when one protects it from being neglected and from others taking control of it; so the husband protects his wife (yuhassinu imra'atahu), meaning he guards her from neglect and from the aggression of men. This is like the naming of virgins as mukhaddarat and maqsurat, which was discussed in Surat al-Nisa. The description "al-muhsanat" is applied only to married free women, not to slave women, because they were not protected according to the custom of people before Islam.

The object of testimony (shahada) is omitted because it is evident that they are witnesses to establishing what the accuser alleged, namely the establishing of the occurrence of fornication in its reality, which is legally recognized. And it is clear

Page 159
that the four witnesses are other than the accuser, because the meaning of ﴿they do not produce four witnesses﴾ is not realized if the accuser is among the witnesses. The flogging was discussed just previously. This flogging was prescribed as a punishment for one who accuses with falsehood or without verification, and to block the means to that.

The verb (yarmuna, "they accuse") is attributed to the masculine relative pronoun, and the pronouns of (tabu and aslahu, "repent and reform") and likewise the description (al-fasiqun, "the defiantly disobedient") are in masculine forms. The verb of accusing is transitive to an object in the feminine form. All of this is based on the general case or on considering an incident that was the occasion of revelation of the verse. But this ruling in all cases includes the opposite of the people of this form in all its positions, by way of analogy. No weight is given to what is imagined to be a difference, namely that the stigma attaches to a woman when she is accused of fornication but not to a man who is accused of fornication; because placing shame on a woman who commits fornication but not on a man who commits fornication is merely a Jahiliyyah custom to which no attention is paid in Islam. Islam has made equal the prohibition, the hadd, the deferred punishment and the immediate blame between woman and man.

It may be considered that a man's transgression by his fornication is worse than a woman's transgression by her fornication, because the fornicating man loses the lineage of his offspring, so he is a wrongdoer against himself; as for the woman, her child is certainly attached to her, so there is no wrong against herself regarding it. And they are equal in the wrong against the child by the loss of its lineage. So this supposed difference is set aside in analogy.

As for the non-acceptance of the accuser's testimony in the future: since he accused without proof, this indicates his laxity regarding testimony, so he is deserving of not being taken by his testimony.

Al-abad: the entire future time.

The demonstrative (ulaika) is for announcing their defiance so that they are distinguished by this blameworthy attribute.

The restriction in His saying ﴿And those are the defiantly disobedient (hum al-fasiqun)﴾ is for emphasis on the enormity of their defiance, as if other kinds of disobedience are not counted as defiance.

The exception in His saying "Except those who repented" should by right return to everything mentioned before it, as is the case with exceptions according to the majority, except that here it refers specifically to the non-acceptance of their testimony and the establishing of their defiance, and does not refer to the carrying out of the hadd, by the context of His saying "after that," meaning after the three rulings have been established. The hadd has already passed. Moreover, it is known from the inductive study of the Shari'ah that legal hadd punishments are not dropped by the repentance of one who commits their cause. Abu Hanifa and a group said: the exception returns to the final sentence, in keeping with its principle regarding an exception that comes after conjoined sentences.

Tawba (repentance): giving up, regret, and the manifest resolve not to return to the like of that. Repentance was discussed in the context of women when His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 17] and the verses following. It is not a condition of repentance, according to the majority, and this is the view of Malik, that he retract his accusation, because he may be truthful but was unable to establish it with four witnesses of the known description. So his repentance is that he reforms, his condition improves, and he is careful in his affair. A group said: his repentance is not considered until he retracts his accusation. This is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and al-Sha'bi. 'Umar did not accept the testimony of Abu Bakrah because he refused to retract his accusation against al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah. Afterward he accepted the testimony of Shibl ibn Ma'bad and Nafi' ibn Kaladah, because they both retracted their accusations in that affair, and 'Umar had given all three of them the hadd of qadhf.

The meaning of (aslahu, "they reform") is that they did righteousness, meaning they became righteous. The object of the verb is omitted, indicated by the context, meaning: they reformed themselves by avoiding what they were forbidden. This was discussed previously in His saying ﴿They said, "We are only reformers"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11] and His saying ﴿except those who repent, reform and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a consequence of what the exception implies, in the sense: so accept their testimony and forgive them what has passed, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful; that is, indeed Allah commanded forgiveness for them because He is Forgiving and Merciful, as He said in the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿except those who repent, reform and make clear, so those I will accept repentance from, and I am the Accepting of Repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160].

What was expressed explicitly in the verse of al-Baqarah, whose counterpart is implied here, is because the situation there is one of elaboration, due to the great concern for their affair, as they returned to faith, reform, and making clear the guidance revealed to them after they had concealed it, as their predecessors had concealed it.

Page 161
The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the hadd of qadhf is a right of Allah, Exalted, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is a right of the one falsely accused. It follows from this disagreement that it is dropped by the pardon of the one accused.

This verse is the foundation for the hadd of slander (fira) and qadhf, which first appeared in accusing chaste women of fornication. Thus every accusation involving something that brings disgrace requires the hadd, by consensus based on analogy.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 24, verses 6–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves, then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah, that he is surely of the truthful.﴾ ﴿And the fifth: that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿And it averts the punishment from her that she testify four testimonies by Allah, that he is surely of the liars.﴾ ﴿And the fifth: that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he is of the truthful.﴾

This is a specification of the two generalities in His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], for among the chaste women are those who are wives of the ones who accuse them. So these, those who accuse their wives, are singled out from the ruling of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], etc., since husbands alone are excused for their undertaking to speak of adultery concerning their wives when they are unable to establish it with four witnesses.

The basis of their excuse in this is the natural disposition (sajiyyah) of jealousy (al-ghayrah) that is in people's souls over their wives, and the inability to bear seeing adultery with them. So He removed from them the legal penalty for slander (hadd al-qadhf) and prescribed for them mutual imprecation (al-mulaʿanah).

In this ruling there is an acceptance of the husband's word about his wife in general, when he is careful (mutathabbitan). Indeed, after the husband's oaths, the woman is required to repel that by her own oaths; otherwise his word is accepted against her together with his oaths, and it is then equivalent to the testimony of four, and it makes her punishment obligatory if she does not repel it with her oaths.

The reason for this is that in the souls of husbands there is a restraint (wazi') that holds them back from accusing their wives of immorality falsely, and it is the restraint of shame (al-taʿyir) from that, and the restraint of love in husbands, generally. For this reason Allah named the husband's claim against her by the name of testimony, with the evident exception in His saying: ﴿And they have no witnesses except themselves﴾. And in their souls there is such jealousy over them that silence about it cannot be tolerated; in the Jahiliyyah they used to kill over it, and the man was believed in what he claimed against his wife. Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said: "If I found a man with my wife, I would strike him with the sword, not turning the flat of it (ghayr musfih)." But jealousy may be excessive, and rivalry among men to be known for it may kindle it in souls; so Islam forbade that, since it is not the right of anyone to destroy a soul except the ruler (al-hakim). And it did not establish placing the lives of wives under the control of the differing dispositions of their husbands.

When the penalty for slander was established, the matter became difficult for husbands who come upon suspicion regarding their wives. The case of ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani with his wife Khawlah bint ʿAsim (and it is said: bint Qays) was revealed; both were from the paternal cousins of ʿAsim ibn ʿAdi from the Ansar. Malik narrated in the Muwatta' from Sahl ibn Sa'd that "ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani came to ʿAsim ibn ʿAdi al-Ansari and said to him: 'O ʿAsim, what do you think of a man who found another man with his wife; would he kill him, and would you kill him, or how should he act? Ask the Messenger of Allah about that for me, O ʿAsim.' So ʿAsim asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about that, and the Messenger of Allah disliked the questions and found fault with them, until what ʿAsim heard from the Messenger of Allah weighed heavily on him. When ʿAsim returned to his family, ʿUwaymir came to him and said: 'O ʿAsim, what did the Messenger of Allah say to you?' ʿAsim said to ʿUwaymir: 'You have not brought me any good; the Messenger of Allah disliked the question which I asked him about.' ʿUwaymir said: 'By Allah, I will not desist until I ask him about it.' So ʿUwaymir stood up until he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the midst of the people and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you think of a man who finds another man with his wife; would he kill him, and would you kill him, or how should he act?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Indeed it has been revealed concerning you and your companion; go and bring her.' Sahl said:
{page 163}
So they performed mutual imprecation while I was among the people at the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ presence," the hadith... So this verse became the beginning of the legislation of the ruling on husbands accusing their wives of adultery. The narrator of the story was confused by some narrators, who named him Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi. And it was added to the story: "That the Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'Evidence, or a penalty on your back.'" The correct view is that the occasion of revelation of the verse is the case of ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani, and this incident occurred in Sha'ban of the ninth year after the return from the expedition of Tabuk. The verification is that they are two stories that occurred at one time or close to it.

When the Prophet ﷺ heard the words of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah at the revelation of the earlier verse of slander, he said: "Do you marvel at Sa'd's jealousy? I am more jealous than him, and Allah is more jealous than me," meaning that it (jealousy) is not moderate in its effects, since he made among its effects that he kill whoever he finds with his wife, while Allah and His Messenger did not permit that; for Allah and His Messenger are more jealous than Sa'd. And they did not make it lawful for the husband who sees his wife committing adultery to kill the adulterer or the woman. For this reason ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani said: "If a man finds another man with his wife, would he kill him, and would you kill him, or how should he act?"

The complement of "witnesses" (shuhada') is elided because it is evident from the context, i.e., witnesses regarding what they claimed of what they accused their wives with.

His saying "except themselves" includes what testimony cannot apply to, such as accusing with denial of a pregnancy, for which the husband had earlier claimed istibra' (the verification of the womb's cleanliness).

It is known from the hadiths on the occasion of revelation, from the reason for specifying husbands with a special ruling in the law of slander, from the wording "accuse" (yarmun), and from the mention of witnesses, that mutual imprecation is a concession (rukhsah) which Allah granted to husbands in cases of necessity, so it is not extended beyond them. For this reason Malik, in the well-known view from him and his last of two opinions, and a group, said: a couple is not made to perform mutual imprecation except when the husband claims to have seen his wife committing adultery, or denies her pregnancy with a denial based on the occurrence of the pregnancy after the certainty of the cleanliness of his wife's womb and his not having intercourse with her. If it is not like that,
{page 164}
and he accuses her of adultery, i.e., merely by hearing, or by seeing a man in the house in a situation other than adultery, or by saying to her "O adulteress" or the like of what functions as insult and abuse, then mutual imprecation is not prescribed. The husband is punished in these cases with the penalty for slander, because it is a false accusation without evidence, and there is no excuse that requires specifying it; for the excuse is the inability to bear seeing one's wife committing adultery, and the inability to bear seeing a pregnancy that is certainly not from him. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and the majority said: if he says to her "O adulteress," mutual imprecation becomes obligatory, going by their view that mutual imprecation between spouses applies to mere slander as well, holding to the unrestricted wording "accuse" (yarmun). Their analogy is weakened by the clear difference, for the jurist, between claiming adultery against a woman and insulting with words that involve attribution of adultery.

The Qur'an's naming of the oaths of mutual imprecation as "testimony" indicates that they serve to repel a claim, and the condition for legal consequences to follow from a claim is that it be established. So Malik's view is weightier than the view of the majority, for it is more penetrating to the legal reality (al-haqiqah al-shar'iyyah).

His saying: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies, by Allah﴾ etc. Since it was impossible for husbands to dispense with testimony in such a situation, and He excused them in making such a claim, and He did not leave the matter neglected, nor did He leave women as a morsel in the mouths of those who want to defame them out of discord, excessive anger or foolishness, He imposed on husbands a testimony that is not difficult for them if they are truthful in what they claim; so He made it obligatory for them to swear by Allah four times, so that oaths stand in place of the four witnesses required for adultery in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not bring four witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 4] etc.

The oath was named testimony because it is a substitute for it; this is a metaphor by the relation of conceptual substitution (ʿalaqat al-hulul al-iʿtibari), and because the form of testimony is frequently used for swearing; here it was made a substitute for testimony, so it is as though the claimant brought forth from himself four witnesses by those four oaths.

The meaning of the oaths being a substitute for testimony is that they stand in its place for the excuse we mentioned just above; so they do not take all the rulings of testimony. And it should not be imagined that the oaths of mutual imprecation are accepted only from a just person (ʿadl); so if he were a transgressor (fasiq), he would not perform mutual imprecation and would not be punished with the penalty of slander; rather every
{page 165}
person whose oath is valid, his mutual imprecation is valid. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah stipulated freedom, and his proof for that is linking mutual imprecation to testimony, since Allah named it testimony.

For the sake of preserving this substitution, the Imams of the four schools required that the oaths of mutual imprecation be in the formula "I bear witness by Allah" (ashhadu billah). As for what follows the formula "I bear witness", it is like an oath according to the claim he swears to, in words that admit no ambiguity.

His saying: (﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies﴾) was read by the majority with the accusative on "four" (arbaʿa), as a cognate accusative (maf'ul mutlaq) of "testimony" (shahadah), so "the testimony of one of them" is with an elided predicate, indicated by the conditional sense in the relative clause and the attachment of the fa' to its predicate; the estimate is: "so the testimony of one of them is binding upon him." It is permissible that the predicate be His saying: ﴿that he is surely of the truthful﴾, by way of quoting the wording, like the saying of them: "Hijjira Abi Bakr: there is no god but Allah." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read "four" with the nominative, as the predicate of the subject, and the clause ﴿that he is surely of the truthful﴾ to its end is a substitute (badal) for "the testimony of one of them." There is no disagreement among the readers on the accusative of the second "four testimonies."

In His saying: ﴿that he is surely of the truthful﴾ there is a quotation of the wording of the oath, with the pronoun kept in the third-person context, i.e., he says: "Indeed I am of the truthful regarding what I claimed against her."

As for His saying: (wal-khamisah), i.e., "the fifth testimony," i.e., the one completing the number five with the four preceding it. The number noun was made feminine because it is an attribute of an elided noun indicated by His saying: (fa-shahadatu ahadihim). The estimate: "and the fifth testimony." There is no counterpart to it in the number of witnesses to adultery. So perhaps the wisdom in adding this oath to the four oaths standing in place of the four witnesses is that it reinforces the four oaths by recalling what follows from his oaths, if they were a false oath (ghamus), of being deprived of Allah's mercy, exalted is He. This is the reason it differs in its form from the forms of the four preceding testimonies. In this there is an indication that the four are those made as substitutes for the witnesses, and that this fifth is a conclusion (tadhyil) to the testimony and an intensification (taghlize) of it.

The majority read ("and the fifth: that the wrath of Allah be upon her") with the nominative, as in His saying: ("and the fifth: that the curse of Allah be upon him"), and it is a coordination of sentences (ʿatf al-jumal). Hafs on the authority of
{page 166}
ʿAsim read it with the accusative, coordinated upon the second "four testimonies," and it is a coordination of single words (ʿatf al-mufradat).

The majority read ("that the curse of Allah be upon him") and ("that the wrath of Allah be upon her") with the nun of "anna" doubled, with the verbal noun in it ("that the wrath of Allah"), and the divine name in the genitive by the annexation of "wrath" to it. On this reading it is necessary to estimate the preposition bi- entering upon "anna" in both places, attached to "the fifth," since it is an attribute of a qualified noun whose estimate is "and the fifth testimony," so that the opening of the hamzah of "anna" in both is correct. The meaning: that the man or the woman testifies that "the curse of Allah" or "the wrath of Allah," i.e., by what corresponds to this sentence.

Nafi' read with the lightening of the nun of "an" in both places, and ("ghadiba Allahu") with the form of the past tense verb, and the divine name after "ghadiba" in the nominative. His reading was interpreted by taking "an" as a lightened form of the heavy one, with its operation cancelled, and its noun being a suppressed pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), elided, meaning: to magnify the matter of the fifth testimony. It was rejected by what has been established: that the predicate of the lightened "an" may not be free of one of four things: "qad," a negative particle, a particle of futurity (tanfis), or "law." What appears to me is that "an" in Nafi's reading should be taken as explanatory (tafsiriyyah), since the fifth is an oath, so it contains the sense of saying without its letters, and the explanatory form suits it.

Ya'qub recited (anna la'nata Allahi) with the (anna) lightened, the (la'natu) in the nominative, and the name of God in the genitive, like the recitation of Nafi'. He alone recited (anna ghadabu Allahi 'alayha) with the (anna) lightened, the (ghadaba) with a fatha on the dad and the ba' in the nominative, as a verbal noun (masdar), and the name of God in the genitive by annexation.

In all the recitations, the two spouses do not mention the word (anna) in the fifth oath of imprecation, for it is not found in the description of the oaths of imprecation in the books of jurisprudence or the books of Sunnah.

The wording of the fifth oath is like the wording of the four oaths. He specified for him in the supplication the particular curse, because if he is lying, he has slandered his wife and exposed her to the people's cursing and the rejection of spouses, so it was fitting that his recompense be the curse.

Al-la'nah and al-la'n: removal with contempt. It has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Hijr: 35] in Surat al-Hijr.

Know that if the husband names a specific man as having committed adultery with his wife, he becomes a slanderer of that man in addition to his slander of the woman. And if he performs imprecation and completes it, the hadd punishment for slander falls from him with respect to the woman, which is clear. What remains to be considered is his slander of that man whom he attributed adultery to. The jurists differ regarding the falling of the hadd punishment for slander with respect to the man. Al-Shafi'i said: it falls from him, the hadd punishment for slander with respect to the man, because God Most High mentioned only one hadd, and because it is not established in the Sunnah that the Messenger of God ﷺ enforced the hadd for slander (qadhf) against 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani or against Hilal ibn Umayya after the imprecation. Malik and Abu Hanifa said: the imprecation removes the hadd of the one performing imprecation for slandering his wife, but it does not remove the hadd of slander for a man he named. Their proof is that God legislated the hadd for slander.

Since these oaths entail the truthfulness of the husband's claim against the wife, it follows that the wife is regarded as an adulteress, or that her pregnancy is not from him, and so it is from fornication. Because she is under his marriage, this requires that the hadd for fornication be enforced upon her. Thus the Shari'ah does not neglect the woman's right, nor does it hold her bound by oaths whose swearer may be lying in them, since he is accused of lying to clear himself. Therefore it granted the wife the right to counter her husband's oaths, just as it granted the one testified against the right to challenge the testimony by impeachment or counter-evidence. God Most High said: ﴿And it averts from her the punishment that she testify four testimonies by God﴾, the verse. Since the wife's oaths serve to repel the husband's oaths, and the husband's oaths substitute for testimony and are called testimony, it is fitting that the wife's oaths for repelling them be called testimony too, and because they are like counter-testimony. And since they stand in the place of counter-testimony, all the wife's oaths are aimed at nullifying his claim, not at establishing her innocence or truthfulness.

Al-dar' (al-dar'): repelling with force, and it is used here metaphorically for nullification. It has been discussed at His words: ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22] in Surat al-Ra'd.

The definite article in (al-'adhab) is clearly for a previously mentioned referent, since the punishment was mentioned in His words: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. From the verse it is taken that if the woman does not swear the oaths of imprecation, the hadd is enforced upon her. This is what the reports of the hadith of imprecation in the Sunnah attest. Abu Hanifa said: if the woman refuses the oaths of imprecation, she is not subjected to the hadd, because in his view the hadd is only established by the testimony of witnesses or by confession. So, in his view, she is returned to the ruling of imprisonment, which is abrogated according to us, and in his view it was abrogated only in some cases and remained in others.

The wording of the wife's oaths is the same as the wording of the husband's oaths, exactly alike. And for her in the fifth oath is specified the supplication for the anger of God upon her if her husband is truthful, because she angered her husband by her action, so it was fitting that her recompense be the anger of her Lord upon her, just as she angered her mate.

Many branches arise from the rulings of imprecation, some of which some exegetes touch upon, and they are the subject matter of the books of furu' (positive law).

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 24, verses 6–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves, then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah, that he is surely of the truthful.﴾ ﴿And the fifth: that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿And it averts the punishment from her that she testify four testimonies by Allah, that he is surely of the liars.﴾ ﴿And the fifth: that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he is of the truthful.﴾

This is a specification of the two generalities in His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], for among the chaste women are those who are wives of the ones who accuse them. So these, those who accuse their wives, are singled out from the ruling of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], etc., since husbands alone are excused for their undertaking to speak of adultery concerning their wives when they are unable to establish it with four witnesses.

The basis of their excuse in this is the natural disposition (sajiyyah) of jealousy (al-ghayrah) that is in people's souls over their wives, and the inability to bear seeing adultery with them. So He removed from them the legal penalty for slander (hadd al-qadhf) and prescribed for them mutual imprecation (al-mulaʿanah).

In this ruling there is an acceptance of the husband's word about his wife in general, when he is careful (mutathabbitan). Indeed, after the husband's oaths, the woman is required to repel that by her own oaths; otherwise his word is accepted against her together with his oaths, and it is then equivalent to the testimony of four, and it makes her punishment obligatory if she does not repel it with her oaths.

The reason for this is that in the souls of husbands there is a restraint (wazi') that holds them back from accusing their wives of immorality falsely, and it is the restraint of shame (al-taʿyir) from that, and the restraint of love in husbands, generally. For this reason Allah named the husband's claim against her by the name of testimony, with the evident exception in His saying: ﴿And they have no witnesses except themselves﴾. And in their souls there is such jealousy over them that silence about it cannot be tolerated; in the Jahiliyyah they used to kill over it, and the man was believed in what he claimed against his wife. {page 163}
So they performed mutual imprecation while I was among the people at the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ presence," the hadith... When the Prophet ﷺ heard the words of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah at the revelation of the earlier verse of slander, he said: "Do you marvel at Sa'd's jealousy? I am more jealous than him, and Allah is more jealous than me," meaning that it (jealousy) is not moderate in its effects, since he made among its effects that he kill whoever he finds with his wife, while Allah and His Messenger did not permit that; for Allah and His Messenger are more jealous than Sa'd. And they did not make it lawful for the husband who sees his wife committing adultery to kill the adulterer or the woman. For this reason ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani said: "If a man finds another man with his wife, would he kill him, and would you kill him, or how should he act?"

and he accuses her of adultery, i.e., merely by hearing, or by seeing a man in the house in a situation other than adultery, or by saying to her "O adulteress" or the like of what functions as insult and abuse, then mutual imprecation is not prescribed.
