When the Prophet ﷺ heard the words of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah at the revelation of the earlier verse of slander, he said: "Do you marvel at Sa'd's jealousy? I am more jealous than him, and Allah is more jealous than me," meaning that it (jealousy) is not moderate in its effects, since he made among its effects that he kill whoever he finds with his wife, while Allah and His Messenger did not permit that; for Allah and His Messenger are more jealous than Sa'd. And they did not make it lawful for the husband who sees his wife committing adultery to kill the adulterer or the woman. For this reason ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani said: "If a man finds another man with his wife, would he kill him, and would you kill him, or how should he act?"

The complement of "witnesses" (shuhada') is elided because it is evident from the context, i.e., witnesses regarding what they claimed of what they accused their wives with.

His saying "except themselves" includes what testimony cannot apply to, such as accusing with denial of a pregnancy, for which the husband had earlier claimed istibra' (the verification of the womb's cleanliness).

It is known from the hadiths on the occasion of revelation, from the reason for specifying husbands with a special ruling in the law of slander, from the wording "accuse" (yarmun), and from the mention of witnesses, that mutual imprecation is a concession (rukhsah) which Allah granted to husbands in cases of necessity, so it is not extended beyond them. For this reason Malik, in the well-known view from him and his last of two opinions, and a group, said: a couple is not made to perform mutual imprecation except when the husband claims to have seen his wife committing adultery, or denies her pregnancy with a denial based on the occurrence of the pregnancy after the certainty of the cleanliness of his wife's womb and his not having intercourse with her. If it is not like that,
{page 164}
and he accuses her of adultery, i.e., merely by hearing, or by seeing a man in the house in a situation other than adultery, or by saying to her "O adulteress" or the like of what functions as insult and abuse, then mutual imprecation is not prescribed. The husband is punished in these cases with the penalty for slander, because it is a false accusation without evidence, and there is no excuse that requires specifying it; for the excuse is the inability to bear seeing one's wife committing adultery, and the inability to bear seeing a pregnancy that is certainly not from him. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and the majority said: if he says to her "O adulteress," mutual imprecation becomes obligatory, going by their view that mutual imprecation between spouses applies to mere slander as well, holding to the unrestricted wording "accuse" (yarmun). Their analogy is weakened by the clear difference, for the jurist, between claiming adultery against a woman and insulting with words that involve attribution of adultery.

The Qur'an's naming of the oaths of mutual imprecation as "testimony" indicates that they serve to repel a claim, and the condition for legal consequences to follow from a claim is that it be established. So Malik's view is weightier than the view of the majority, for it is more penetrating to the legal reality (al-haqiqah al-shar'iyyah).

His saying: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies, by Allah﴾ etc. Since it was impossible for husbands to dispense with testimony in such a situation, and He excused them in making such a claim, and He did not leave the matter neglected, nor did He leave women as a morsel in the mouths of those who want to defame them out of discord, excessive anger or foolishness, He imposed on husbands a testimony that is not difficult for them if they are truthful in what they claim; so He made it obligatory for them to swear by Allah four times, so that oaths stand in place of the four witnesses required for adultery in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not bring four witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 4] etc.

The oath was named testimony because it is a substitute for it; this is a metaphor by the relation of conceptual substitution (ʿalaqat al-hulul al-iʿtibari), and because the form of testimony is frequently used for swearing; here it was made a substitute for testimony, so it is as though the claimant brought forth from himself four witnesses by those four oaths.

The meaning of the oaths being a substitute for testimony is that they stand in its place for the excuse we mentioned just above; so they do not take all the rulings of testimony. And it should not be imagined that the oaths of mutual imprecation are accepted only from a just person (ʿadl); so if he were a transgressor (fasiq), he would not perform mutual imprecation and would not be punished with the penalty of slander; rather every
{page 165}
person whose oath is valid, his mutual imprecation is valid. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah stipulated freedom, and his proof for that is linking mutual imprecation to testimony, since Allah named it testimony.

For the sake of preserving this substitution, the Imams of the four schools required that the oaths of mutual imprecation be in the formula "I bear witness by Allah" (ashhadu billah). As for what follows the formula "I bear witness", it is like an oath according to the claim he swears to, in words that admit no ambiguity.

His saying: (﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies﴾) was read by the majority with the accusative on "four" (arbaʿa), as a cognate accusative (maf'ul mutlaq) of "testimony" (shahadah), so "the testimony of one of them" is with an elided predicate, indicated by the conditional sense in the relative clause and the attachment of the fa' to its predicate; the estimate is: "so the testimony of one of them is binding upon him." It is permissible that the predicate be His saying: ﴿that he is surely of the truthful﴾, by way of quoting the wording, like the saying of them: "Hijjira Abi Bakr: there is no god but Allah." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read "four" with the nominative, as the predicate of the subject, and the clause ﴿that he is surely of the truthful﴾ to its end is a substitute (badal) for "the testimony of one of them." There is no disagreement among the readers on the accusative of the second "four testimonies."

In His saying: ﴿that he is surely of the truthful﴾ there is a quotation of the wording of the oath, with the pronoun kept in the third-person context, i.e., he says: "Indeed I am of the truthful regarding what I claimed against her."

As for His saying: (wal-khamisah), i.e., "the fifth testimony," i.e., the one completing the number five with the four preceding it. The number noun was made feminine because it is an attribute of an elided noun indicated by His saying: (fa-shahadatu ahadihim). The estimate: "and the fifth testimony." There is no counterpart to it in the number of witnesses to adultery. So perhaps the wisdom in adding this oath to the four oaths standing in place of the four witnesses is that it reinforces the four oaths by recalling what follows from his oaths, if they were a false oath (ghamus), of being deprived of Allah's mercy, exalted is He. This is the reason it differs in its form from the forms of the four preceding testimonies. In this there is an indication that the four are those made as substitutes for the witnesses, and that this fifth is a conclusion (tadhyil) to the testimony and an intensification (taghlize) of it.

The majority read ("and the fifth: that the wrath of Allah be upon her") with the nominative, as in His saying: ("and the fifth: that the curse of Allah be upon him"), and it is a coordination of sentences (ʿatf al-jumal). Hafs on the authority of
{page 166}
ʿAsim read it with the accusative, coordinated upon the second "four testimonies," and it is a coordination of single words (ʿatf al-mufradat).

The majority read ("that the curse of Allah be upon him") and ("that the wrath of Allah be upon her") with the nun of "anna" doubled, with the verbal noun in it ("that the wrath of Allah"), and the divine name in the genitive by the annexation of "wrath" to it. On this reading it is necessary to estimate the preposition bi- entering upon "anna" in both places, attached to "the fifth," since it is an attribute of a qualified noun whose estimate is "and the fifth testimony," so that the opening of the hamzah of "anna" in both is correct. The meaning: that the man or the woman testifies that "the curse of Allah" or "the wrath of Allah," i.e., by what corresponds to this sentence.

Nafi' read with the lightening of the nun of "an" in both places, and ("ghadiba Allahu") with the form of the past tense verb, and the divine name after "ghadiba" in the nominative. His reading was interpreted by taking "an" as a lightened form of the heavy one, with its operation cancelled, and its noun being a suppressed pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), elided, meaning: to magnify the matter of the fifth testimony. It was rejected by what has been established: that the predicate of the lightened "an" may not be free of one of four things: "qad," a negative particle, a particle of futurity (tanfis), or "law." What appears to me is that "an" in Nafi's reading should be taken as explanatory (tafsiriyyah), since the fifth is an oath, so it contains the sense of saying without its letters, and the explanatory form suits it.

Ya'qub recited (anna la'nata Allahi) with the (anna) lightened, the (la'natu) in the nominative, and the name of God in the genitive, like the recitation of Nafi'. He alone recited (anna ghadabu Allahi 'alayha) with the (anna) lightened, the (ghadaba) with a fatha on the dad and the ba' in the nominative, as a verbal noun (masdar), and the name of God in the genitive by annexation.

In all the recitations, the two spouses do not mention the word (anna) in the fifth oath of imprecation, for it is not found in the description of the oaths of imprecation in the books of jurisprudence or the books of Sunnah.

The wording of the fifth oath is like the wording of the four oaths. He specified for him in the supplication the particular curse, because if he is lying, he has slandered his wife and exposed her to the people's cursing and the rejection of spouses, so it was fitting that his recompense be the curse.

Al-la'nah and al-la'n: removal with contempt. It has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Hijr: 35] in Surat al-Hijr.

Know that if the husband names a specific man as having committed adultery with his wife, he becomes a slanderer of that man in addition to his slander of the woman. And if he performs imprecation and completes it, the hadd punishment for slander falls from him with respect to the woman, which is clear. What remains to be considered is his slander of that man whom he attributed adultery to. The jurists differ regarding the falling of the hadd punishment for slander with respect to the man. Al-Shafi'i said: it falls from him, the hadd punishment for slander with respect to the man, because God Most High mentioned only one hadd, and because it is not established in the Sunnah that the Messenger of God ﷺ enforced the hadd for slander (qadhf) against 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani or against Hilal ibn Umayya after the imprecation. Malik and Abu Hanifa said: the imprecation removes the hadd of the one performing imprecation for slandering his wife, but it does not remove the hadd of slander for a man he named. Their proof is that God legislated the hadd for slander.

Since these oaths entail the truthfulness of the husband's claim against the wife, it follows that the wife is regarded as an adulteress, or that her pregnancy is not from him, and so it is from fornication. Because she is under his marriage, this requires that the hadd for fornication be enforced upon her. Thus the Shari'ah does not neglect the woman's right, nor does it hold her bound by oaths whose swearer may be lying in them, since he is accused of lying to clear himself. Therefore it granted the wife the right to counter her husband's oaths, just as it granted the one testified against the right to challenge the testimony by impeachment or counter-evidence. God Most High said: ﴿And it averts from her the punishment that she testify four testimonies by God﴾, the verse. Since the wife's oaths serve to repel the husband's oaths, and the husband's oaths substitute for testimony and are called testimony, it is fitting that the wife's oaths for repelling them be called testimony too, and because they are like counter-testimony. And since they stand in the place of counter-testimony, all the wife's oaths are aimed at nullifying his claim, not at establishing her innocence or truthfulness.

Al-dar' (al-dar'): repelling with force, and it is used here metaphorically for nullification. It has been discussed at His words: ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22] in Surat al-Ra'd.

The definite article in (al-'adhab) is clearly for a previously mentioned referent, since the punishment was mentioned in His words: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. From the verse it is taken that if the woman does not swear the oaths of imprecation, the hadd is enforced upon her. This is what the reports of the hadith of imprecation in the Sunnah attest. Abu Hanifa said: if the woman refuses the oaths of imprecation, she is not subjected to the hadd, because in his view the hadd is only established by the testimony of witnesses or by confession. So, in his view, she is returned to the ruling of imprisonment, which is abrogated according to us, and in his view it was abrogated only in some cases and remained in others.

The wording of the wife's oaths is the same as the wording of the husband's oaths, exactly alike. And for her in the fifth oath is specified the supplication for the anger of God upon her if her husband is truthful, because she angered her husband by her action, so it was fitting that her recompense be the anger of her Lord upon her, just as she angered her mate.

Many branches arise from the rulings of imprecation, some of which some exegetes touch upon, and they are the subject matter of the books of furu' (positive law).

**Tadhyil** (a concluding phrase that summarizes and closes a passage) for the great rulings mentioned earlier, which contain Allah's favor and mercy, and which indicate that He is Accepting of repentance from His servants who repent. It also points to the perfection of His wisdom, since He placed severity where it belongs and leniency where it belongs, and restrained some people from others. When those rulings fell under the general heading of these attributes, mentioning the attributes became a concluding phrase.

The answer to **(la-wla)** ("had it not been for") is omitted, to magnify its content. The omission makes its import grand, and this magnification indicates the greatness of the conditional clause's content, which was the cause of that clause's non-occurrence. The implied meaning is: Had it not been for Allah's favor upon you, He would have repelled from you the harm some of you inflict on others through the deterrents He prescribed, and you would have attacked one another. And had it not been for Allah's mercy toward you, He would have granted you a relaxation from the deterrents He legislated in cases of necessity and excuse, and no one would have been able to remain silent about what he sees of the causes of jealousy (*ghayra*). Then, if he disclosed that, he would be punished, and if he avenged himself, he would destroy some people, or he would remain silent about what should not be overlooked by someone of his standing. Had it not been that Allah is Accepting of repentance and Wise, He would not have restored the one who repents and set right what he had forfeited of uprightness (*'adala*) and the acceptability of testimony.

Mentioning the attribute "the Wise" here alongside "Accepting of repentance" indicates that there is wisdom in this repentance, namely the reform of people.

The answer to **(la-wla)** has been omitted for magnification and exaltation, and omitting it is a method used by the people of eloquence (*ahl al-balagha*). It has recurred in this surah, and it is similar to the omission of the answer to **(law)**. The omission of the answer to **(law)** was previously mentioned at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if only those who did wrong could see when they see the punishment﴾ [al-Baqara: 165] in Surat al-Baqara. As for the answer to **(la-wla)**, I do not now recall a witness for its omission. Some of the scholars (*a'imma*) have said that **(la-wla)** is composed of **(law)** and **(la)**.

[Page 170]

It is a new (resumptive) statement (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a sentence that begins a fresh topic). These ten verses, up to His words ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Nur: 21], were revealed at a time far removed from the time of the verses at the beginning of this surah, as you will come to know.

Al-ifk is a noun denoting a lie that admits no doubt; it is a slander that takes people by surprise. It is derived from *al-afk* (with an open *hamzah*), which means turning a thing upside down. From this comes the name of the people of Sodom, 'Amurah, Adamah and Sabuyim, the towns of the people of Lot, called the *Mu'tafikah* (the overturned), because their towns were overturned: God made the upper part of them their lower part and sank them into the earth. Thus, reporting a thing contrary to its actual state is a turning of it away from its reality, and so it is called *ifk*. This was discussed earlier, at His words ﴿Then it swallows what they fabricate﴾ [al-A'raf: 117] in Surat al-A'raf.

The phrase *jā'ū bi-l-ifk* (they brought the slander) means: they intended and were preoccupied with it. Its origin is that the one who brings a strange report is said to have "come with such-and-such news." Strange reports are usually carried by those who arrive from journeys or who have been away from the tribe. God said: ﴿If a deviator comes to you with news﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6]. He likened the report to the arrival of a traveller or newcomer, by way of metaphor (*makniyya*, the implied comparison), and made "coming" a supporting element (*tarshih*, a metaphor-sustaining term), and it was connected with the particle of accompaniment *bi-* in order to complete the sustaining element.

Al-ifk is a story invented by the hypocrites, which circulated among the hypocrites and some naive Muslims, either merely out of following rumour or to stir up strife among the Muslims. The substance of this report is: when the Prophet ﷺ returned from the expedition against the Banu al-Mustaliq of Khuza'ah, which is also called the expedition of al-Muraysi', and only one stage remained between him and Madinah, he gave the order to depart at the end of the night. When 'A'ishah learned of this, she left her howdah and moved away from the army to attend to her needs, as is the custom of women before the departure. When she had finished, she came back to her camel-litter and missed a necklace of Zafar onyx that had been on her chest. She went back along her path looking for it, and her searching held her back, and it was night. When she found it, she returned to where her litter had been placed, but she found neither the army nor her litter. That was because the men charged with the departure had gone to the howdah, lifted it and carried it off, thinking that 'A'ishah was in it; she was light and slight of flesh. They lifted the howdah and set off. When she found no one, she lay down in her place, hoping that they would miss her and return to her, and she fell asleep. Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal (with a kasra on the *ta'*) al-Sulami (with a damma on the *sin* and a fatha on the *lam*, attributed to the Banu Sulaym, and he was settled in Madinah among the migrants of the Arabs) had been assigned by the Prophet ﷺ to guard the rear of the army. When he learned that the army had moved away, and he was secure from any treachery of the enemy, he mounted his mount to catch up with the army. When he reached the place where the army had been, he saw the figure of a person; it was 'A'ishah, and he had seen her before the veiling. He said *innā lillāh* (inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un), and 'A'ishah awoke at the sound of his words of recitation. He dismounted from his she-camel, brought it close to her and made it kneel. 'A'ishah mounted it, and he began to lead it until he caught up with the army at the height of midday. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites in the army, said: "By God, she has not escaped from him, nor has he escaped from her." This statement spread to Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthathah (with a kasra on the *mim* of Mistah, a fatha on its *ta'*, and a damma on the *hamzah* of Uthathah), and Hamnah bint Jahsh, the sister of Zaynab, the Mother of the Believers. Jealousy for her sister, a co-wife of 'A'ishah, moved her, and a group of hypocrites, the companions of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, aided them in their talk.

Thus, al-ifk becomes a proper name by dominance for what is fabricated in this story.

Al-'usbah means a group of ten to forty; this is what the majority of lexicographers say. It is also said that *al-'usbah* is a group from three to ten, which is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is said that in the codex of Hafsah the reading was (*'usbah arba'ah minkum*, a group of four among you). It is a collective noun with no singular of its own from its form, and it is also said *'iṣābah*. This was discussed at the beginning of Surat Yusuf.

*'Usbah* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *jā'ū* (they came).

The clause ﴿Do not think it an evil for you﴾ is the predicate of *inna*. The meaning is: do not think their slander an evil for you. Because the object pronoun in *taḥsabūhu* refers back to *al-ifk*, and *al-ifk* is connected to the verb *jā'ū*, the pronoun has the force of a definite noun with the definite article of previous mention (*lām al-'ahd*). The sense is: do not consider the aforementioned slander an evil for you. It is also permissible for the predicate of *inna* to be His words ﴿for every person among them is what he has earned of sin﴾, and the clause ﴿do not think it﴾ would then be a parenthetical insertion.

It is also permissible to make *'usbah* the predicate of *inna*, and the statement would then be used to express wonder at their deed, given that they are a group of the people who are most reprehensible, as Tarafah said:

*The wronging of close kin is more painful to a man than the strike of a keen-edged Indian sword.*

Mentioning *'usbah* is a belittling of them and of their statement, meaning that their talk is not heeded against the whole community's commendation of those whom they accused of slander. Describing the group as ﴿from among you﴾ indicates that they are Muslims, and in this there is an implied reproach that they have deviated from the morals of Islam by setting themselves against the harm done to the Muslims.

His words ﴿Do not think it an evil for you; rather, it is good for you﴾ are meant to remove what had arisen in the souls of the believers of grief at the audacity of a group in this calumny contained in the story. Thus the pronoun in *taḥsabūhu* refers to *al-ifk*.

The evil that was thought of is that it caused, among some, the sin of lying and false accusation, while the believers wished that their community be free of defects, for they are the people of the virtuous city. When disorder arose among them, they thought it an evil that had befallen them.

The meaning of denying that this is an evil for them is that it harms them by more than that passing grief, and it is less than an evil, because it leads to the repentance of the believers among them, so that its sin is confined to the hypocrites, who are another group whose misguidance does not harm the Muslims.

Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi said: The reality of good is that its benefit exceeds its harm, and the reality of evil is that its harm exceeds its benefit. Good with no evil in it is Paradise, and evil with no good in it is Hell. Thus God alerted 'A'ishah and those like her among those who were struck by grief from this report, that no evil had befallen them from it, but rather it was good, according to the way God set good and evil in this world, by the comparison between harm and benefit, the preponderance of benefit on the side of good, and the preponderance of harm on the side of evil. End quote. The mention of good was discussed at His words ﴿Wherever he directs himself, he brings no good﴾ [al-Nahl: 76] in Surat al-Nahl.

After removing the thought that this might be an evil for the believers, He established that it is good for them. He used the transition *bal* (rather) to nullify their thinking it an evil and to affirm that it is good for them, because in it are many benefits: through it the sincere believers are distinguished from the hypocrites; legal rulings are enacted through it that deter the people of wickedness from their wickedness; the innocence of their virtuous people becomes evident through it; the hypocrites become more enraged and become despised and blamed; and they do not rejoice in their supposition the grief of the Muslims. For when they fabricated this report, they wanted nothing but to harm the Muslims. Through it come miracles, by the revelation of these verses that inform of the unseen. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: ... and religious benefits and moral lessons that are not hidden from the one who reflects on them. End quote.

He chose not to conjoin *khayran* (good) to *sharran* (evil) with the particle *bal*, saying *bal khayran lakum* (rather, good for you), in preference for the nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity.

Al-ithm means sin. It was discussed at His words ﴿Say: in both there is great sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] in Surat al-Baqarah and at His words ﴿Abandon the outward and inward of sin﴾ [al-An'am: 120] in Surat al-An'am.

*Tawalli al-amr* means to directly undertake its work and to be preoccupied with it.

*Al-kibr* is with a kasra on the *kaf* in the reading of the majority, and a damma on the *kaf* is also permissible. Ya'qub alone recited it so, and its meaning is the greatest part of a thing and its bulk. The two are dialectal variants according to the majority of the lexicographers' imams. Ibn Jinni and al-Zajjaj said: the kasra form means sin, and the damma form means the greater part of a thing. ﴿And the one who undertook its greater part﴾ is 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, who was a hypocrite and was not among the Muslims.

The pronoun in *minhum* refers back to ﴿those who brought the slander﴾. It is also said that the one who undertook its greater part was Hassan ibn Thabit, because of what occurred in Sahih al-Bukhari: From Masruq, who said: Hassan entered upon 'A'ishah and recited in her presence some verses, among them:

*Chaste and steadfast, she is not accused of doubt, and she wakes up hungry from the flesh of the heedless.*

'A'ishah said to him: "But you are not like that." Masruq said: I said: "Do you permit such a man to enter upon you when God has revealed ﴿and the one who undertook its greater part among them, for him is a great punishment﴾?" She said: "What punishment is greater than blindness?"

The threat that for him there is a great punishment indicates that he is 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. It contains information that he will die in disbelief and will be punished with the great punishment in the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the lowest level of the Fire. As for the rest of the group, they bear sin in proportion to their wrongdoing. It also contains a hint that God will turn to them in forgiveness if they repent, as is the custom in this religion.

[Page 174]

﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of one another, and say, "This is an obvious lie"?﴾ This is a resumed statement (isti'naf) rebuking the faction of the slander (ʿusbat al-ifk) among the believers and reproaching them, after it has been called a lie (ifk).

Here (لولا) (lawla) is a particle meaning (هلا) (halla, "why not"), used for rebuke, as is its usual function when a past-tense verb follows it. Here that verb is (﴿ظن المؤمنون﴾) ("the believers thought"). As for (إذ سمعتموه) (idh samiʿtumūhu, "when you heard it"), it is an adverbial phrase governed by the verb of thinking (ẓann), and it has been placed before it. The object of the rebuke is the clause ﴿ظن المؤمنون والمؤمنات بأنفسهم خيرا﴾ ("the believing men and believing women did not think well of themselves"). The hearing is attributed to all the addressees, but the rebuke is specifically directed at those who heard the report and did not deny it.

The speech is couched in vagueness in the rebuke, by using the plural form, although the intended number is less than a plural. Two men did not think well, and so the verse refers to them with (المؤمنين) (al-muʾminīn, the believing men), and one woman, and so it refers to her with (المؤمنات) (al-muʾminat, the believing women), in the manner of His saying: ﴿Those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173].

His saying (بأنفسهم خيرا) (bi-anfusihim khayran, "well of themselves") occurs in contrast to (﴿ظن المؤمنون والمؤمنات﴾), so it implies distribution (tawzīʿ), meaning that each one of them should think well of the others among those who cast the slander, since a person does not think well of himself in this sense.

This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not defame one another [lit. "yourselves"]﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], meaning that some of you defame others, and like His saying: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another [lit. "yourselves"]﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

It is reported that when Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu) heard the report of the slander, he said to his wife: "Do you not see what is being said?" She said to him: "If you were in place of Safwan, would you think evil of the sanctity of the Messenger of Allah?" He said: "No." She said: "And if I were in place of ʿAʾisha, I would not have betrayed the Messenger of Allah. ʿAʾisha is better than me, and Safwan is better than you." He said: "Yes."

The placement of the adverbial phrase (إذ سمعتموه) (idh samiʿtumūhu) before its governing verb, which is (قلتم) (qultum, "you said"), is for the sake of emphasis on the meaning of that phrase, as an alert that it was their duty for the thought of good to occur to their hearts immediately upon hearing the good report, and that they should disassociate themselves from engaging in it at the moment of hearing it.

The turn away from the pronoun of address in attributing the verb of thinking to the believers is an iltifat (shift of pronoun, a rhetorical turn). The apparent expectation would be to say: "You thought well of yourselves," but He turned from address for the sake of emphasis on the rebuke, since iltifat is a kind of emphasis on the report. It is also to state explicitly the word (الإيمان) (al-iman, belief), indicating that sharing in belief requires that no believer should give credence against his brother or sister in religion, nor any believing woman against her brother or sister in religion, to the words of a critic or a slanderer. It also contains an alert that when a believer hears an accusation against a believer, his duty is to base the matter on a presumption of innocence (ẓann) and not on doubt, and then to examine the circumstantial evidence and the suitability of the situation. If something bad is attributed to someone known for goodness, he should think that this is a lie and a calumny until the proof becomes clear. It also contains an allusion (taʿrīḍ) that the presumption of evil which occurred is one of the traits of hypocrisy (nifaq), which seeped into some believers through delusion (ghurur) and lack of insight, and that this is sufficient to disgrace them.

This is a rebuke for their failure to exercise judgment in rejecting a statement whose very nature cries out its falsehood, and for their silence about it and their failure to denounce it.

The conjunction of (﴿وقالوا هذا إفك مبين﴾) ("and said, 'This is an obvious lie'") is a legislation (tashrīʿ) for the obligation to hasten to denounce what a Muslim hears of slander against a Muslim by speech, just as he denounces it in his heart, and likewise changing the wrong (taghyīr al-munkar) with the heart and the tongue.

The (ب) (bāʾ) in (بأنفسهم) (bi-anfusihim) is for transitivity of the verb of thinking to the second object, because here it is transitive to only one object, since it carries the meaning of accusation (ittihām).

Al-Mubin (المبين) means one who has reached the utmost in clarity (bayān), that is, in obviousness, as if, due to the strength of its clarity, it has come to make others clear.

Second resumptive statement, rebuking the band who brought the slander and censuring them. This "lawla" is like the earlier "lawla," meaning "why did they not" (halla).

﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses to it? Since they did not bring the witnesses, it is they who are the liars in the sight of Allah.﴾

The meaning: whoever reports a matter he did not witness must base his report on the testimony of an eyewitness, and the witnesses who report must be numerous enough that their report produces certainty of the truth of such a report. Those who brought the slander fabricated it out of their evil suspicions; they did not base it on witnessing what they reported, nor on the testimony of anyone who witnessed it from those whose testimony is accepted. Therefore their report was a lie (ifk). This rests on the ruling established earlier at the beginning of the surah, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses—lash them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. You know that the beginning of Surat al-Nur was revealed at the end of the second year or the beginning of the third year (AH), before the martyrdom of Marthad ibn Abi Marthad.

The restrictive form in His saying, ﴿it is they who are the liars﴾, is for emphasis, as if their lying, owing to its intensity and monstrousness, means that others are not counted as liars in comparison; it is as if the very quiddity of those described as liars is confined to them.

The demonstrative noun ("they") serves to further distinguish them by this attribute, so that people may beware of their like.

The qualification "in the sight of Allah" serves to further confirm their lying; that is, it is a lie in the knowledge of Allah, for the knowledge of Allah is never other than in accordance with reality itself. The intended meaning is not what many exegetes have stated, that the meaning of "in the sight of Allah" is "in His law" (shar'ihi), because that would make it a qualifier for restriction, so that the meaning would become: "they are the liars in the application of the rulings of the Sharia." This contradicts the purpose of the discourse and does not fit with what accompanies it of emphasis on describing them as liars. Moreover, that this is the law of Allah is already known from His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses—lash them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4], through to His saying: ﴿it is they who are the liars in the sight of Allah.﴾ Thus the question of acting on the apparent in applying the legal rulings is a separate matter, not derived from this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 14:

﴿And were it not for Allah's favor upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, you would have been touched, for what you plunged into, by a tremendous punishment.﴾

(Law la) here is a particle of prohibition of something due to the existence of something else (imtina' li-wujud). The favor (fadl) in this world is clearly the lifting of the punishment of the prescribed penalty (hadd) from them through the pardon of 'A'isha and Safwan concerning them, and in the Hereafter it is the lifting of punishment from them through repentance. The address is to the believers, not to the head of the hypocrites. This verse supports what most scholars hold: that the Prophet ﷺ did not impose the hadd for slander (hadd al-qadhf) on any of the group (al-'usbah) who spoke about the slander (al-ifk). This is the most correct of the reports, either because of the pardon of 'A'isha and Safwan, or because their speech about the slander was whispered and secretive; they did not speak openly about it, but they spread it among their circles and gatherings. This is what the hadith of 'A'isha about the slander in the Sahih of al-Bukhari indicates, and how she heard the news from Umm Mistah, and her saying: "Has this been spoken of and reached the Prophet ﷺ and my parents?"

It is said that the hadd was imposed on Hassan, Mistah and Hamnah. This was stated by Ibn Ishaq and a group of scholars. As for 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, a group said that he was not given the hadd for slander, in order to win over his heart to faith. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Ubayy was flogged with the hadd for slander as well.

The "plunging" (al-ifadah) in speech is a metaphor taken from pouring water into a vessel, meaning abundance of it within it. So the meaning is: you spoke a great deal about it and discussed it among yourselves.

**[p. 178]**

*Idh* (when) is an adverbial clause dependent on *afaḍtum* (you plunged into it). Its purpose, together with the clause it is attached to, is to call to mind the scene of their talk about the slander (al-ifk) and to make it appear more abhorrent.

The original form of *talaqqawnahu* was *tatalaqqawnahu* with two tā's, one of which was elided. The basic meaning of *talaqqī* is to make oneself ready to meet another. It was mentioned in His words, *"Then Adam received words from his Lord"* (2:37), meaning that he learned them and was taught them. Then *talaqqī* is used for taking a thing with the hand from another's hand, as al-Shammākh said:

*"When a banner is raised for glory, ʿArāba receives it with the right hand."*

In the hadith: "Whoever gives a charity from lawful earnings, and God accepts only what is good, the Merciful receives it with His right hand..." (the hadith continues). This is by likening the readiness to take the gift to the readiness to meet another. This is the usage in His words, *"when you received it with your tongues."* So in His words, *"with your tongues,"* there is an allegorical likening of the report to a person, and of the one who relates the report to one who prepares and readies himself to meet it. This is a metaphor in implicit form (*istiʿāra makniyya*). The tongues are made the instrument of receiving, in an imaginative mode (*takhyīliyya*), by likening the tongues in relating the report to hands in taking hold of a thing. The tongues are made the instrument of receiving even though receiving reports is done by the ears, because this receiving has as its purpose the telling of the report. So the tongues are put in place of the ears, as a figurative usage through the relation of "what something becomes" (*ʿalāqat al-ayūla*). In this there is also an oblique rebuke of their eagerness to receive this report: when they receive it, they rush to report it without deliberation or patience. This is also an oblique rebuke with reproach.

As for His words, *"and you say with your mouths,"* the reason for mentioning "with your mouths" even though speech cannot occur without mouths is that it is intended as a preface to His words, *"what you have no knowledge of."* That is: it is speech that does not agree with knowledge, but is merely from bare imagination, because the proofs of knowledge stand against the meaning of this speech. Thus the utterance becomes merely words that run over the mouths.

In this there is a point of moral etiquette: a person should not say with his tongue except what he knows and has verified. Otherwise he is one of two kinds: a man of weak judgment who says a thing before the matter has become clear to him, and so is likely to say a falsehood, and people will consider him a liar. In the hadith: "It is enough of a lie for a man that he relates everything he hears." Or he is a dissembler and hypocrite who says what he believes to be otherwise. God said: *"And among people is one whose speech in the life of this world pleases you, and he calls God to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of adversaries"* (2:204), and He said: *"Greatly hateful in the sight of God is that you say what you do not do"* (61:3).

This applies to reports. The same holds for promises: one should not promise except what he knows he is able to fulfil. In the hadith: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays."

He added to their reproach with His words, *"and you consider it a small matter, while it is grave in the sight of God,"* that is: you consider the report of the slander a trivial matter. They regarded it as trivial because they treated backbiting and defaming people lightly, carrying over what they had been accustomed to in the time of ignorance (*al-jāhiliyya*), when they had no religious restraint to hold them back. Therefore they were wary of people, and did not attack them with hand or abuse out of fear of them; but when they were alone, they felt safe from that. This is the reason for their considering the talk of the slander a light matter. Islam came to remove the vices of the *jāhiliyya* and to complete the noble characteristics of morality.

*Al-hayyin* (the light/easy) is derived from *al-hawān* (humiliation, lowliness). The lowliness of a thing is the absence of regarding it with respect and attention to its importance. One says, "such-and-such is *hāna ʿalā* so-and-so," meaning he did not consider it an important matter. The meaning is: a light thing. They considered it light even though the *ḥadd* (the prescribed punishment) was established before the revelation of this verse, according to the apparent order of the verses in His words, *"And those who accuse chaste women and do not bring four witnesses, lash them"* (24:4). This is because it is possible that no case of slander occurred between the revelation of that verse and the revelation of this one; or the case of Uwaymir al-ʿAjlānī occurred and the people of the slander did not know of it; or they considered it light because they were heedless of the ruling on the *ḥadd* that had been mentioned earlier, since their acquaintance with it was recent. In this there is a lesson in the etiquette of the Sacred Law: respect for the legal rules must be the same in absence and presence, in private and in public.

The meaning of *"in the sight of God"* is in the knowledge of God, from what He has legislated for you of rulings, as was mentioned just before in His words, *"Those are, in the sight of God, the liars"* (24:13).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 16:

﴿Had it not been that, when you heard it, you said, "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander."﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Had it not been that, when you heard it, the believing men and believing women thought well of their own kind﴾ [al-Nur: 12], and so on. The phrase (lawlā) together with its condition and its response was repeated to add emphasis to the sentence. For this reason, the (qultum) in this sentence was not conjoined to the (qultum) in the sentence before it, so that it would be clear that these are conjoined sentences.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase (idh samiʿtumūhu), before its governing verb (qultum mā yakūnu lanā), is like the fronting of its counterpart in His words ﴿Had it not been that, when you heard it, the believing men thought well...﴾ [al-Nur: 12], and its purpose is to emphasize the meaning of the adverbial phrase.

صفحة ١٨٠

The pronoun in (samiʿtumūhu) refers to the slander (al-ifk), like the similar pronouns in the preceding verses.

The demonstrative (hādhā) refers to the slander together with the fabrication it contains, which is spoken of by the hypocrites and the weak-minded. Thus the demonstrative points to what is present in every gathering where the slander was heard.

The meaning of ﴿qultum mā yakūnu lanā﴾ is that they should say to those who reported this lying news to them, i.e., "You said to them, rebuking and admonishing them."

The pronoun in (lanā) is intended to refer to both the speakers and the addressees. As for the addressees, it is because they spoke of it when they related the news of the slander to them; the meaning is: "It is not for you to speak of this." As for the speakers, it is that they should be cleared of having such lies pass over their tongues.

He said ﴿mā yakūnu lanā an natakallama bihādhā﴾ rather than saying "It is not permissible for us to speak of this" (laysa lanā an natakallama bihādhā), to draw attention to the fact that speaking about this, and the very existence of engaging in it, is truly to be negated. For your saying "mā yakūnu lī an afʿala" is stronger in negating the act from you than your saying "laysa lī an afʿala." An example of this is His words, quoting Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116].

This is directed as a rebuke for their passing on the false report, and the usual course would have been for the speaker to say within himself, "It is not for us to speak of this," and to say it to the one sitting with him and hearing it from him. This is an addition to the rebuke for remaining silent about it, in His words ﴿and they said, "This is a manifest lie."﴾ [al-Nur: 12].

(Subhanaka) is an expressive (inshaʾ) sentence placed parenthetically between the clause ﴿mā yakūnu lanā an natakallama bihādhā﴾ and the clause ﴿hādhā buhtānun ʿaẓīm﴾. (Subhanaka) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that stands in place of its verb, i.e., "We glorify, a glorifying of You." Its annexation to the second-person pronoun is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object, and here it is used metaphorically to express amazement, as was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1] and His words ﴿Glory be to God, and I am not of the polytheists﴾ [Yusuf: 108] in Surah Yusuf. It is best that it here serves to declare the speaker's innocence of something, by representing the state of his own self as that of one who calls God to witness to what he says. He therefore begins by addressing God with glorification, then says ﴿this is a tremendous slander﴾, disavowing what follows from it. This is an exaggeration in denying the matter and in expressing wonder at its occurrence.

Directing the address to God in His words (subhanaka) indicates that God is angry with those who engage in this. Therefore, they must turn to God in repentance for it if they have engaged in it, and must guard against participating in it if they have not engaged in it.

The clause ﴿hādhā buhtānun ʿaẓīm﴾ is an explanation (taʿlīl) of the clause ﴿mā yakūnu lanā an natakallama bihādhā﴾, so it falls within the rebuke of those to whom it was said.

Describing the slander as (ʿaẓīm, tremendous) means that it is great in its occurrence, i.e., it reaches the full reality of slander to a powerful degree.

It was tremendous because it contains many abominations: the lie itself; the lie's injury to the soundness of honor; its causing great enmity between the fabricators and those slandered, who are among the best of people, and who are connected to the worst of people in terms of wives, fathers and kin; and, greater than all that, its audacity against the station of the Prophet ﷺ and the station of the Mother of the Believers, may God be pleased with her.

Al-buhtān is a verbal noun like al-kufrān and al-ghufrān. Al-buhtān is a false report that stupefies the hearer, because there is no doubt in it. It has already been discussed at His words ﴿and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nisa: 156] in Surah al-Nisa.

[Page 182]

After Allah, exalted is He, had explained the consequences that befell those who spread the slander of the false report (ifk) and those who accepted it, which included many reproaches and threats, the exposure of those who circulated it, and a disappointment brought upon them that was the opposite of what they intended, and the benefit that accrued to the believers from this, He stated at the outset that it is not to be counted as evil for them but is in fact good for them. He also stated that those who brought the report had gained nothing from it but sin, and that no harm reached the Muslims from it. He censured the believers for their negligence and heedlessness regarding the bad intention of those who fabricated it, and for how they had failed to think well of those about whom they knew nothing but good, so they did not refute the report. He also stated that by this they had ventured into what would cause punishment to befall them in this world and in the Hereafter, and how they had regarded it as a trivial matter when it is great in the sight of Allah. Had they reflected, they would have known its greatness in the sight of Allah, and their silence about changing this (state of affairs)... He followed all of this with a warning to the believers against returning to the like of it: rashness in receiving reports, and rushing after every messenger without verification, and without consideration of the consequences of their undertakings.

Al-wa'z (admonition): speech by which one seeks to make the one addressed avoid an ugly matter. It was discussed at the end of Surat al-Nahl.

The verb (ya'izukum) does not take a second object directly. Therefore the verbal noun derived from (an ta'udu) cannot be an object of the verb (ya'izukum) except by assuming an omitted element, or by construing the verb of admonition with the meaning of another transitive verb, or by assuming an omitted preposition. So you may construe the verb (ya'izukum) with the meaning of warning. The sense would then be: "He warns you against returning to the like of it." Or it may be assumed: "Allah admonishes you concerning returning to the like of it." Or a negative particle may be assumed, meaning: "that you should not return to the like of it." The omission of the negative particle is common when the context indicates it. Under all these interpretations, the sentence contains concision (ijaz).

Al-abad (ever): the entire future time. Generally it occurs as an adverb of time with a negation.

His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾ is an incitement and a spurring on of them, which stirs their eagerness not to return to the like of it, because they are keen to affirm their faith. The conditional in such a case is not intended as a restriction, for the meaning is not: "If you are not believers, then return to the like of it." Rather, since the possibility of the implied converse of the condition is avoided, the mention of the condition serves as an incitement to compliance. Thus, if anyone speaks of the slander after this verse, believing it to have occurred, [Page 183] the implication of the condition is that he would be a disbeliever. Malik said this as well. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Hisham ibn 'Ammar said: "I heard Malik say: Whoever reviles Abu Bakr and 'Umar is to be disciplined, and whoever reviles 'A'isha is to be put to death, because Allah says: ﴿Allah admonishes you that you should never return to the like of it, if you are believers﴾. So whoever reviles 'A'isha has contradicted the Qur'an, and whoever contradicts the Qur'an is put to death." End of quotation. By "contradiction" he means denying what the Qur'an has stated explicitly, while holding that the reference of "returning to the like of it" is the affair of the slander, because Allah cleared her with texts that admit of no interpretation, and it is widely transmitted that these verses were revealed concerning 'A'isha. Ibn al-'Arabi reported from the Shafi'is that this is not disbelief. As for reviling her for any other reason, it is equivalent to reviling the other Companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿And Allah makes the verses clear to you﴾: that is, He makes them clearly indicative of the intended meaning for you. The verses (al-ayat) are the verses of the Qur'an revealed concerning the punishment for slander (qadhf) and the admonition of those who are heedless of the forbidden matters.

The reminder with the two attributes, knowledge and wisdom, is evident in its relevance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾

Page 184

When Allah warned the believers against returning to the like of what they engaged in of slander at all times in the future, He followed their warning with a threat concerning what might arise from them in the future: a threat concerning the love of the spread of indecency among the believers. The sentence is therefore a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) encompasses everyone who has the attribute stated in the relative clause, so it includes believers, hypocrites and polytheists. Thus it is a warning to the believers and an informing about the hypocrites and polytheists.

He made the threat concerning the love of the spread of indecency among the believers an alert that the love of that is deserving of punishment, because the love of that indicates an evil intention toward the believers. It is the nature of such an inclination that its bearer does not remain long before there issues from him what he loves, or before he is pleased by its issuing from someone else. So the love here is a metonymy (kinayah) for readiness to bring into being what one loves to occur. The present tense verb form is used to indicate continuity. The essence of a metonymy is that it combines the explicit meaning with its implication. Hence it is inevitable that from that love there arises the punishment of this world, which is the prescribed penalty for slander (hadd al-qadhf), and the punishment of the Hereafter, which is more evident, because it is what evil intentions deserve. That love is something other than resolving upon an evil deed or inner whispering of the soul, because those two are passing thoughts from which their bearer can refrain. As for sustained love, it is a desire for the attainment of the beloved. This is analogous to the metonymy in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the poor﴾ [al-Haqqah: 34], a metonymy for the non-occurrence of feeding the poor. So the threat here is upon loving that such things occur in the future, as is required by His saying "that indecency should spread," because "an" (أن) makes the present tense verb specific to the future. As for past love, Allah has pardoned it by His saying: ﴿Had it not been for Allah's favour upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, a great punishment would have touched you for what you plunged into﴾ [al-Nur: 14].

The meaning of "that indecency should spread" (أن تشيع الفاحشة) is that its report should spread, because spreading (al-shuyu') is an attribute of reports and accounts, like diffusion (al-fushuww), and it means: the publicising of talk about it. Thus it is necessary to posit an elided noun, i.e., "that the report of it should spread," since indecency is an act that has reached a great degree of atrocity.

The use of the term "indecency" (al-fahishah) for fornication and the like is widespread, and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And those of your women who commit indecency﴾ [al-Nisa': 15] in Surat al-Nisa'. And the term indecency in the sense of a reprehensible matter was mentioned earlier in His saying:

Page 185

﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say: "We found our fathers doing it"﴾ [al-A'raf: 28] in Surat al-A'raf. And al-fahsha' was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Among the etiquette of this verse is that it is the duty of the believer not to love for his believing brothers except what he loves for himself. Just as he does not love that a report of evil about himself should spread, likewise he must not love the spreading of evil about his believing brothers. The spread of reports of indecency among the believers, whether true or false, entails a moral corruption, for among the things that restrain people from corruptions is their awe of committing them and their aversion to the evil reputation of such acts; this turns their thoughts away from recalling them, let alone undertaking them, until they are gradually forgotten and their images fade from the souls. But when news of some indecency spreads among the community, the thoughts recall it, and the impact of its report on the ears lessens, so that complacency about its occurrence creeps into souls, and the lightness of its impact on the ears follows; then wicked souls soon proceed to commit it. In proportion to the frequency of its occurrence and the frequency of talk about it, it becomes commonplace. In addition, the spreading of indecency entails harm and injury to people, of varying degree according to the variation of reports in truth and falsehood.

For this reason, this noble etiquette is indicated by His saying: ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾, meaning: He knows what corruptions lie in that, so He admonishes you that you may avoid them, while you do not know, and so you suppose that talking about it entails no harm. This is like His saying: ﴿and you consider it trivial, while with Allah it is grave﴾ [al-Nur: 15].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 20:

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you, and His mercy, and that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful.﴾

This is the third time he repeats ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾. In the first and third occurrences he omits the answer of (lawla) (the conditional "were it not for"), so that the mind may go every possible way in estimating it according to the context.

Page 186
331 He mentioned in the first occurrence the description of Allah as Oft-Returning (tawwab), Wise (hakim), owing to the preceding context; and he mentions here that He is Most Kind (ra'uf), Most Merciful (rahim). This is because the admonition contained in the concluding phrase (tadhyil) is a rescue of the community from a great turmoil in its morals and manners and from the severing of the bonds of its unity; He saved them from that out of kindness (ra'fah) and mercy (rahmah) toward its individuals and its collective, and to preserve its ties.

He mentions the attribute of kindness (ra'fah) and mercy (rahmah) here because it was preceded by His rescuing them from the evil of the love that the sins of indecency should spread among those who believed, a love that was harbored in the hearts of the hypocrites. Saving the believers from adopting it was kindness toward them from punishment and mercy toward them with the reward of return (to Him).

This verse is the end of the ten verses that were revealed about the People of the Slander concerning 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. They were revealed successively to the Prophet ﷺ, and he recited them upon their revelation while he was in his house.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 21:

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan. And whoever follows the steps of Satan - indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing. And if not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would have been pure, ever. But Allah purifies whom He wills. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

This verse was revealed after the ten preceding verses, so the sentence is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i). Its placement right after the ten verses concerning the slander (al-ifk) indicates that everything those verses contained of prohibited acts, evil suspicions, and love for the spread of indecency all comes from the whisperings of Satan. Thus the state of one who performs these acts, being afflicted by Satan's whispering, is likened to Satan walking, and the one who acts on his command follows the steps of that Satan. So in His saying: ﴿Do not follow the steps of Satan, and whoever follows the steps of Satan﴾ there is a metaphor (tamthil) based on likening a perceptible state to an imagined state, since the listeners do not know steps for Satan, so that they would be forbidden to follow them.

In it there is also a likening of Satan's whispering in the souls of those who brought the slander to walking. The word (khutuwat) is the plural of (khutwah), with a dammah on the kha'. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir, read it with a sukun on the ta' as it is in the singular, so it is a sound plural (jam' salamah). The others read it with a dammah on the ta', because moving the sakin 'ayn or the 'ayn that follows a noun's fa' which carries a dammah or kasrah is common and permitted.

Al-khutwah, with a dammah on the kha', is the name for the movement of a walker lifting one of his feet, which was behind the other, and placing it ahead of it. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 208] in Surat al-Baqarah.

(Man) is conditional (shart), and therefore the verb (yattabi') is in the jussive mood by the consensus of the readers.

The clause ﴿indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing﴾ is the response of the condition, and the link is the omitted object of (ya'muru) intended for generality, for its generality includes the doer of the conditional verb, and by this the connection between the conditional clause and the response clause is achieved. The two pronouns in (fa-innahu ya'muru) refer to Satan. The meaning: whoever follows the steps of Satan commits immorality and wrongdoing, because Satan enjoins immorality and wrongdoing; that is, enjoins their commission. So whoever follows the steps of Satan falls into immorality and wrongdoing, because he is one of the instances of the generality.

Al-fahsha' (immorality) is every deed or statement that is ugly. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-munkar (wrongdoing) is what the Sharia denounces and what people of sound nature (ahl al-khabar) deny. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104] in Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying: ﴿And if not for the favor of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Nur: 20] to the end of the verse means: if not for His favor, by guiding you to good, and His mercy, by forgiveness upon repentance, no one among people would have been pure, because the temptation of Satan is great, and people hardly escape it without the guidance of the religion. Allah the Exalted said, relating the words of Satan: ﴿He said, "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them"﴾ [Sad: 82].

(Zaka) with a lightened kaf is the well-known reading among the recitations. In the Mushaf, (zaka) is written with an alif in the form of a ya'. Its proper form would have been written with a pure alif, since it is not imala and its root is not a ya', for its final radical is waw. The orthography of the Mushaf does not always follow analogy. Its reading with a lightened kaf is not considered a violation of the Mushaf's orthography, because the violation that weakens a reading is the violation that leads to a difference in the pronunciation of the letters of the word; as for something like this, it belongs to matters of performance (al-ada'), and transmission (al-riwayah) protects against error in it.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) between promise and threat; that is, He hears those who spread indecency, and knows what is in their souls of love for its spread; and He hears those who deny that, and knows what is in their souls of dislike for that; so He recompenses each for his deed.

The mention of the divine name (Allah) here is so that the concluding appendage stands independently by itself, because it is of the kind that functions as a proverb (yajri majra al-mathal).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 22:

﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear against giving to the near of kin, the needy, and those who emigrated in the way of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

It is coordinated with the sentence (﴿Do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-Nur: 21]) as the coordination of the particular over the general, for the sake of emphasis on it, because it may be hidden that it is among the footsteps of Satan. For among the guile of Satan is that he comes with whispering in the form of thoughts of goodness, when he knows that the one whispered to is among those who seek out righteousness and obedience, and that he is one for whom it is difficult to market his whispering when it is exposed.

And among the appendages of the story of the slander is that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) used to spend on Mistah ibn Uthathah al-Muttalibi, since he was the son of the maternal aunt of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and he was among the poor emigrants. When he learned of his involvement in the matter of the slander, he swore that he would not spend on him. When Mistah repented and Allah accepted his repentance, Abu Bakr still remained resentful toward Mistah in his heart,

page 189
so this verse was revealed. The intended meaning of "those of virtue" initially is Abu Bakr, and the intended meaning of "the near of kin" initially is Mistah ibn Uthathah, and the verse encompasses others besides them from among those who took part in the matter of the slander and others who are covered by the general wording of it, for Mistah had a family who received Abu Bakr's maintenance. Ibn 'Abbas said: The community of believers cut off their benefits from everyone who spoke in the slander, and they said: "By Allah, we will not connect with anyone who spoke concerning 'A'isha's affair," so the verse was revealed concerning all of them.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the verse up to his words ﴿Do you not love that Allah should forgive you﴾, Abu Bakr said: "Yes, I love that Allah should forgive me," and he returned to Mistah and his household what he used to spend on them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu Bakr expiated for his oath. He narrated it from 'A'isha.

The majority read (﴿wa la ya'tali﴾). The ita' (ايتلاء, to swear) is an iftu'al form from al-alliyyah, which is the oath, and the most common usage of al-alliyyah is in an oath of abstention; it is said: "ala" and "a'tala." It has been mentioned previously at His words, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226] in Surat al-Baqarah. Abu Ja'far read (﴿wa la yata'all﴾) from ta'alla, which is a taf'il form from al-alliyyah.

Al-fadl (virtue): its origin is excess, so it is the opposite of deficiency, and its use has become common for excess in goodness and religious perfection, and this is the intended meaning here. It is also applied to an excess of wealth beyond the need of its owner, but this is not intended here, because the coordination of (﴿wa al-si'ah﴾, and the wealth) with it makes that unlikely. The one meant by "those of virtue" initially is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Al-si'ah: wealth. The attributes in His words: ﴿the near of kin, the needy, and those who emigrated in the way of Allah﴾ each require support on their own, so swearing to withhold support from any one of them is a blocking of a great door of goodness, and how much more so for one who combined all these attributes, such as Mistah, concerning whom the verse was revealed.

The interrogation in His words (﴿Do you not love﴾) is reproachful, used in the sense of urging the striving toward that by which forgiveness comes, which is the pardoning and overlooking in His words: ﴿Let them pardon and overlook﴾. In it there is an indication that there was a conflict for Abu Bakr between the cause of goodness and the cause of piety in the oath, and that he was inclined to the side of piety in his oath, and left the side of what he would miss of the reward of spending, supporting kin, and maintaining family ties. It seems he gave precedence to the side of avoiding sin over the side of seeking reward, so Allah alerted him that he should take the side of preferring goodness, because for an oath there is an exit, which is expiation.

This indicates that the expiation of an oath was prescribed before this story, but they used to be reluctant to proceed to breaking an oath, as in the report of 'A'isha: that she would not speak to 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr when news reached her that he was restricting her because of her great spending of wealth. It is in Sahih al-Bukhari in the Book of Manners, chapter on Abandonment (al-hijran).

The coordination of ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ with the sentence ﴿Do you not love that Allah should forgive you﴾ is an addition of encouragement toward pardoning and overlooking, a reassurance to Abu Bakr's soul regarding his breaking of the oath, and an alert to the command to adopt the attributes of Allah, exalted is He.

[p. 191]

The clause ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*) following another resumptive sentence, the words ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [Q. 24:19]. Both are an elaboration of the admonition in the words ﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of this, if you are believers﴾ [Q. 24:17]. So the warning against returning to their love of that (indecency) comes first, and then the warning against returning to spreading the slander. The present tense in His words (*yarmūna*, "they accuse") refers to the future.

It was not joined by a conjunction to the clause that is related to it, because of the separation between them by the verses revealed in between, namely His words ﴿O you who believe, do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [Q. 24:21].

The relative pronoun clearly refers to a group, namely ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and those with him. The words *al-ghāfilāt* ("unwary") refer to those women who have no knowledge of what they were accused of. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for their not having committed what they were accused of, because one who commits an act is not unaware of it. The meaning is: indeed, those who accuse chaste women falsely of such things, so do not think that "unwary" means unaware of what people say about them. The attribute *al-muʾmināt* ("believing") is mentioned to make the accusation of those who falsely slander them more shameful, because the quality of faith restrains them from indecency.

His words *luʿinū* ("they have been cursed") are a report of God's curse upon them for the sin that was decreed for them and the punishment that was prescribed for them.

Cursing (*al-laʿn*) in this world means declaring them wicked (*tafsīq*), depriving them of the eligibility to give testimony, the believers' shunning of them, and the prescribed punishment for slander (*ḥadd al-qadhf*). Cursing in the Hereafter means being removed from God's mercy.

The great punishment is the punishment of Hell. There is no benefit in lengthening the discussion here with the question of whether it is permissible to curse a specific Muslim, nor in whether the intended ones are among the disbelievers.

The adverbial phrase in His words ﴿on the day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them﴾ is connected to what the adverbial phrase governs, which is the predicate of the subject in His words ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾. Mention of the testimony of their tongues, hands and feet is to terrify them, so that perhaps they will guard against that station and repent.

The testimony of the limbs against their owner is among the conditions of the reckoning of the disbelievers.

The singling out of these limbs for mention, although testimony comes from the whole body, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Q. 41:21], is because these limbs have a role in the accusation of chaste women. They speak the slander, point with their hands at the women being slandered, and walk with their feet to the gatherings of people to convey the slander.

[p. 192]

Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read *yashhadu ʿalayhim* ("it will testify against them") with the third person masculine prefix (*yāʾ*), which is a permissible reading for a verb whose subject is a broken plural pronoun.

His words ﴿On that day God will pay them their due recompense in truth﴾ form a clarifying resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf bayānī*), because mention of the testimony of the limbs raises the question of the consequences of that testimony. It is answered that its consequence is that God will repay them for what their limbs testified against them. Their due recompense (*dīnahum*) is their requital, as in His words "Master of the Day of Judgment" [Q. 1:4].

*Al-ḥaqq* ("in truth") is an attribute of *dīn* ("recompense"), meaning the just requital in which there is no injustice. It is described by a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) for emphasis.

His words ﴿and they will know that God is the Manifest Truth﴾ mean that it will become clear to people that God is the Truth. Describing God as "the Truth" is a description by a verbal noun, to convey the certainty of His being characterised by truth, like the words of al-Khansāʾ:

*She grazes as long as she grazes, until she remembers; then she is nothing but coming and going.*

The description of God as "the Truth" has two meanings:

The first is that it means the Established, the Necessary Reality. His existence is necessary, so His essence is a reality realised, which was never preceded by non-existence or negation, and so the possibility of non-existence is not accepted for Him. Al-Ghazālī, in his explanation of the Beautiful Names, restricted himself to this meaning of His name "the Truth."

The second is that it means He is possessor of truth, that is, justice. This is the meaning that suits the attribute coming after His words "their due recompense in truth." The author of *al-Kashshāf* explained it in this way, so it is possible that he intended to explain the meaning of "truth" here, that is, to describe God by a verbal noun, and his aim was not to explain the Name. This is what Ibn Barrajān al-Ishbīlī followed in his book *Sharḥ al-Asmāʾ al-Ḥusnā* ("Explanation of the Beautiful Names"), and al-Qurṭubī in his commentary.

[p. 193]

*Al-Ḥaqq* ("the Truth") is one of God's Beautiful Names. Since He was described by a verbal noun, the attribute *al-mubīn* ("the Manifest") is added to the description of the verbal noun. *Al-Mubīn* is an active participle of *abāna*, which is used transitively with the meaning "to make manifest", in keeping with the basic meaning of the *hamza* as making transitive, and it is also used with the meaning *bāna*, "to become manifest", on the basis that the *hamza* is extra. So you may take it as an attribute of *al-ḥaqq* in the sense of justice, as al-Kashshāf explicitly states, that is, the clear truth. Or you may take it as an attribute of God, exalted is He, in the sense that God is manifest and a guide. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Barrajān inclined to this view, for they both counted *al-Mubīn* among His Names.

If the description of God as "the Truth" is in the verbal-noun sense, then the restriction derived from the pronoun of separation (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*) is a claim-based restriction (*ḥaṣr iddiʿāʾī*), because the truth that comes from others among the judges is not reckoned as truth, since even if it hits the target, it is nonetheless subject to change, deficiency and error. It is as if it were not truth, or not manifest. If the report that God is "the Truth" is in the nominal sense, as a Name of God, then the restriction is real (*ḥaqīqī*), since no one is named by the Name "the Truth" other than the essence of God, exalted is He. So the meaning is: God is the possessor of this Name, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Do you know anyone who shares His name?﴾ [Q. 19:65]. On these two aspects, the discussion of His description as "the Manifest" proceeds in the same way.

The meaning of their knowing that God is the Manifest Truth is that they will verify it on that day with certain knowledge that admits neither concealment nor doubt, even though they knew it before. This is because the discourse is an admonition to believers. But their knowledge, which requires reflection and is liable to concealment and heedlessness, is treated as the equivalent of the absence of knowledge.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of ﴿those who accuse chaste, unwary women﴾ is specifically ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and those who associate with him among the hypocrites who conceal disbelief, let alone persisting in the sin of the slander. There is no repentance for them, for they continue in the slander among themselves, because it was made attractive to their own selves, so they did not seek to abandon it in their hearts, even though they knew it was a fabrication by them. But because of the corruption of their hidden intentions, they treat the doubt that entered their souls as if it were certainty. So they are cursed by God in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter. And they will know that God is the Manifest Truth regarding what He disproved them of in the story of the slander. They had previously been [p. 194] concealing associationism with God, making the truth belong to their idols. In that case the restriction is relative (*qaṣr idāfī*), meaning: they will know that God alone, and not their idols, is the Truth.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of ﴿those who accuse chaste, unwary women﴾ is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl alone, and that he is referred to in the plural to conceal his name, as an allusion to him, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿those to whom people said﴾ [Q. 3:173], and as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is wrong with people who stipulate conditions that are not in the Book of God?"

They had previously been [p. 194] concealing associationism with God, making the truth belong to their idols. In that case the restriction is relative (*qaṣr idāfī*), meaning: they will know that God alone, and not their idols, is the Truth.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of ﴿those who accuse chaste, unwary women﴾ is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl alone, and that he is referred to in the plural to conceal his name, as an allusion to him, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿those to whom people said﴾ [Q. 3:173], and as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is wrong with people who stipulate conditions that are not in the Book of God?"

[p. 191]

The clause ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*) following another resumptive sentence, the words ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [Q. 24:19].
