Both are an elaboration of the admonition in the words ﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of this, if you are believers﴾ [Q. 24:17]. So the warning against returning to their love of that (indecency) comes first, and then the warning against returning to spreading the slander. The present tense in His words (*yarmūna*, "they accuse") refers to the future.

It was not joined by a conjunction to the clause that is related to it, because of the separation between them by the verses revealed in between, namely His words ﴿O you who believe, do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [Q. 24:21].

The relative pronoun clearly refers to a group, namely ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and those with him. The words *al-ghāfilāt* ("unwary") refer to those women who have no knowledge of what they were accused of. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for their not having committed what they were accused of, because one who commits an act is not unaware of it. The meaning is: indeed, those who accuse chaste women falsely of such things, so do not think that "unwary" means unaware of what people say about them. The attribute *al-muʾmināt* ("believing") is mentioned to make the accusation of those who falsely slander them more shameful, because the quality of faith restrains them from indecency.

His words *luʿinū* ("they have been cursed") are a report of God's curse upon them for the sin that was decreed for them and the punishment that was prescribed for them.

Cursing (*al-laʿn*) in this world means declaring them wicked (*tafsīq*), depriving them of the eligibility to give testimony, the believers' shunning of them, and the prescribed punishment for slander (*ḥadd al-qadhf*). Cursing in the Hereafter means being removed from God's mercy.

The great punishment is the punishment of Hell. There is no benefit in lengthening the discussion here with the question of whether it is permissible to curse a specific Muslim, nor in whether the intended ones are among the disbelievers.

The adverbial phrase in His words ﴿on the day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them﴾ is connected to what the adverbial phrase governs, which is the predicate of the subject in His words ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾. Mention of the testimony of their tongues, hands and feet is to terrify them, so that perhaps they will guard against that station and repent.

The testimony of the limbs against their owner is among the conditions of the reckoning of the disbelievers.

The singling out of these limbs for mention, although testimony comes from the whole body, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Q. 41:21], is because these limbs have a role in the accusation of chaste women. They speak the slander, point with their hands at the women being slandered, and walk with their feet to the gatherings of people to convey the slander.

[p. 192]

Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read *yashhadu ʿalayhim* ("it will testify against them") with the third person masculine prefix (*yāʾ*), which is a permissible reading for a verb whose subject is a broken plural pronoun.

His words ﴿On that day God will pay them their due recompense in truth﴾ form a clarifying resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf bayānī*), because mention of the testimony of the limbs raises the question of the consequences of that testimony. It is answered that its consequence is that God will repay them for what their limbs testified against them. Their due recompense (*dīnahum*) is their requital, as in His words "Master of the Day of Judgment" [Q. 1:4].

*Al-ḥaqq* ("in truth") is an attribute of *dīn* ("recompense"), meaning the just requital in which there is no injustice. It is described by a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) for emphasis.

His words ﴿and they will know that God is the Manifest Truth﴾ mean that it will become clear to people that God is the Truth. Describing God as "the Truth" is a description by a verbal noun, to convey the certainty of His being characterised by truth, like the words of al-Khansāʾ:

*She grazes as long as she grazes, until she remembers; then she is nothing but coming and going.*

The description of God as "the Truth" has two meanings:

The first is that it means the Established, the Necessary Reality. His existence is necessary, so His essence is a reality realised, which was never preceded by non-existence or negation, and so the possibility of non-existence is not accepted for Him. Al-Ghazālī, in his explanation of the Beautiful Names, restricted himself to this meaning of His name "the Truth."

The second is that it means He is possessor of truth, that is, justice. This is the meaning that suits the attribute coming after His words "their due recompense in truth." The author of *al-Kashshāf* explained it in this way, so it is possible that he intended to explain the meaning of "truth" here, that is, to describe God by a verbal noun, and his aim was not to explain the Name. This is what Ibn Barrajān al-Ishbīlī followed in his book *Sharḥ al-Asmāʾ al-Ḥusnā* ("Explanation of the Beautiful Names"), and al-Qurṭubī in his commentary.

[p. 193]

*Al-Ḥaqq* ("the Truth") is one of God's Beautiful Names. Since He was described by a verbal noun, the attribute *al-mubīn* ("the Manifest") is added to the description of the verbal noun. *Al-Mubīn* is an active participle of *abāna*, which is used transitively with the meaning "to make manifest", in keeping with the basic meaning of the *hamza* as making transitive, and it is also used with the meaning *bāna*, "to become manifest", on the basis that the *hamza* is extra. So you may take it as an attribute of *al-ḥaqq* in the sense of justice, as al-Kashshāf explicitly states, that is, the clear truth. Or you may take it as an attribute of God, exalted is He, in the sense that God is manifest and a guide. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Barrajān inclined to this view, for they both counted *al-Mubīn* among His Names.

If the description of God as "the Truth" is in the verbal-noun sense, then the restriction derived from the pronoun of separation (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*) is a claim-based restriction (*ḥaṣr iddiʿāʾī*), because the truth that comes from others among the judges is not reckoned as truth, since even if it hits the target, it is nonetheless subject to change, deficiency and error. It is as if it were not truth, or not manifest. If the report that God is "the Truth" is in the nominal sense, as a Name of God, then the restriction is real (*ḥaqīqī*), since no one is named by the Name "the Truth" other than the essence of God, exalted is He. So the meaning is: God is the possessor of this Name, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Do you know anyone who shares His name?﴾ [Q. 19:65]. On these two aspects, the discussion of His description as "the Manifest" proceeds in the same way.

The meaning of their knowing that God is the Manifest Truth is that they will verify it on that day with certain knowledge that admits neither concealment nor doubt, even though they knew it before. This is because the discourse is an admonition to believers. But their knowledge, which requires reflection and is liable to concealment and heedlessness, is treated as the equivalent of the absence of knowledge.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of ﴿those who accuse chaste, unwary women﴾ is specifically ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and those who associate with him among the hypocrites who conceal disbelief, let alone persisting in the sin of the slander. There is no repentance for them, for they continue in the slander among themselves, because it was made attractive to their own selves, so they did not seek to abandon it in their hearts, even though they knew it was a fabrication by them. But because of the corruption of their hidden intentions, they treat the doubt that entered their souls as if it were certainty. So they are cursed by God in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter. And they will know that God is the Manifest Truth regarding what He disproved them of in the story of the slander. They had previously been [p. 194] concealing associationism with God, making the truth belong to their idols. In that case the restriction is relative (*qaṣr idāfī*), meaning: they will know that God alone, and not their idols, is the Truth.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of ﴿those who accuse chaste, unwary women﴾ is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl alone, and that he is referred to in the plural to conceal his name, as an allusion to him, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿those to whom people said﴾ [Q. 3:173], and as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is wrong with people who stipulate conditions that are not in the Book of God?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 26:

﴿The wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. Those are cleared of what they say; for them is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾

After God cleared 'Ā'isha (may God be pleased with her) of what the slanderers (ʿuṣbat al-ifk) had said, He exposed them, for they had come only with evil assumption and the fabrication of accusation, and He threatened and warned them. Then He forgave those among them who repented, and He once more praised the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for being cleared of having wicked wives, because his infallibility (ʿiṣma) and his honour before God require that God would not allow his wives to be other than good. Thus the high station of the Messenger (ﷺ) is sufficient as evidence of the innocence of his wife and the purity of all his wives. This is a form of inference about the state of a thing from the state of what is associated with it and similar to it. In this there is also an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to those who fabricated the slander: that what they invented is not befitting except for their own wives. So His saying ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men﴾ is an allusion to the hypocrites who fabricated the slander.

The beginning with the mention of "the wicked women" is because the purpose of the speech is to infer the innocence of ʿĀ'isha and the rest of the Mothers of the Believers. The lām in His saying "for wicked men" (li-l-khabīthīna) is the lām of entitlement (lām al-istiḥqāq). "The wicked women, the wicked men, the good women and the good men" are attributes applied to omitted nouns (mawṣūfāt maḥdhūfa) that the context indicates. The estimated noun in all of them is: "the wives" (al-azwāj).

The conjunction of "and wicked men are for wicked women" is an elaboration (iṭnāb) for the sake of further care in establishing this ruling, and so that the sentence stands like a proverb, independent in its indication of the ruling, and so that the inference about the state of the companion from the state of his associate is achieved from whichever side the listener begins.

The mention of "and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women" is likewise an elaboration, to indicate that association is also evidence of the state of the two partners in goodness.

The conjunction of "and good men are for good women" is like the conjunction of "and wicked men are for wicked women."

The discussion of the wicked and the good has already preceded at His saying: ﴿That God may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [al-Anfāl: 37] in Surat al-Anfāl; and His saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 38] in Surat Āl ʿImrān; and His saying: ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the wicked things﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 157] in Surat al-Aʿrāf.

The masculine pronoun prevailed in His saying "are cleared" (mubarra'ūn), and this is a universal rule; for this reason it was fit that it should take the course of a proverb, and it was placed at the end of the story as a concluding appendage (tadhyīl).

By "wickedness" is meant the wickedness of human qualities, such as indecencies. Likewise by "goodness" is meant the purity of human qualities from the virtues known among mankind. So disbelief is not part of wickedness but is among its completers. Likewise belief is among the completers of goodness. Therefore the disbelief of the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot did not contradict the generality of His saying: ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men﴾, for what is meant by His saying: ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 10] is that they betrayed their two husbands by concealing disbelief. This is supported by the contrast of their state with the state of the wife of Pharaoh: ﴿when she said: My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 11], up to His saying: ﴿and deliver me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 11].

The turning away from naming the slander by its name to "what they say" indicates that it is nothing more than a saying, i.e., that it does not correspond to reality, as in His saying: ﴿and We shall inherit from him what he says﴾ [Maryam: 80], because he will have no wealth or children in the Hereafter.

"Generous provision" is the delight of Paradise. It has already been stated that "generous" (karīm) means precious in its kind, at His saying: ﴿They have ranks with their Lord, and forgiveness and generous provision﴾ [al-Anfāl: 4] in Surat al-Anfāl.

With these verses the admonitions of the story of the slander come to an end.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verses 27–28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their occupants. That is better for you, that you may remember.﴾ ﴿But if you find no one in them, do not enter them until you are given permission. And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

We have mentioned that among the major aims of this surah is the legislation of the system of social dealings and family interaction among neighbours. These verses are a new subject, explaining the rules of visiting and teaching the etiquette of seeking permission (al-istidhan), and specifying what achieves its intended purpose, so that people do not differ about its manner according to the variation in their understanding of its aim and benefit.

Seeking permission was known in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) and at the beginning of Islam, and its form varied according to the condition of the person being visited, whether a king or a commoner, so it was not uniform. Some people neglect it or fall short in it, namely those concerned only with fulfilling their own purpose and hastening their own needs. It is not unlikely that their entering would embarrass the one visited or burden him. These verses came to specify its manner and to incorporate it into the etiquette of the religion, so that people do not neglect it, or part of it, due to their differing levels of modesty and self-respect, and their differing assumptions about whether there is any accountability for it or how severe that accountability is.

Seeking permission was prescribed for one who visits someone at his house, because people made houses as shelter from what harms the body, such as heat, cold, rain and dust, and from what harms honour and the self, such as the exposure of what the occupant does not wish people to see. So when a person is in his house and someone comes to him, he should not admit him until he has put his house in order and covered what must be covered. Then he gives him permission, or he goes out to him and speaks to him from outside the door.

The meaning of (tasta'nisu) is that you seek companionship with them, that is, you seek that the owner of the house be at ease with you, and his being at ease with you is by the absence of estrangement and aversion. This is a subtle metaphor (kinaya) for seeking permission: that the one entering should seek permission, that is, seek a permission which by its nature ensures that the owner of the house does not feel estranged by the one entering. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "Al-istina's (seeking companionship) — in our view, and Allah knows best — is al-istidhan (seeking permission)." He means that this is what is intended, either as a metaphor or as a synonym, and it derives from (uns) companionship. And what Malik said is the decisive statement. It is reported from Ibn al-Qasim in Jami' al-'Utbiyya that al-istina's is greeting (al-taslim). Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is far-fetched."

I say: Ibn al-Qasim meant the greeting made with the intention of seeking permission, so the conjunction of (wa tusallimu) is an explanatory conjunction. The intended meaning of al-istina's is not that it is derived from (anasa) in the sense of (knowing), because that is a different usage which does not fit here, and there is no benefit in mentioning it. That is according to the apparent meaning, for when the person is given permission, his permission indicates that he does not dislike the other's entering, and when he dislikes it he does not give permission. Allah is the One who knows what is in the heart, and therefore He expressed seeking permission by seeking companionship, along with the implicit indication of the reason for the legislation of seeking permission.

In this there is etiquette: a person should not be a burden on others, nor should he expose himself to aversion and being unwelcome. And the visitor and the one visited should be in harmony, at ease with each other, and this helps to strengthen Islamic brotherhood.

The command to greet is conjoined with seeking companionship, and both are made the goal of the prohibition against entering houses, to draw attention to the obligation of performing both, because the prohibition is lifted only when both are achieved. From Ibn Sirin: "A man sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'May I enter?' The Prophet (ﷺ) instructed a man near him, or a female servant named Rawda, saying: 'He does not know how to seek permission properly; let him say: As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?' The man heard it and said: 'As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?' He said: 'Enter.'" Mutarrif related from Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, that he sought permission from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and said: "Ala-j?" (may I enter?). Ibn 'Umar gave him permission, and when he entered Ibn 'Umar said to him: "What is the matter with you and the seeking of permission by the Arabs?" He meant the people of the Jahiliyyah. "When you seek permission, say: As-salamu 'alaykum. When the greeting is returned to you, say: May I enter? If you are given permission, then enter."

The apparent meaning of the verse is that seeking permission is obligatory, and that greeting is obligatory, except that the context of the verse is the legislation of seeking permission. As for greeting, its legislation was established earlier, at the beginning of Islam, and it was not specific to the situation of entering houses, so greeting is not particularly singled out here. It was mentioned together with seeking permission only to ensure its observance alongside seeking permission, lest seeking permission distract the one knocking so that he forgets the greeting, or thinks that seeking permission is sufficient in place of the greeting. Al-Mazari said in Kitab al-Mu'lim 'ala Sahih Muslim: "Seeking permission is prescribed (mashru')." Ibn al-'Arabi said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: "A group said: seeking permission is obligatory (fard) and greeting is recommended (mustahabb)." It is reported from 'Ata': "Seeking permission is obligatory upon every person who has reached puberty." Nothing has clarified the ruling on seeking permission except the jurists of the Malikis. Shaykh Abu Muhammad said in al-Risala: "Seeking permission is obligatory. Do not enter a house in which there is anyone until you have sought permission three times; if you are given permission, well and good, otherwise you return." Ibn Rushd said in al-Muqaddimat: "Seeking permission is obligatory." Abu al-Hasan al-Maliki, in his commentary on al-Risala, related the consensus (ijma') on the obligation of seeking permission. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "Seeking permission is prescribed," and this is the statement of al-Mazari in his commentary on Muslim.

I say: The juxtaposition of seeking permission with greeting in the verse does not necessarily require that they be equal in ruling, since there are other evidences distinguishing their rulings, and these evidences are from the Sunnah and from the meaning. The benefit of seeking permission is to avert what is disliked from the one visited, to cut off the causes of denial, insult, or harshness of speech, and to block the means of suspicion. All of these, or their combination, require that seeking permission be obligatory.

As for the benefit of greeting together with seeking permission, it is to strengthen the established familiarity, so it does not require more than the emphasis of recommendation. The Qur'an commanded the complete situation and left the details of its parts to the clarification of the Sunnah, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44].

The wisdom of seeking permission has been summarized in His saying: ﴿That is better for you, that you may remember.﴾ That is, that seeking permission is better for you, meaning there is good and benefit in it for you; if you reflect, you will know the good in it for you, as is hoped from you.

The verse has combined seeking permission and greeting with the conjunction (wa), which indicates only joint association. So it indicates that if seeking permission is placed before greeting, or greeting before seeking permission, the required aim has been achieved. Many hadiths report the command to put greeting before seeking permission, so that is better, and it does not contradict the verse.

There is no fixed formula for seeking permission. What has come in some reports is either understood as what was customary among them, or as a phrase more comprehensive than others in its meaning. The Sunnah has clarified that if the one seeking permission is not given permission to enter, he repeats it three times, and if he is still not given permission, he leaves.

Concerning this, there is the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in Sahih al-Bukhari, which is what was reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "I was in a gathering of the Ansar when Abu Musa al-Ash'ari came, as if frightened. He said: 'I sought permission from 'Umar three times, and he did not give me permission, so I went back.'" In another report they explained that 'Umar was occupied with some of his affairs, then he remembered and said: "Did I not hear the voice of 'Abdullah ibn Qays?" They said: "He sought permission three times and then went back." So he sent after him, and Abu Musa came, and 'Umar said: "What prevented you?" He said: "I said: I sought permission three times and was not given permission, so I went back." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said: "When one of you seeks permission three times and is not given permission, let him go back." 'Umar said: "By Allah, you must bring evidence for this!" Abu Musa said: "Is there anyone among you who heard it from the Prophet?" Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "By Allah, none will go with you except the youngest of us." So I was the youngest of them, and I went with him, and I informed 'Umar that the Prophet had said that. 'Umar said: "This matter of the Messenger of Allah was hidden from me; the trading in the markets distracted me."

It is known that seeking permission has three outcomes: permission given, refusal, or silence. If permission is given, that is that. If refusal is expressed in explicit words, then that is His saying: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you.﴾ The pronoun refers to the act of returning (al-ruju') understood from (irji'u, "go back"), as in His saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8].

The meaning of (azka lakum, "purer for you") is that it is better and more excellent for you than that they grant permission reluctantly. In this there is a great lesson: teaching frankness in speaking the truth without evasion, as long as there is no harm in it, and teaching the acceptance of truth, because it is more reassuring to the soul of the one who receives it than receiving what one does not know to be true or evasion. If people became accustomed to speaking the truth plainly among themselves, the suspicions they hold about one another would disappear.

As for silence, its ruling is clarified by the hadith of Abu Musa. The verb (tusallimu) means that you say: "As-salamu 'alaykum." It is one of the verbs derived from the quotation of statements that occur in sentences, like (rahhaba, "he welcomed") and (ahhala, "he greeted with 'ahlan'"), when he says "marhaban" (welcome) and "ahlan" (you are among family); and (hayya, "he greeted"), when he says "hayyaka Allah" (may Allah give you life); and (jazza, "he thanked"), when he says to him "jazaka Allah khayran" (may Allah reward you with good); and (sahhala, "he made easy"), when he says "sahlan" (ease), that is, you have alighted in ease. Al-Bu'ayth ibn Hurayth said:

"I said to her, 'Ahlan wa sahlan wa marhaban,'
and she replied with welcome, ease and marhaban."

In the hadith: "You glorify (tusabbihun), praise (tuhammidun) and magnify (tukabbirun) after every prayer thirty-three times." These are close to what is called (naht, "word-formation by compounding" or "blending"), like (basmala, "he said Bismillah") when he says "Bismillah," and (hasbala, "he said hasbuna Allah") when he says "hasbuna Allah" (Allah is sufficient for us).

The phrase (ʿala ahliha, "upon its occupants") is connected to (tusallimu), because its origin is from the rest of the sentence from which the verb was formed, which originally was: "As-salamu 'alaykum," just as (rahhaba bihi, "he welcomed him") is transitive with a preposition when he says "marhaban bika" (welcome to you). Likewise (ahhala bihi) and (sahhala bihi). From this is His saying: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

The formula of greeting is: "As-salamu 'alaykum." The Prophet (ﷺ) taught it to his companions, and he forbade Abu Juzayy al-Hujaymi from saying: "'Alayka as-salam." He said to him: "'Alayka as-salam is the greeting of the dead," three times, meaning that it is the initiation of the greeting in that way. As for the reply, one says: "Wa 'alaykum as-salam" with the conjunction (wa), and by this the reply is distinguished from the greeting of the dead, "wa rahmatullah." Al-Tirmidhi recorded this in the Book of Seeking Permission. Greeting has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 54] in Surah al-An'am.

[Page 201]

As for His saying: ﴿But if you find no one in them,﴾ etc., it is to guard against the supposition that someone might think that uninhabited dwellings may be entered by people in the absence of their owners without permission from them, assuming that the reason for the legislation of seeking permission is only what the occupants dislike, namely being seen unprepared. Rather, the reason is their dislike of others seeing what they wish to keep hidden of their affairs. So the condition here resembles the conditional clause that connects with what precedes it (al-shart al-wasli), because it is intended to emphasise the affirmation of what precedes it, and for this reason it has no implication of contrast (mafhum mukhalafa).

The purpose of His saying: ﴿until you are given permission﴾ is to reinforce the prohibition expressed by His saying: "do not enter them," that is: until its occupants come and give you permission.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ is a conclusion (tadhyil) to these instructions, reminding them that Allah is aware of their actions, so that those who insist on pressing their requests be restrained from insistence and from burdening others, and so that those who resort to tricks or peeking through cracks and the like be restrained. This is an allusive warning (ta'rid bi-al-wa'id), because doing this is disobedience to what Allah has commanded. His knowledge of it is therefore a metaphor (kinaya) for His recompense to its doers according to what they deserve.

The address in (do not enter) is general, but it is specified by the implication of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ [al-Nur: 58], as will come. Therefore the slaves and the children are also excepted from this generality, as will come.

The majority of readers recited (houses) wherever it occurs with a kasra on the ba'. Abu 'Amr, Warsh from Nafi', Hafs from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited it with a damma on the ba'. This has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verses 27–28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their occupants. That is better for you, that you may remember.﴾ ﴿But if you find no one in them, do not enter them until you are given permission. And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

We have mentioned that among the major aims of this surah is the legislation of the system of social dealings and family interaction among neighbours. These verses are a new subject, explaining the rules of visiting and teaching the etiquette of seeking permission (al-istidhan), and specifying what achieves its intended purpose, so that people do not differ about its manner according to the variation in their understanding of its aim and benefit.

Seeking permission was known in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) and at the beginning of Islam, and its form varied according to the condition of the person being visited, whether a king or a commoner, so it was not uniform. Some people neglect it or fall short in it, namely those concerned only with fulfilling their own purpose and hastening their own needs. It is not unlikely that their entering would embarrass the one visited or burden him. These verses came to specify its manner and to incorporate it into the etiquette of the religion, so that people do not neglect it, or part of it, due to their differing levels of modesty and self-respect, and their differing assumptions about whether there is any accountability for it or how severe that accountability is.

Seeking permission was prescribed for one who visits someone at his house, because people made houses as shelter from what harms the body, such as heat, cold, rain and dust, and from what harms honour and the self, such as the exposure of what the occupant does not wish people to see. So when a person is in his house and someone comes to him, he should not admit him until he has put his house in order and covered what must be covered. Then he gives him permission, or he goes out to him and speaks to him from outside the door.

The meaning of (tasta'nisu) is that you seek companionship with them, that is, you seek that the owner of the house be at ease with you, and his being at ease with you is by the absence of estrangement and aversion. This is a subtle metaphor (kinaya) for seeking permission: that the one entering should seek permission, that is, seek a permission which by its nature ensures that the owner of the house does not feel estranged by the one entering. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "Al-istina's (seeking companionship) — in our view, and Allah knows best — is al-istidhan (seeking permission)." He means that this is what is intended, either as a metaphor or as a synonym, and it derives from (uns) companionship. And what Malik said is the decisive statement. It is reported from Ibn al-Qasim in Jami' al-'Utbiyya that al-istina's is greeting (al-taslim). Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is far-fetched."

I say: Ibn al-Qasim meant the greeting made with the intention of seeking permission, so the conjunction of (wa tusallimu) is an explanatory conjunction. The intended meaning of al-istina's is not that it is derived from (anasa) in the sense of (knowing), because that is a different usage which does not fit here, and there is no benefit in mentioning it. That is according to the apparent meaning, for when the person is given permission, his permission indicates that he does not dislike the other's entering, and when he dislikes it he does not give permission. Allah is the One who knows what is in the heart, and therefore He expressed seeking permission by seeking companionship, along with the implicit indication of the reason for the legislation of seeking permission.

In this there is etiquette: a person should not be a burden on others, nor should he expose himself to aversion and being unwelcome. And the visitor and the one visited should be in harmony, at ease with each other, and this helps to strengthen Islamic brotherhood.

The command to greet is conjoined with seeking companionship, and both are made the goal of the prohibition against entering houses, to draw attention to the obligation of performing both, because the prohibition is lifted only when both are achieved. From Ibn Sirin: "A man sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'May I enter?' The Prophet (ﷺ) instructed a man near him, or a female servant named Rawda, saying: 'He does not know how to seek permission properly; let him say: As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?' The man heard it and said: 'As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?' He said: 'Enter.'" Mutarrif related from Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, that he sought permission from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and said: "Ala-j?" (may I enter?). Ibn 'Umar gave him permission, and when he entered Ibn 'Umar said to him: "What is the matter with you and the seeking of permission by the Arabs?" He meant the people of the Jahiliyyah. "When you seek permission, say: As-salamu 'alaykum. When the greeting is returned to you, say: May I enter? If you are given permission, then enter."

The apparent meaning of the verse is that seeking permission is obligatory, and that greeting is obligatory, except that the context of the verse is the legislation of seeking permission. As for greeting, its legislation was established earlier, at the beginning of Islam, and it was not specific to the situation of entering houses, so greeting is not particularly singled out here. It was mentioned together with seeking permission only to ensure its observance alongside seeking permission, lest seeking permission distract the one knocking so that he forgets the greeting, or thinks that seeking permission is sufficient in place of the greeting. Al-Mazari said in Kitab al-Mu'lim 'ala Sahih Muslim: "Seeking permission is prescribed (mashru')." Ibn al-'Arabi said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: "A group said: seeking permission is obligatory (fard) and greeting is recommended (mustahabb)." It is reported from 'Ata': "Seeking permission is obligatory upon every person who has reached puberty." Nothing has clarified the ruling on seeking permission except the jurists of the Malikis. Shaykh Abu Muhammad said in al-Risala: "Seeking permission is obligatory. Do not enter a house in which there is anyone until you have sought permission three times; if you are given permission, well and good, otherwise you return." Ibn Rushd said in al-Muqaddimat: "Seeking permission is obligatory." Abu al-Hasan al-Maliki, in his commentary on al-Risala, related the consensus (ijma') on the obligation of seeking permission. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "Seeking permission is prescribed," and this is the statement of al-Mazari in his commentary on Muslim.

I say: The juxtaposition of seeking permission with greeting in the verse does not necessarily require that they be equal in ruling, since there are other evidences distinguishing their rulings, and these evidences are from the Sunnah and from the meaning. The benefit of seeking permission is to avert what is disliked from the one visited, to cut off the causes of denial, insult, or harshness of speech, and to block the means of suspicion. All of these, or their combination, require that seeking permission be obligatory.

As for the benefit of greeting together with seeking permission, it is to strengthen the established familiarity, so it does not require more than the emphasis of recommendation. The Qur'an commanded the complete situation and left the details of its parts to the clarification of the Sunnah, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44].

The wisdom of seeking permission has been summarized in His saying: ﴿That is better for you, that you may remember.﴾ That is, that seeking permission is better for you, meaning there is good and benefit in it for you; if you reflect, you will know the good in it for you, as is hoped from you.

The verse has combined seeking permission and greeting with the conjunction (wa), which indicates only joint association. So it indicates that if seeking permission is placed before greeting, or greeting before seeking permission, the required aim has been achieved. Many hadiths report the command to put greeting before seeking permission, so that is better, and it does not contradict the verse.

There is no fixed formula for seeking permission. What has come in some reports is either understood as what was customary among them, or as a phrase more comprehensive than others in its meaning. The Sunnah has clarified that if the one seeking permission is not given permission to enter, he repeats it three times, and if he is still not given permission, he leaves.

Concerning this, there is the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in Sahih al-Bukhari, which is what was reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "I was in a gathering of the Ansar when Abu Musa al-Ash'ari came, as if frightened. He said: 'I sought permission from 'Umar three times, and he did not give me permission, so I went back.'" In another report they explained that 'Umar was occupied with some of his affairs, then he remembered and said: "Did I not hear the voice of 'Abdullah ibn Qays?" They said: "He sought permission three times and then went back." So he sent after him, and Abu Musa came, and 'Umar said: "What prevented you?" He said: "I said: I sought permission three times and was not given permission, so I went back." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said: "When one of you seeks permission three times and is not given permission, let him go back." 'Umar said: "By Allah, you must bring evidence for this!" Abu Musa said: "Is there anyone among you who heard it from the Prophet?" Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "By Allah, none will go with you except the youngest of us." So I was the youngest of them, and I went with him, and I informed 'Umar that the Prophet had said that. 'Umar said: "This matter of the Messenger of Allah was hidden from me; the trading in the markets distracted me."

It is known that seeking permission has three outcomes: permission given, refusal, or silence. If permission is given, that is that. If refusal is expressed in explicit words, then that is His saying: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you.﴾ The pronoun refers to the act of returning (al-ruju') understood from (irji'u, "go back"), as in His saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8].

The meaning of (azka lakum, "purer for you") is that it is better and more excellent for you than that they grant permission reluctantly. In this there is a great lesson: teaching frankness in speaking the truth without evasion, as long as there is no harm in it, and teaching the acceptance of truth, because it is more reassuring to the soul of the one who receives it than receiving what one does not know to be true or evasion. If people became accustomed to speaking the truth plainly among themselves, the suspicions they hold about one another would disappear.

As for silence, its ruling is clarified by the hadith of Abu Musa. The verb (tusallimu) means that you say: "As-salamu 'alaykum." It is one of the verbs derived from the quotation of statements that occur in sentences, like (rahhaba, "he welcomed") and (ahhala, "he greeted with 'ahlan'"), when he says "marhaban" (welcome) and "ahlan" (you are among family); and (hayya, "he greeted"), when he says "hayyaka Allah" (may Allah give you life); and (jazza, "he thanked"), when he says to him "jazaka Allah khayran" (may Allah reward you with good); and (sahhala, "he made easy"), when he says "sahlan" (ease), that is, you have alighted in ease. Al-Bu'ayth ibn Hurayth said:

"I said to her, 'Ahlan wa sahlan wa marhaban,'
and she replied with welcome, ease and marhaban."

In the hadith: "You glorify (tusabbihun), praise (tuhammidun) and magnify (tukabbirun) after every prayer thirty-three times." These are close to what is called (naht, "word-formation by compounding" or "blending"), like (basmala, "he said Bismillah") when he says "Bismillah," and (hasbala, "he said hasbuna Allah") when he says "hasbuna Allah" (Allah is sufficient for us).

The phrase (ʿala ahliha, "upon its occupants") is connected to (tusallimu), because its origin is from the rest of the sentence from which the verb was formed, which originally was: "As-salamu 'alaykum," just as (rahhaba bihi, "he welcomed him") is transitive with a preposition when he says "marhaban bika" (welcome to you). Likewise (ahhala bihi) and (sahhala bihi). From this is His saying: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

The formula of greeting is: "As-salamu 'alaykum." The Prophet (ﷺ) taught it to his companions, and he forbade Abu Juzayy al-Hujaymi from saying: "'Alayka as-salam." He said to him: "'Alayka as-salam is the greeting of the dead," three times, meaning that it is the initiation of the greeting in that way. As for the reply, one says: "Wa 'alaykum as-salam" with the conjunction (wa), and by this the reply is distinguished from the greeting of the dead, "wa rahmatullah." Al-Tirmidhi recorded this in the Book of Seeking Permission. Greeting has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 54] in Surah al-An'am.

[Page 201]

As for His saying: ﴿But if you find no one in them,﴾ etc., it is to guard against the supposition that someone might think that uninhabited dwellings may be entered by people in the absence of their owners without permission from them, assuming that the reason for the legislation of seeking permission is only what the occupants dislike, namely being seen unprepared. Rather, the reason is their dislike of others seeing what they wish to keep hidden of their affairs. So the condition here resembles the conditional clause that connects with what precedes it (al-shart al-wasli), because it is intended to emphasise the affirmation of what precedes it, and for this reason it has no implication of contrast (mafhum mukhalafa).

The purpose of His saying: ﴿until you are given permission﴾ is to reinforce the prohibition expressed by His saying: "do not enter them," that is: until its occupants come and give you permission.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ is a conclusion (tadhyil) to these instructions, reminding them that Allah is aware of their actions, so that those who insist on pressing their requests be restrained from insistence and from burdening others, and so that those who resort to tricks or peeking through cracks and the like be restrained. This is an allusive warning (ta'rid bi-al-wa'id), because doing this is disobedience to what Allah has commanded. His knowledge of it is therefore a metaphor (kinaya) for His recompense to its doers according to what they deserve.

The address in (do not enter) is general, but it is specified by the implication of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ [al-Nur: 58], as will come. Therefore the slaves and the children are also excepted from this generality, as will come.

The majority of readers recited (houses) wherever it occurs with a kasra on the ba'. Abu 'Amr, Warsh from Nafi', Hafs from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited it with a damma on the ba'. This has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 29:

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

This is a specification of the generality of His saying: ﴿houses other than your own houses﴾ [al-Nur: 27], restricting it to the houses prepared for dwelling. As for houses that are not prepared for dwelling, if anyone has a need to enter them, then he may enter them, because their not being prepared for dwelling means that the one who resides in them is not guarded against the entry of others; rather, he is prepared for whoever visits him. Such a house is either empty of occupants, like the houses built on the roads of travellers for their lodging, as there were houses on the road between the Hijaz and al-Sham on the route of the merchants, where they would take shelter and set down their goods there for rest, then depart from them and resume their journey. These are called al-khanat (caravanserais), the plural of khan, with the letter kha' pointed from above; it is a word arabicized from Persian. Similar to these are houses that existed in some quarters of the city, where people would place goods and saddles, and some of those in need of them built them, and others benefited from them.

As for those houses being inhabited by people who dwell in them, sheltering travellers, their baggage and their mounts, guarding their belongings, and lodging them until they resume the stage of their journey, like inhabited khans and hostels (funduq), the same applies to houses prepared for the sale of goods, bathhouses, shops of merchants, and likewise libraries and reading rooms. These are inhabited but are not called "maskun" (dwelt-in), because dwelling (sukna) is the residence in which a person lives, settles, and conducts his affairs. So the meaning of His saying "not inhabited" (ghayra maskunatin) is that they are not inhabited in the state of settled residence, or that they are not inhabited at all.

As for al-Khawaniq, the plural of khanqah, and it is said al-Khankat, the plural of khankah: these are dwellings with rooms in which the students of Sufism reside; likewise the madrasas, where students of knowledge reside; and likewise al-Rubut, the plural of ribat, which is the shelter of guards on the frontiers. There is no need for seeking permission among their residents, because they have dispensed with formality among themselves and have become like the people of one house. But a stranger among them must seek permission to enter upon them, and their supervisor, their senior, or whoever conveys on their behalf grants him leave.

His saying ﴿wherein is provision for you﴾ is a second attribute of (houses).

Al-mata' (provision) is equipment of goods, merchandise, and saddles. The apparent meaning of His saying "wherein is provision" is that the provision is placed there before the entrant enters, so this attribute has no implied restriction (mafhum), because it came as a reminder of the excuse for entering. This includes that one enters it to place his goods, by the indication of the implicit meaning of the discourse (lahn al-khitab). Likewise it includes the entry of a traveller, even if he has no goods, for the purpose of seeking shade or lodging, by the indication of the implicit meaning of the discourse or by analogy (qiyas).

Al-mata' has also been explained as a verbal noun, i.e., enjoyment and benefit. Jabir ibn Zayd said: "All the benefits of this world are mata'." Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "This is a good explanation from the statement of one of the imams of the Muslims, and it agrees with the language." Al-Zamakhshari followed him in this in al-Kashshaf. Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi also drew attention to this interpretation, which implies that whoever has no benefit in entering them is not permitted to enter them, because that would constrict those in need of their space.

His saying ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ is used as a warning against exceeding the restrictions indicated by the verse, namely that the houses are not inhabited and that the entrant is in need of entering them, far less entering them with the intention of spying on their residents, harming them, or stealing their belongings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 30:

﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾

Having mentioned the ruling on seeking permission to enter, [the Qur'an] follows it with the etiquette that applies to sitting together after entering, namely that the one who enters the house should not fix his gaze upon a woman within it. Rather, when a woman sits with him, he lowers his gaze, keeps to speech, and looks at her only with a glance that it would be difficult to turn away from.

Since complete lowering of the gaze is not possible, the particle (min) (meaning "some of," indicating partiality) was used in the verse, as an indication of this. For it is understood that what is commanded to be lowered is what it is not fitting to stare at. The Muslim recalls this from keeping in mind the rulings of the lawful and the unlawful in this matter, and so he knows that lowering the gaze has degrees: some of it is obligatory, and some of it is less than that. Thus lowering the gaze covers what people customarily dislike to scrutinize, such as looking into the hidden corners of houses, unlike what is not of that kind.

In the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he entered the upper chamber (mashraba) of the Prophet ﷺ, "I raised my gaze to the ceiling and saw a hide (uhba) hanging." 

And the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Ali: "Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours, but the second is not yours."

In this command to lower the gaze there is a great legal etiquette of restraining the soul from looking at what might lead it into the unlawful, or what might impose upon it severe patience.

Al-ghadd (lowering): the person turning his gaze away from staring and fixing his look. It may arise from modesty, as 'Antarah said:

"I lower my glance when my neighbour appears, until she has hidden her dwelling-place from my neighbour."

And it may arise from humiliation, as Jarir said:

"So lower your glance, for you are of Numayr."

The root gh-d-d conveys the sense of lowering and diminishing.

The command to guard the private parts, following the command to lower the gaze, [is mentioned] because the gaze is the precursor of fornication. Since it is a means to it, the one who pursues it by means of guarding is directed toward it, as an alert to exaggerating in lowering the gaze from the beauty of women. Thus, guarding the private parts means guarding them from engaging in anything other than what the religion has permitted.

The demonstrative (dhalika) refers to what has been mentioned, i.e., that thing mentioned: lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts.

The superlative in the phrase (azka) is stripped of comparison. The intended meaning is strengthening that purification, since this is a shield against committing great sins.

It is concluded with the clause (﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do﴾), because it is a metonymic indication of the recompense for what the command includes of lowering and guarding, since the purpose of the command is compliance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze, guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what appears thereof; and let them draw their head-coverings (khumur) over their chests (juyub), and not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or their husbands' fathers, or their sons, or their husbands' sons, or their brothers, or their brothers' sons, or their sisters' sons, or their women, or those their right hands possess, or male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who have not yet attained awareness of the private matters of women.﴾

He follows the command to the believing men with a command to the believing women, because the wisdom in both commands is one, and to make explicit what had been established in the legal commands addressed to men, namely that they include women as well. However, since this command might be thought to apply only to men, because they are more prone to violating it, the text explicitly extends it to women as well.

He then moves from this to the prohibition on women regarding things in which they are known to be lax, and the prohibition on displaying things to which they have become accustomed to wanting to show, which the Qur'an gathers under the term adornment (zinah), in His saying: ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾.

Zinah is that by which beauty (zayn) is obtained. Zayn is beauty, the verbal noun of zanah. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

"God adorned that face with beauty"

It is said: zayyana means "made beautiful" (hassana). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The love of desires has been made attractive to people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran, and He said: ﴿And We adorned it for the observers﴾ [Al-Hijr: 16] in Surat al-Hijr.

Adornment is of two kinds: natural (khilqiyyah) and acquired (muktasabah). The natural is the face and the palms, or half the forearms; the acquired is what causes adornment, such as fine clothing, jewelry, kohl,
page 206
and dyeing with henna. The term adornment has been applied to clothing in His saying: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prostration﴾ [Al-A'raf: 31], and His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 32] in Surat al-A'raf, and to good clothing in His saying: ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59]. Adornment increases a woman's beauty and draws people's glances to her, because it is among the states that are not sought except to display beauty; so it attracts men's eyes. For this reason women are forbidden to display their adornment except to those men who by kinship or marriage are not expected to feel desire toward them because of the sanctity of the relationship.

What is excepted is what appears of the adornment, which is what covering it entails hardship for the woman, or what leaving it uncovered would cause difficulty for women; this is the adornment in places of work that need not be covered, such as kohl, henna, and rings.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: adornment is of two kinds, natural and manufactured (mustan'ah). As for the natural, it is most of a woman's body, especially: the face, the wrists, the upper arms, the breasts, the shins, and the hair. As for the manufactured, it is what women customarily do not do without, such as jewelry, embroidery and dyeing of garments, as well as kohl, dyeing with henna, and the siwak. The apparent of the natural adornment is what covering it entails hardship, such as the face, the two palms, and the two feet; its opposite, the hidden, is such as the upper parts of the shins, the wrists, the upper arms, the chest, and the ears. The apparent of the manufactured adornment is what leaving it entails hardship for the woman from the side of her husband and from the side of her appearance among her peers, and whose removal is not easy when she is seen in front of men, and whose restoration is not easy when she is alone at home; likewise what is placed in a spot not commanded to be covered, such as rings, unlike earrings and bracelets. There is disagreement regarding anklets and bangles, and the correct view is that they are of the apparent adornment; the Qur'an has confirmed the anklet in His saying: ﴿nor let them stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known﴾, as will come. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik: "Dyeing is not part of adornment." Ibn al-'Arabi said: and dyeing is part of the hidden adornment if it is on the two feet. [Ibn al-'Arabi's statement ends.]

page 207
So the meaning of (what appears thereof) is what is in a place that a woman does not cover, namely the face, the two palms, and the two feet.

A group of exegetes interpreted adornment as the entire body, and interpreted what appears as the face, the two palms, and it is said the two feet and the hair. On this interpretation, the apparent adornment is that which God, by the dictate of nature, made manifest, such that covering it would nullify its benefit or cause hardship to its bearer; that is the face and the palms. As for the feet, their covering does not nullify their use but makes it harder; because going barefoot is the usual state of desert women. For this reason the jurists differed about covering them: in the school of Malik there are two opinions, the more well-known being that she must cover her feet, and it is said that it is not required; Abu Hanifah said that covering her feet is not required.

As for a woman's attractive features, which do not involve hardship in covering, these are not part of the apparent adornment, such as the chest, the breast, the upper arm, the wrist, and the upper parts of the shins; likewise what has a beautiful shape on a woman, even if it is not bare, such as the buttocks, the flanks, and the thighs, provided that draping the garment over it does not cause her hardship. Malik narrated in the Muwatta' from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Women who are clothed yet naked, leaning and causing others to lean, will not enter Paradise." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: he meant those who wear thin clothing that describes the body and does not conceal it; that is, they are clothed in name but naked in reality. [Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's statement ends.] In the version of the Muwatta' by Ibn Bashkuwal, from al-Qunazi', he said: Malik explained: they wear thin garments that do not conceal them. [End of statement.]

In the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from the Jami' of al-'Utbiyyah, Malik said: "It reached me that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab forbade women from wearing qabati garments." Ibn Rushd said in his commentary: these are tight garments that cling to the body because of their tightness, so that the wearer's thickness appears thin, and they reveal what is admired, in compliance with His saying: ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾. [Ibn Rushd's statement ends.] In the transmissions of Ibn Wahb from the Jami' of al-'Utbiyyah, Malik said concerning slave women who wear cloaks: "I do not like it; if she fastens it on herself it becomes a revealing of her shape."

The majority of the imams hold that the exception of displaying the face and the two palms from the general prohibition on displaying their adornment requires that the face and palms may be displayed in all circumstances, because

page 208
the rule is that the exception should cover all circumstances of what is excepted from. Al-Shafi'i interpreted it as an exception only during prayer, and not otherwise, but this is a specification for which there is no evidence.

They were forbidden to be lax regarding the khimar. The khimar is a garment a woman places on her head to cover her hair, her neck, and her ears. Women sometimes let the khimar hang down behind them, as the women of the Anbat do, leaving the neck, the chest, and the ears uncovered; therefore they were commanded by His saying: ﴿and let them draw their khimar over their chests﴾. Darb means fixing a placement, and it was discussed in His saying: ﴿Indeed God is not ashamed to strike an example﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: let them tighten the placement of the khimar over the chests, so that no part of the skin of the chest appears.

The ba' in His saying (bi-khumurihinna) is for emphasizing adhesion, an intensification in firmly placing the khimar over the chest, beyond the emphasis derived from the verb (yadribna).

Juyub is the plural of jayb, with a fatha on the jim, which is the collar of a shirt at the neck. The meaning is: let them place their khimar over the collars of their garments, such that between the end of the khimar and the beginning of the collar there remains no part of the neck showing.

His saying: ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾ repeats the phrase ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ as an emphasis of the earlier ﴿and not display their adornment﴾, and in order to build upon it the exception in His saying (except to their husbands), etc., whose apparent sense would require it to be coordinated with (except to their husbands) because of the distance between the first and the second. That is: they should not display their hidden adornment except to those mentioned after the particle of exception, because of the great hardship in concealing hidden adornment at many times, since the contact between a woman and her relatives and in-laws who are excepted is frequent; so if it were obligatory for her to conceal her adornment at all times, that would be a hardship for her.

The verse mentions twelve excepted persons, all of whom are those who frequently enter. The verse is silent about others who share their status in meaning; we will mention these after finishing with those explicitly named in the verse.

page 209
335 The buʿūlah is the plural of baʿl, which means husband and the master of a female slave. The root of baʿl is lord and owner (and the greatest idol among the ancient people of Iraq was called Baʿl, and its mention came in the Qur'an in the story of the people of Nineveh and their messenger Elias). It was applied to the husband because the origin of marriage is ownership, and traces of ownership remain in it in the dowry, since it is like a price. The pattern fu'ulah in plurals is rare and not regular; it is the plural of fu'ul with the ta' added.

Every man counted among those excepted from the prohibition is among those who have a strong bond with the woman, which serves as a barrier against their desiring her. In the Sama' of Ibn al-Qasim from the Jami' of al-'Utbiyyah: Malik was asked about a man whose wife's mother leaves her cloak with him. He said: there is no harm in that. Ibn Rushd said in his commentary: because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and let them draw their khimar over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾, etc., so God permitted that she remove her khimar from her chest and display her adornment in the presence of her unmarriageable kin by blood or marriage. [End of statement.] That is, Malik analogized the husband of a woman's daughter to the son of a woman's husband, because both share the prohibition by affinity.

The possessive in His saying (nisa'ihinna), referring to the pronoun of (the believing women): if it is taken in its apparent sense of possession, it indicates that they are the women with whom they have special closeness. It has been said that what is meant is the women of their community, that is, believing women, like the usage in His saying: ﴿and call to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 282], meaning from among the men of your religion. It is also possible that what is meant is simply women. The possessive was attached to the pronoun for women only to match the rest of the counted items.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: this verse contains twenty-five pronouns, so this was for the sake of consistency. That is, the possessive would then be for a non-semantic reason, but for a verbal reason required by eloquence, like the two pronouns attached in His saying: ﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ [Al-Shams: 8], meaning: He inspired it with wickedness and piety. Their attachment to the pronoun is for consistency with the pronouns from the beginning of the surah: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [Al-Shams: 1], and likewise His saying in it: ﴿Thamud denied by its transgression﴾ [Al-Shams: 11]

page 210
meaning: by its transgression, which is rebellion; so the pronoun for Thamud was mentioned without need, but was brought in for the sake of the embellishment of parallelism.

From these two possibilities the jurists differed on the permissibility of women who are polytheists or People of the Book looking at what a Muslim woman may display of her body to a non-kin man. The statements of the Maliki exegetes and jurists on this are not precise. What may be deduced from their statements is the words of Khalil in al-Tawdih, at the words of Ibn al-Hajib: "The awrah of a free woman is everything other than the face and the two palms": and the implication of the words of my lord Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hajj is: as for the disbelieving woman, she is like the non-kin woman with respect to men, by consensus. [End of statement.]

Al-Shafi'i's school has two opinions. The first is that a non-Muslim woman may see of a Muslim woman only her face and hands. Al-Baghawi and the author of al-Minhaj, al-Baydawi, gave this view preference, and al-Fakhr (al-Razi) chose it in his tafsir. Something similar is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas gave as its reason that a non-Muslim woman does not refrain from describing a Muslim woman to her husband. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah: "It has reached me that the women of the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimma) enter the bathhouses with the women of the Muslims. Prevent that and stand between them and it, for it is not permissible for a dhimmi woman to see the nakedness of a Muslim woman."

The second opinion is that a non-Muslim woman is like a Muslim woman. Al-Ghazali gave this view preference.

Abu Hanifa's school likewise has two opinions. The more sound of them is that a non-Muslim woman is like an unrelated man, so she may see of a Muslim woman only her face, hands and feet. It is also said that she is like a Muslim woman.

As for "what their right hands possess" (ma malakat aymanuhunna), it is a concession, because a woman covering her adornment from them is a hardship for her, given how often they come and go in her presence. Also, the fact that he is her property is a restraint on him and on her against anything forbidden arising between them, and Islam is a restraint on him from describing the woman to men.

As for the male attendants who have no physical desire (al-tabi'in ghayr uli al-irba) among men, they are a category of free men whose members share two attributes: dependence (tab'iyya) and lack of desire (adam al-irba).

The dependence is that they are among the dependents of the woman's household. They are not her property, but they come and go to her house to receive charity or for service.

Al-irba means need, and what is meant by it is the need for intercourse with women. The absence of this need is evident in the castrated (majbub), the impotent (unnin) and the very old man, so God permitted the display of adornment to these men's gaze, to remove hardship from women, with the general safety from the arousal of desire and its effects on both sides.

It is disputed whether the eunuch who is not a dependent is to be included with these, on two opinions transmitted from the early scholars. Both opinions have been reported from Malik. Ibn al-Faras mentioned that the sound view is the permissibility of his entering upon the woman when both conditions, dependence and lack of desire, are met. This was also reported from Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan.

As for the case of Hit, the effeminate (mukhannath) or castrated man, and the Prophet ﷺ forbidding his wives to let him enter upon them, that was a specific case tied to a particular condition in him, namely that he described women to men. It is limited to such people. Do you not see that he was not forbidden from entering upon women before he heard what he heard from him?

The majority read ﴿غَيْرِ أُولِي الإرْبَةِ﴾ with a kasra on ghayr. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read ghayr with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). "Al-tifl" is singular but is meant generically, so the plural is applied to it in His saying ﴿الَّذِينَ لَمْ يَظْهَرُوا﴾, as in His saying ﴿ثُمَّ نُخْرِجُكم طِفْلًا﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], meaning children (atfal).

The meaning of ﴿لَمْ يَظْهَرُوا عَلى عَوْراتِ النِّساءِ﴾ is that they have not come to know of them. This is a metaphor for their minds being free of desire for women, which is the state before the age of puberty (murahaqa).

The paternal uncle and maternal uncle are not mentioned among those excepted, so the scholars differed over whether they are equal to them in this. Al-Hasan and the majority said they are equal to those mentioned among the mahram relatives, and this is the apparent position of Malik's school, since the Malikī commentators such as Ibn al-Faras and Ibn Juzayy did not mention a prohibition from him. Al-Sha'bi held that they are prohibited. He justified the distinction by saying that the paternal and maternal uncles may describe the woman to their sons, and the sons are not mahram. This justification is weak, because the restraint of Islam prevents describing the woman.

The apparent reason the verse is silent about the uncles is not that their ruling differs from the rest of the mahram relatives, but that it limits itself to those who frequently attend the woman's house, so the enumeration follows what is usual. Relatives by foster-suckling who are in the same degrees are included with these, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "What is forbidden by nursing is forbidden by lineage." al-Hasan affirmed this, and I have not found a Malikī opinion on it. The apparent meaning of the hadith is that they share in the same concession as the mahram by lineage and by marriage.

* * *

﴿ولا يَضْرِبْنَ بِأرْجُلِهِنَّ لِيُعْلَمَ ما يُخْفِينَ مِن زِينَتِهِنَّ﴾
"Striking with the feet" (al-darb bi'l-arjul) is walking with force, as in His saying "yadrib fi al-ard" (who strikes the earth).

Al-Tabari related from a Hadrami that a woman had two bura (a type of anklet of silver, the word being the dual of bura, with a damma on the ba' and a light ra') and had made a jaz' (onyx/agate) for her feet. She passed by a group of people and struck with her foot, so the anklet fell upon the jaz' and it made a sound, and this verse was revealed.

The reality is that some women, when they wore anklets, would strike with their feet forcefully as they walked, so the jingling of the anklets would be heard, out of coquetry and vanity in their beauty. They were forbidden this, together with the prohibition on displaying adornment.

Al-Zajjaj said: the hearing of this adornment is more stirring of desire than looking at adornment. As for the sound of an ordinary anklet, there is no harm in it.

In the narrations of Ibn Wahb from the Jami' al-'Utbiyya: Malik was asked about anklets on women's feet and said: "What is this that the hadith has come about?" and leaving them is dearer to me, without forbidding them. Ibn Rushd said in his commentary: he meant that what is forbidden is only that they intend, in their walking, to make the anklets jingle, to display their adornment.

This implies the prohibition of everything that by its nature reminds a man of women's allure and stirs in him desire for them through whatever he sees or hears of adornment or movement, such as swaying, singing, and words of flirtation. Among this is women dancing in men's gatherings, and among it is smearing oneself with perfume whose fragrance is strong. His saying ﴿لِيُعْلَمَ ما يُخْفِينَ مِن زِينَتِهِنَّ﴾ points to the reason for this. The Prophet ﷺ cursed women who tattoo and women who file their teeth for beauty.

Makki ibn Abi Talib said: there is no verse in the Book of God with more pronouns than this verse; it gathers twenty-five pronouns for the believing women, both in the genitive and the nominative. Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi named it "the verse of pronouns."

* * *

﴿وتُوبُوا إلى اللَّهِ جَمِيعًا أيُّها المُؤْمِنُونَ لَعَلَّكم تُفْلِحُونَ﴾
The commands and prohibitions addressed to the believers are followed by the command to all of them to repent to God. This signals that in what they were commanded and forbidden there is a defense against a call the human nature inclines to, from approval and desire, so that it issues from a person through heedlessness, and then he becomes absorbed in it. They were therefore commanded to repent, so that they would hold themselves accountable for what slips from them of that lapse (lamam), which leads to something greater.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿قُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [al-Nur: 30]. There is a shift (iltifat) from addressing the Messenger ﷺ to addressing the community, because this is a reminder of the obligation of repentance established earlier, not the beginning of a new legislation.

By saying "jami'an" (all of you) he indicates that the addressees are the believing men and women, even though the address came with the masculine pronoun by way of predominance (taghlib). They should hope for success if they repent and turn back.

The discussion of repentance has already been given in Surat al-Nisa' at His saying ﴿إنَّما التَّوْبَةُ عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Nisa': 17].

In the Mushaf, "ayyuhah" was written with a ha' at its end, in consideration of the dropping of the alif in continuous speech with the word "al-mu'minun." The majority read it with a fatha on the ha' without an alif in continuous speech. Abu 'Amir read it with a damma on the ha', following the vowel of "ayy." Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i pause on it with an alif at its end. The rest pause on it with a sukun on the ha', in consideration of how it was written.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 32:

﴿Marry off the unmarried among you, and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty. Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

The commands concerning chastity are followed by guidance toward what helps to achieve it, what keeps the souls of the believing men and women chaste, and what lowers their gaze. He commanded the guardians to marry off their unmarried women (ayama-hum) and not leave them as widows (mutaʼayyimat), because that is more chaste for them and for the men who marry them. He commanded masters to marry off their male and female slaves. This is a means to eliminating prostitution (al-bigha'), as the end of the verse will indicate.

*Al-ayama* is the plural of *ayyim*, with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the kasra-marked ya, in the pattern *fayʿil*. It refers to a woman who has no husband, whether she was previously married (thayyib) or a virgin (bikr). The common usage of *ayyim* applies to a woman who had a husband and then became free of him through separation or death. Its application to a virgin who has no husband is not common, so it is understood as a figurative usage that became frequent. Originally *ayyim* is an attribute of women. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i said: For this reason the feminine *ta'* is not attached to it, so one does not say *imra'a ayyima*. Applying *ayyim* to a man who is without a wife is either by way of association (*mushakala*) or comparison (*tashbih*). Some lexicographers, such as Abu 'Ubayd and al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, consider *ayyim* to be shared (*mushtarak*) between woman and man, and al-Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf* and the *al-Qamus* follow this view.

According to al-Zamakhshari, the pattern of *ayama* is *afa'il*, because it is the plural of *ayyim* in the pattern *fayʿil*, and *fayʿil* is not pluralized as *faʿali*. The original form of *ayama* is *ayaʾim*, and a metathesis (*qalb makani*) occurred in it: the *mim* was moved forward to escape the heaviness of the *ya'* after the long vowel, and the *mim* was given a fatha for lightness, so the *ya'* became an *alif*. According to Ibn Malik and a group of scholars, its pattern is *faʿali* by way of irregular formation (*ala ghayr qiyas*), which is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's statement.

*Al-ayama* (in the verse) is a general expression, because it is a plural defined by the article *al-*, so it includes prostitutes (*al-baghaya*). Their guardians were commanded to marry them off, so this generality abrogated (*nasikh*, i.e., abrogated) the statement of God Most High: ﴿The adulterous woman is not married except to an adulterer or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. Most jurists said that this verse abrogates the earlier verse, and this is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad. It has been reported that the view that the earlier one is *muhkam* (not abrogated) is held without specifying anyone. Abu Bakr married a woman to a man who had committed adultery with her, after her father complained about him.

The partitive sense in His words *minkum* ("among you") is that they are of the Muslims, because non-Muslims, according to the Muslims, are either married to some Muslims, so the verse has no relevance to them, or they are slaves, in which case they are included in His words: ﴿and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾, according to the possibilities that follow concerning the meaning of *al-salihin* ("the righteous"). As for others, their guardianship belongs to the people of their own religion.

The intended meaning is that *al-ayama* refers to free women, and this is specified by His words after it: ﴿and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾. The apparent meaning of describing the male and female slaves as "the righteous" is that what is intended is their being characterized by religious righteousness, that is, being God-fearing. The meaning is: the certainty of their righteousness should not lead you to neglect their marriage, because you are secure from their falling into fornication. Rather, you must marry them, out of kindness toward them and to repel the hardship of distress (*al-'anat*) from them.

This indicates that if they were not righteous, their marriage would be even more urgent. This is by implication (*dalalat al-fahwa*), so it includes non-righteous slaves who are not chaste, and the chaste slaves who are Muslim, and it includes slaves who are non-Muslim. With this interpretation the perplexity that confronted the exegetes concerning the restriction by this description is dispelled. It has been said that *al-salihin* is meant as suitability for marriage, in the sense of fitness for the husband's affairs, that is, if they are likely to fulfill the rights of marriage.

The imperative form in His words: ﴿Marry off the unmarried among you﴾ to the end is general and admits of obligation (*wujub*) or recommendation (*nadb*), according to the circumstances of those whose marriage is commanded. If they are likely to fall into harm in religion or in worldly life, their marriage is obligatory. If they are not like that, then according to Malik and Abu Hanifa, their marriage is recommended (*mustahabb*). Al-Shafi'i said it is not recommended, and the imperative is taken to mean permissibility (*ibaha*).
