This is a weak interpretation in this context, since the context is not one where there is likely to be doubt about the permissibility of marrying them.

The clause ﴿If they are poor﴾ etc. is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), because the generality of the unmarried women, male slaves and female slaves in the imperative form raises the question for guardians and masters: what if the suitor for the unmarried woman is poor, should the guardian reject him? And what if the master of the slaves is poor and cannot find what he needs to spend on his wife? Likewise, the master of a female slave who is proposed to by a poor man, whether free or a slave. So this came to clarify that the generality in circumstances is intended. God promised the one who marries among them, if he is poor, that God will enrich him. His enriching him means facilitating wealth for him if he is free, and expanding the wealth of his master if he is a slave. So there is no excuse for the guardian or the master to reject his proposal in these circumstances.

God's enriching them is the granting of success to what they undertake of the means of provision that they are accustomed to, which is connected to their particular efforts, along with the general or particular causes that make their efforts successful and their trade profitable. The meaning is that God has guaranteed for them that He will suffice them for the burden of what marriage adds to their expenses.

The divine attribute *al-Wasi'* ("All-Encompassing") is derived from the verb *wasi'a* (to be vast/encompassing), in the sense that it is metaphorical, because what is described as vast is His beneficence. The Proof of Islam (Hujjat al-Islam, al-Ghazali) said: "Vastness is ascribed sometimes to knowledge, when it is extensive and encompasses many known things, and sometimes to beneficence and the bestowal of blessings. However it is determined and on whatever it is based, the absolutely All-Encompassing is God Most High, because if one considers His knowledge, there is no shore to the sea of His known things, and if one considers His beneficence and blessings, there is no end to His capabilities." End of quote.

What is derived from the inductive study of the Qur'an is that the absolute attribute "All-Encompassing" is meant to express vastness of bounty and blessing. That is why it is paired with the attribute of knowledge and the like. God Most High said: ﴿And if they separate, God will enrich each of them from His abundance, and God is ever All-Encompassing, All-Wise﴾ [al-Nisa': 130]. As for when vastness is mentioned in the verbal form, what is meant by it is comprehensiveness regarding what it is distinguished by, as in His words: ﴿Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾ [al-A'raf: 89].

The mention of ﴿All-Knowing﴾ after ﴿All-Encompassing﴾ is an indication that He gives His bounty according to what He knows of wisdom in the measure of the giving.

[p. 216]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 33 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And let those who cannot find a marriage (nikah, marriage) keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty.﴾

He commanded everyone to whom the matter of marrying off relates to keep chaste (al-'afaf) during the period in which they await the facilitation of marriage for them, whether by themselves or with the permission of their guardians (awliya') and masters (mawali). The sin and the ta' in (ﷺ)... [see note below] *al-sin wa al-ta'* ("the sin and the ta'") are for emphasis in the action, meaning: let those who cannot find a marriage strive hard to be chaste. The way in which this indicates emphasis is that it is originally a metaphor. He made the request for the action equivalent to a request for striving in it, so as to indicate exerting one's full effort.

The meaning of (﴿لا يَجِدُونَ نِكاحًا﴾) "they do not find a marriage" is: they do not find the ability to marry. So there is an omitted modifier here. It has been said that *nikah* here is the name of that which is the cause of obtaining marriage, like clothing and covering. So what is meant is the dowry (mahr) that is given to the woman.

The "enrichment" (al-ighna') here is their being made rich through marriage. And *al-fadl* (bounty) is the increase in giving.

* * *

﴿And those among your slaves who seek a contract (al-kitab), write it for them if you know good in them, and give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you.﴾

When the promise of Allah to those among the poor slaves who marry, that they will be made rich, was mentioned, and one of the means of their enrichment is that they go out and earn through their work, and this is not something the slave can accomplish independently because he is in the service of his master, [p. 219] Allah made for the slaves a right to earning, so that they may free themselves from slavery. And there would be enrichment for the slave in that, if he is among those who have spouses. Allah commanded the masters to respond to whoever among their slaves seeks a contract (kitabah, contractual manumission), in order to realize the objective of the Shari'ah of spreading freedom among the community, and its objective of increasing offspring in the community, and its objective of purifying the community and the rectitude of its religion.

*Alladhina* (those who) is in the nominative by way of the beginning (mubtada'), or in the accusative by a hidden verb which is explained by (*fakatibuhum*, "write for them"). This second is the preference of Sibawayh and al-Khalil.

The entry of the *fa'* (then) into (*fakatibuhum*) is because the relative clause (al-mawsul) implies the meaning of a conditional, as if it were said: "If the one who seeks the contract is among what your right hands possess, then write for them," as an emphasis on the consequence of the statement upon the realization of the content of the relative clause, such that it is like the consequence of conditions upon the condition.

*Al-kitab* is the verbal noun of *kataba*, when one contracts (aqada) for obtaining freedom from slavery upon a specified amount of wealth which is paid to the master of the slave in installments (munajjaman), meaning distributed over specified times. They in most cases fixed these times by the risings of the lunar mansions (nujum al-manazil), like the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). Therefore they called the fixing of its payment *najm* (a star/stage), and called its distribution *tanjim* (payment in installments). Then this became dominant for every fixed time, so it is said concerning it: *tanjim*. Likewise the blood-money (diyat) and the burdens (hamalat) they used to make distributed over fixed times, and they called that *tanjim*. The paying of blood-money in three years in equal parts was the practice. Zuhayr said:

*Wounds are left unpaid for with the hundreds (of camels), so the one who is not guilty pays them in installments.*

They called that *kitabah* because the master and his slave would record the contract of installment payment in exchange for freedom with a document (sakk) which a scribe writes between them. Since writing contains preservation of the right of both of them, the name *kitabah* was applied to that recording, because what it includes is a contract from both sides, even if the scribe is one and the writing is one. In the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf: "I made a *kitab* with Umayyah ibn Khalaf, that he would protect me in my property in Mecca and I would protect him in his property in Medina."

The meaning of (﴿if you know good in them﴾) is: if you think that they do not seek by this except the freeing of themselves, and do not seek by it a capacity for running away. That good consists of the ability to earn and the quality of trustworthiness. It is not required that the continuation of this be certain, because if he fails to complete what is upon him, he returns a slave as he was.

[p. 220] The *kitabah* was known since the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah), but it was at the discretion of the master. So this verse came, commanding the masters to do this if the slave desired it, or to urge them to do it, with differences among the scholars regarding the implication of the command in His saying (*fakatibuhum*). Concerning this, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Masruq, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, and the Zahiriyyah, is that *kitabah* is obligatory upon the master if he knows good in his slave, and Allah has left this to his knowledge and religion. Al-Tabari chose this, and it is the preponderant view, because it combines the objective of the Shari'ah with preserving the right of the masters in their property. So if the slave proposes buying himself from his master, it becomes obligatory upon him to accept. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab intended to strike Anas ibn Malik with the whip (durrah) when Sirin, his slave, asked him to make a contract with him, and Anas refused. The majority went to interpret the command as recommendation (nadb).

In the Sunnah there is the hadith of the *kitabah* of Barirah with her masters, and how 'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, paid all of the money of the *kitabah* on her behalf. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned from al-Naqqash and Makki ibn Abi Talib that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was: a slave of Hutayb ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, or of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, whose name was Subayh al-Qibti (or Subh), asked his master for *kitabah*, but he refused him, so Allah revealed this verse, and his master made the contract with him. In al-Kashshaf it is said that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab made a contract with a slave of his who was called Abu Umayyah, the first slave to be given a *kitabah* contract in Islam.

It is apparent that the address in His saying (﴿and give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾) is directed to the masters of the slaves, so that the two addresses are consistent. It is a command to the masters to help their *mukatabun* (slaves in a *kitabah* contract) with money from what Allah has bestowed upon them. That would be by reducing for them some of the amount of money on which the contract was made. Likewise Malik said: "From the last installment of the *kitabah*, what the master's soul permits is remitted for the *mukatab*." Some of the early scholars determined it as a quarter, and some as a third, and some as a tenth.

This reduction was described with the word *ita'* (giving), and there is no actual giving here. But since it was a remission of what was due upon the *mukatab*, it was treated as being equivalent to giving, just as the completion of the full dowry by a husband who divorces before consummation to his divorced wife was called *'afw* (pardon) in His saying: ﴿or that the one in whose hand is the marriage tie should pardon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. [p. 221] In the view of a group, regarding the meaning of ﴿the one in whose hand is the marriage tie﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], among them al-Shafi'i, it is the husband.

Some of the exegetes said: the address in His saying (*wa atuhum*, "and give them") is to the Muslims, and Allah commanded them to help the *mukatabin* (those in contracts). The command is interpreted as recommendation according to most scholars, but al-Shafi'i interpreted it as obligation. Isma'il ibn Hammad al-Qadi said: "Al-Shafi'i made the *kitabah* not obligatory, and made the command to give obligatory, so he made the origin non-obligatory and the branch obligatory, and this has no parallel." Hmm, and this is open to examination.

The attribution of the wealth to Allah is because He facilitates the means of obtaining it. In it there is an allusion that giving from that wealth is gratitude, and withholding is denial of the blessing, which may expose the withholder to the removal of the blessing from him.

The relative pronoun in His saying (*alladhi atakum*, "which He has given you") may be a description of (*mal Allah*, "the wealth of Allah"), with the returning pronoun omitted, its estimate being: *atakumuhu* ("He gave it to you"). It may also be a description of the name of Majesty (Allah), so that it is a reminder of favor and an incitement to compliance, by reminding that He is the guardian of the blessing. In that case the object of (*ataka*, "He gave") is omitted for generality, meaning: He gave you blessings in abundance, as in His saying: ﴿and He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

The rulings of the *kitabah*, the inability of the *mukatab* to pay his installments and his return to being a slave, the death of the *mukatab*, the inheritance of the *kitabah*, and the payment of the installments by the children of the *mukatab* are explained at length in the books of jurisprudence (furu').

* * *

﴿And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution if they desire chastity, seeking the goods of the worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

[p. 222] A transition to legislation regarding matters of dealings between men and women which have an effect on lineages, and regarding matters of the rights of masters and slaves. This transition is due to the connection with what preceded of the ruling on earning, which relates from slaves to their masters, which is the *kitabah*, so it moved on to the ruling on prostitution (al-bigha').

*Al-bigha'* is the verbal noun of: *baghati al-jariyah*, when the slave-girl engages in fornication for pay as a profession for herself. So *al-bigha'* is fornication for a wage. The derivation of the form *mufa'alah* in it is for emphasis and repetition, and for this reason one only says: *baghat al-amah* ("the female slave engaged in *bigha'*"), and one does not say *baghat*. It is derived from *al-baghy* in the meaning of seeking, as 'Iyad said in *al-Mashariq*, because the master of the slave-girl sought gain through her. The woman who practices it as a profession is called *baghiyy*, on the pattern of *fa'ul* in the meaning of *fa'il*, and for this reason the feminine *ha'* does not join it. So the origin of *baghiyy* is *baghuwy*, the *waw* and *ya'* gathered, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the *waw* was changed to *ya'* and the *ya'* was assimilated into the *ya'*.

This *bigha'* was prescribed in earlier religious laws. It has come in the Book of Genesis, chapter 38: "So she took off her widow's garments, covered herself with a veil and wrapped herself, and sat at the entrance of 'Aynaim, which is on the road." Then it says: "Yahudha saw her and considered her a harlot, because she had covered her face, so he turned to her on the road and said: 'Come, let me come in to you.' She said: 'What will you give me?' He said: 'I will send you a young goat from the flock.' ... Then he went in to her and she conceived by him."

In Medina there were slave-girls who were prostitutes. Among them were six slave-girls belonging to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and they are: Mu'adhah, Musaykah, Umaymah, 'Amrah, Arwa and Qutaylah. He used to compel them to prostitution after Islam. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik narrated from al-Zuhri that a man among the captives of Quraysh on the day of Badr had been placed with 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, and this captive wanted Mu'adhah for himself, and she refused him, because she had become Muslim. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy used to beat her for her refusal of him, hoping that she would conceive from him, that is, from the Qurashi captive, so that he would seek the ransom of her child, that is, the ransom of its enslavement, from Ibn Ubayy. Perhaps this captive was wealthy and had property in Mecca, and the one who fornicated with a slave-girl would ransom his child by a hundred camels which he would give to the master of the slave-girl. She complained of him to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse was revealed.

It has also been said: "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy had prepared Mu'adhah for the honoring of his guests. When a guest alighted with him, he would send her to him to have intercourse with him, out of intent to honor him. Mu'adhah came to Abu Bakr and complained of that to him. Abu Bakr mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ordered Abu Bakr to take her into custody. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy shouted: 'Who will excuse us from Muhammad, who overcomes us regarding our slaves?' So Allah revealed this verse," meaning: and that was before 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy openly professed Islam. All of these reports converge on the point that this verse contained the prohibition of *bigha'* upon the Muslims, men and women, who own the matter of their own persons.

In Mecca there were nine famous prostitutes who used to place banners on their houses like the banners of the farrier (baytar), so that men would recognize them. They were, as al-Wahidi mentioned: Umm Mahzul, slave-girl of al-Sa'ib al-Makhzumi; Umm Ghalid, slave-girl of Safwan ibn Umayyah; Hayyah al-Qibtiyyah, slave-girl of al-'As ibn Wa'il; Muznah, slave-girl of Malik ibn 'Umaylah ibn al-Sabbaq; Jullalah, slave-girl of Suhayl ibn 'Amrah; Umm Suwayd, slave-girl of 'Amr ibn 'Uthman al-Makhzumi; Sharifah, slave-girl of Rabi'ah ibn Aswad; Qarinah or Qaribah, slave-girl of Hisham ibn Rabi'ah; and Qarinah, slave-girl of Hilal ibn Anas. Their houses were called *al-mawakhir* (brothels) in the time of ignorance.

I say: It has already passed that among the prostitutes was 'Inaq, and perhaps she is Umm Mahzul, as the words of al-Qurtubi in his commentary on the saying of Allah, ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3], imply. I have not found that any of these who were in Mecca embraced Islam. As for those who were in Medina, Mu'adhah, Musaykah and Umaymah embraced Islam among them. I have not found the names of the other three among the Companions, so perhaps they died before they embraced Islam.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 24, verse 33 (part 2 of 2):

Prostitution (al-bigha') in the Jahiliyya was counted among the types of marriage. In the Sahih, from the hadith of 'A'isha, that marriage in the Jahiliyya was of four kinds. One of them was the marriage of people today: a man proposes to another man for his ward or his daughter, gives her a dowry, and then marries her.

صفحة ٢٢٤

Another marriage was that a man would say to his wife when she became clean from her menses: "Send to so-and-so and seek to have intercourse with him (istabdi'i)," while her husband kept away from her and did not touch her until her pregnancy from that man whom she sought out became evident. When her pregnancy became evident, her husband would have intercourse with her if he wished. He did this only out of desire for noble offspring, and this marriage was called the marriage of istibda' (seeking seed).

Another marriage was that a group of fewer than ten men would gather and enter upon a woman, all of them having intercourse with her. When she conceived and gave birth, and after some nights had passed following her delivery, she would send for them, and none of them could refuse to come. They would gather before her, and she would say to them: "You know what has happened between you, and I have given birth. This is your son, O so-and-so," naming whomever she wished, and the child would be attributed to him.

A fourth marriage was that people would enter upon a woman who did not refuse anyone who came to her; these were the prostitutes (al-bagaya), who would set up banners at their doors as a sign, so that whoever desired them would enter upon them. When one of them conceived and gave birth, they would gather for her and call the physiognomists (al-qafa), who would then attribute her child to the one they saw fit, and he would be joined to him and called his son. When Muhammad was sent with the truth, he demolished all the marriages of the Jahiliyya except the marriage of people today. End of quotation.

Thus prostitution among free women was by their own choice, for the sake of earning a livelihood. 'Inaq, the companion of Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, whose mention preceded at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ [al-Nur: 3], was one such. Among slave women there were those whom their masters compelled to this for the acquisition of the wages of their prostitution. Just as they used female slaves for service and for concubinage, so they used some of them for earning, and they called their earnings a dowry (mahr), as came in the hadith of Abu Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "forbade the mahr of the prostitute." For this reason the verse is restricted to mentioning the fata'at (young women), the plural of fata meaning a slave woman, just as they said for a male slave: ghulam.

Know that the interpretation of this verse is difficult, and the exegetes did not give it its due explanation. They only spent words repeating the varied narrations about its occasion of revelation and the names of those whose names appear in its case, without clarifying what the observer can extract from its meanings and rulings.

صفحة ٢٢٥

There is no doubt that the address in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not compel your young women to prostitution﴾ is directed at the Muslims. If the case of the slave woman of Ibn Ubayy occurred after her master had declared Islam, then he was the cause of revelation and is included in the generality without doubt. If it occurred before Islam had become manifest, then he is a cause but the ruling does not include him, because he was not among the Muslims on that day; rather, the grumbling of his slave woman against him was what prompted the prohibition to the Muslims against compelling their young women to prostitution. In any case, the young women are Muslims, because idolatresses are not addressed with the branches of the Shari'a. Abdullah ibn Ubayy declared Islam during the second year after the Hijra; he hesitated for a time regarding Islam, and when he saw his people enter Islam, he entered it unwillingly, persisting in hypocrisy. It appears that the case of his slave woman occurred during the period when his disbelief was open, as you know from what is narrated from al-Zuhri of Ibn Ubayy's saying when it was revealed: "Who will excuse us from Muhammad? He overcomes us regarding our slaves." The revelation of Surah al-Nur was around the second year, as you know from the beginning of the discussion of it. There is no doubt that prostitution, which is an action of the Jahiliyya, continued for a time after the Hijra, about a year.

There is no doubt that prostitution resembles fornication in some respects, in that it exposes lineages to confusion, although it does not reach the extent of fornication in breaching the universal necessity of preserving lineage, since the fornicator acts in secret, known only to the one who committed it, whereas prostitution was openly practiced. They used to refer, in attributing children born to prostitutes to their fathers, to the acknowledgment of the prostitute that the pregnancy was from the one she specified. They agreed to act upon this in matters of lineage, so it was similar to acknowledgment of paternity (istilhaq), except that among prostitutes there may be some who have no control in this matter, so the matter leads to the child not being attributed to anyone.

There is no doubt that fornication was forbidden with great severity upon the Muslim from the very beginning of Islam. Its punishment was prescribed during the first year after the Hijra by the revelation of Surah al-Nur, as mentioned at its beginning. 'A'isha affirmed that Islam demolished the three marriages of the Jahiliyya and kept the known marriage, but she did not specify the precise time of that demolition.

صفحة ٢٢٦

It is not conceivable that prostitution was forbidden before the revelation of this verse, since nothing was known before it in the Book and the Sunna indicating the prohibition of prostitution; and because if it had been so, the incidents that were the occasion of the verse's revelation could not have been imagined, for there is no way for those among the Muslims like them to commit a forbidden act.

Therefore the verse was revealed as a preparation for its abolition, just as the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], as a preparation for the absolute prohibition of wine. This is what the exegetes such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi followed, by the apparent wording of their expressions, though not explicitly, but by the interpretations they gave to the meanings of the verse. They interpreted the saying: ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ to mean that the condition is not intended to imply the absence of prohibition of compelling them to prostitution when their desire for chastity is absent; rather the condition came out as what is generally the case, because desire for chastity is the general state of believing slave women who were prostitutes, since they loved abstinence; or because the case that was the occasion of revelation involved the desire for chastity.

The purpose of mentioning the qualifier is to denounce the state of prostitution in Islam as being both under compulsion and under prevention from chastity. In mentioning both qualifiers there is an indication of the wisdom of its prohibition, its corruption, and the evil of earning through it.

The mention of ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ is for the state of compulsion, since their compelling them cannot be conceived except while they refuse, and the usual reason for refusal is the desire for chastity. This is the interpretation of the majority, and they relied, in the factor prompting the interpretation, on the consensus of the Community upon the prohibition of prostitution, whether the consensus was based on this verse or on another proof upon whose content the consensus was formed. There is no dispute that the consensus is on the prohibition of prostitution, but the question is whether its prohibition was by this verse.

I say: the mention of compulsion proceeds from considering the circumstances of the case that was the occasion of revelation.

What appears from the words of Ibn al-'Arabi is that some scholars inclined to regard the condition in the verse as evidence for the prohibition of compelling slave women to prostitution, with the qualification of their desire for chastity.

صفحة ٢٢٧

It may be that the verse was a preparation for the absolute prohibition of prostitution, so that it became forbidden for the Muslims to compel their slave women to prostitution, because Muslim slave women dislike that and there is no benefit to them in it. Then it was not long before it was prohibited absolutely, as the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari indicates: "that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the mahr of the prostitute," for the prohibition of taking its earnings requires the nullification of prostitution.

This possibility may be supported by the saying of the Exalted after it: ﴿And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, as will come.

In the tafsir of al-Asfahani: It was said: the prohibition came against compulsion, not against prostitution, because the hadd for fornication was revealed after this. This implies that the one who holds this view places the beginning of the surah as revealed after these verses, and this is not known.

His saying: ﴿that you may seek the goods of worldly life﴾ is connected to (do not compel), meaning: do not compel them for this reason. He mentioned this reason to add to the denunciation, like the mention of ﴿if they desire chastity﴾.

"The goods of worldly life" is the wage that masters earn from their slave women, which is also called the mahr.

As for the saying: ﴿And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, it is explicit that it is a ruling concerning the future, since it is a present-tense verb within the conditional clause, and it is explicit that it is a pardon for compulsion.

What this statement comprises has two sides: the side of the compellers and the side of the compelled (mukrahat, with a fatha on the ra'). As for the side of the compellers, it does not come to mind that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward them after He forbade them from compulsion, since there is no parallel to such glad tidings in the Qur'an.

As for the compelled slave women, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to them. This assumed reading was recited by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, as narrated from them, and from al-Hasan, who used to say:

صفحة ٢٢٨

"Forgiving and Merciful to them, by Allah, to them, by Allah." They took the benefit of this statement to be that Allah excused the compelled women because of the compulsion, and that it is of the kind of His saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 115]. On this basis it is an allusion to a threat against those who compel slave women to prostitution.

Some exegetes supposed the omitted element to be the pronoun of (min) in the conditional, meaning: Forgiving and Merciful to him, and they interpreted this as meaning after he desists and repents, but this interpretation is remote.

His saying "then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" is the indicator of the response of the condition, since the response was omitted for brevity and dispensed with by mentioning its cause, which encompasses it and other than it. The implied meaning is: then there is no sin upon them, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to the like of them, from among those compelled to commit a crime.

The fa' is the binding particle of the response.

The particle (inna), in this context, indicates causation and does the work of the causal lam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 34:

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses explaining [everything], and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-conscious.﴾

The rulings and admonitions that preceded this were concluded (by this verse), affirming their benefit and usefulness, for what they contain is beneficial to people, sustains the pillar of their community, distinguishes truth from falsehood, and removes from minds the confusion of right with wrong, so that people come to know the paths of sound reasoning and correct thinking. This is a reminder of the reflection they deserve and of God's blessing upon the community in sending them down, so that they may give thanks to God as He deserves.

It describes these sent-down verses with three attributes, just as it described the surah at its opening with three attributes. The purpose of the attributes in both places is to express favour (imtinan), so this resembles the repetition of the final part at the beginning (radd al-'ajz 'ala al-sadr). The sentence ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses explaining [everything]﴾ is resumed as a concluding statement (isti'naf al-tadhyil), and the apparent rule would be that it not be joined by a conjunction, since the nature of a concluding or resumptive statement is disjunction, as its sister verse that follows shortly after it is disjoined by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly sent down verses explaining [everything]﴾ [al-Nur: 46]. He departed from disjunction to conjunction because this is the conclusion of the legislations and rulings for whose causes the surah was revealed. It has been interspersed with a similar concluding statement twice before this, by His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We sent down in it clear verses﴾ [al-Nur: 1], then His saying: ﴿And Allah makes the verses clear to you, and Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾ [al-Nur: 18], then His saying here: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses explaining [everything]﴾. Each of these concluding statements adds to the one before it. The first adds with His saying: ﴿Allah makes the verses clear to you﴾ [al-Nur: 58], for it conveyed that the clarification of the verses is for the benefit of the community. What is here adds with His saying: ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-conscious﴾. Each addition from these two therefore required conjunction, because of the difference that arose between it and its sister, and each one is regarded as a conjunction upon its counterpart. Thus the whole surah is described with three attributes, and what in this surah contained rulings on slander, the hadd punishments, and what leads to them or to what is close to them of the matters of association between men and women, is described with three attributes. So His saying here: ﴿verses explaining [everything]﴾ corresponds to His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We sent down in it clear verses﴾ [al-Nur: 1]. His saying: ﴿an example from those who passed away before you﴾ corresponds to His saying at the beginning of the surah: "(And We imposed it)", according to what we have chosen in explaining that as meaning determination and measurement, because in illustration (tamthil) there is a measuring and a depiction of meanings by their like, and in that is a disclosure of realities. His saying: "(﴿and an admonition for the God-conscious﴾)" corresponds to His saying at its beginning: "so that you may remember."

The verses (ayat) are the sentences of the Qur'an; for because of the perfection of their eloquence and their inimitability, they rendered the obstinate unable to produce the like of them, and they were proofs that it is speech sent down from Allah.

The speech was introduced with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq) for the sake of giving it importance. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (mubayyanat) with a fatha on the ya' in the form of the passive participle. The meaning is that Allah made them clear and explained them. The rest read it with a kasra on the ya', meaning that the verses made clear the purposes for which they were sent down. The two readings' meanings are mutually implicating, so there is no difference between the import of this verse and the import of its counterpart: ﴿And We sent down in it clear verses﴾ [al-Nur: 1] at the beginning of the surah, because "clear" (bayyinat) means evident, that is, evident in indication and conveyance.

The "example" (mathal) means a counterpart or a likeness. It may also be intended to mean a remarkable state.

The "min" in His saying ﴿from those who passed away﴾ is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), that is, an example arising and taking shape from those who passed away. What is meant is the emergence of resemblance. In the speech there is an elision of a modifier which the context indicates, its estimate being: "from the likes of those who passed away before you." Elision of the modifier in such a context is an eloquent method, as al-Nabigha said:

"And I have feared, until my fear has not exceeded
That of a ram on the mountain of al-Mutara, which is wise."

He meant: "beyond the fear of a ram."

"Those who passed away before you" are the nations who preceded the Muslims, and he meant: from the likes of my righteous one who passed away before you.

This example is the story of the slander (al-ifk), which is the counterpart of the story of Yusuf and the story of Maryam in the fabrication of falsehood against the righteous, who were innocent.

The admonition (maw'izah) is a speech or a condition by which a person recognizes the places of slipping, and so he refrains from committing their like. It has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying: ﴿an admonition and an explanation of all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 145] in Surat al-A'raf.

The admonitions of these verses from the beginning of the surah are many, such as His saying: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2], and His saying: ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾ [al-Nur: 12] and the verses following, and His saying: ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever﴾ [al-Nur: 17].

The God-conscious (al-muttaqun) are those who guard themselves (yattaquna), that is, who avoid what they have been forbidden.

**[p. 231]**

﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth.﴾

He follows the favor of specific guidance, concerning specific rulings, which is implied by His saying, ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing [the truth]﴾ [al-Nur: 34], with a favor: that Allah is the One who creates the foundations of general guidance and the true knowledge for all people, by sending His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth. Along with this favor comes an announcement of the greatness, glory, and all-encompassing knowledge and power of Allah, exalted is He.

What appears to me is that the clause ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ is parenthetical, placed between the preceding clause and the clause ﴿The example of His light is like a niche﴾. The clause ﴿The example of His light is like a niche﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing [the truth]﴾ [al-Nur: 34], as will come in its explanation. So the clause ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ serves as a preparation for the clause ﴿The example of His light is like a niche﴾.

The reason the clause ﴿The example of His light is like a niche﴾ comes after ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing [the truth]﴾ [al-Nur: 34] is that the verses of the Qur'an are light. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174] in Surat al-Nisa', and He says: ﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 15] in Surat al-'Uqud. So His saying ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a comprehensive expression for many meanings that follow the meanings of light in its general usage in speech.

The placement of this clause is remarkable in several respects, and it is a transition from the explanation of rulings to another purpose of guidance and the various forms of admonition and proof.

Light (al-nur): its true meaning is brightness and radiance. It is a non-derived noun (ism jamid) denoting a meaning, so it is like a verbal noun (masdar), because we find it to be the root from which verbs of illumination are derived. Thus, it resembles verbs derived from non-derived nouns, such as اسْتَنْوَقَ الجَمَلُ (the camel became like a she-camel), since the verb أنارَ (to illuminate) is like the verb أفْلَسَ (to become bankrupt), and the form فَعَلَ اسْتَنارَ (to become luminous) is like the form اسْتَحْجَرَ الطِّينُ (the clay hardened into stone). For this reason, describing Allah with it is like describing Him with a verbal noun or a generic noun in conveying emphasis, because it names an essence among essences, and it and the verbal noun are equal in the attribute. Thus, the meaning of ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ is that the heavens and the earth become manifest from Him. The word "light" here can refer to several meanings that are likened to light, and applying the name light to them is established in the language.

So describing Allah, exalted is He, as light is necessarily a figurative (majazi) use of the word light, by the evidence of the foundational creed of Islam that Allah, exalted is He, is not a body, a substance, or an accident. No one among the people of the Arabic tongue doubts this. The true meaning of light cannot be free of being either a substance or an accident. The most fitting of the usages of light in the language for this context is that it means the clarity of matters whose nature is to be hidden from human perception and to be confused, so that guidance to them becomes rare. Applying it to that is a metaphor, with the relation of causation in the senses and the intellect as its linking element.

Al-Ghazali said in his well-known treatise Mishkat al-Anwar (The Niche of Lights): "Light is that manifest thing by which every manifestation occurs," i.e., that by which things are revealed, that to which they are revealed, and that from which they are revealed. It is the true light, and there is no light above it. Making His name "the Light" indicates His transcendence above nonexistence, and indicates bringing all things out of the darkness of nonexistence into the manifestation of existence. This leads to what the name Light implies of the meaning of manifestation, clarification, creation, guidance, and legislation. Ibn Barrajan al-Ishbili followed him in his commentary on the Beautiful Names, saying: "His name the Light leads to the attributes of acts." End of quotation.

As for describing the light here, it must be fitting to what precedes the verse, namely His saying ﴿We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing [the truth]﴾ [al-Nur: 34], and what follows it, namely His saying ﴿The example of His light is like a niche﴾ up to His saying ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾, and His saying after that: ﴿And whoever Allah has not granted light—for him there is no light﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. We have already pointed out that light has many usages and other applications that could be intended by describing Him, exalted is He, as light. It has appeared in several places in the Qur'an and the Hadith. So the usage in each context is interpreted according to what suits the context of the speech, and this does not follow one pattern wherever it occurs. An example is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «To You be praise; You are the light of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them». The conjunction of "and whoever is in them" indicates that what is meant by "the heavens and the earth" is their very essence, not the existents within them. Therefore, what is meant by light there must be the bestowal of existence, expressed by the term "splitting" (fatq) in His saying: ﴿that the heavens and the earth were a joined entity, and We separated them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30]. The meaning is that by His power, exalted is He, their affairs became upright.

The Illuminationist philosophers (hukama' al-ishraq) among the Muslims and the Sufi philosophers have adopted meanings from the various usages of light. The most famous of these are three: scientific proof, perfection of the soul, and that by which the luminous realms are witnessed. Shihab al-Din Yahya al-Suhrawardi alluded to these three at the beginning of his book Hayakil al-Nur (The Temples of Light) with his saying: "O Self-Subsisting, strengthen us with light, establish us upon light, and gather us toward light," as Jalal al-Din al-Dawani explained in his commentary.

Also included among these meanings is applying the word light to guidance toward righteous deeds, which is guidance (huda).

The Qur'an has used the word light for something more general than guidance, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44], and His saying: ﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought as light and guidance for the people?"﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. The conjunction of one of the two words with the other indicates that they are different. None of the meanings of the word light in these verses is suitable to be the one ascribed to Allah, exalted is He, neither literally nor figuratively. Therefore it is established that the word "light" (nur) in His saying ﴿The example of His light is like a niche﴾ is not the same as the word "light" in His saying ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. Thus "light" is a homonym (mushtarak), used in one meaning at one time and in another meaning at another time.

The best way to interpret His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ is that Allah originates everything that is described as light, especially the means of true knowledge, the established proof, and the guide to righteous deeds by which there is a good outcome in both the upper and lower worlds. This is an instance of using a homonym in all its meanings.

It is also possible that by "the heavens and the earth" is meant those in them, by way of ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. This is more eloquent than mentioning the omitted genitive (mudaf mahdhuf), because this omission gives the impression that the heavens and the earth are receptive to this light, just as the town itself bears witness to what is asked of it. This is more eloquent in indicating comprehensiveness regarding the intended meaning and more subtle in its indication. It thus encompasses instilling the true creed and guidance to righteousness. As for the guidance of humans to good and righteousness, it is evident. As for the guidance of the angels to that, it is that Allah created them upon the natural disposition (fitra) of righteousness and goodness; and that He commanded them to direct their powers toward good; and that He commanded some of them to convey guidance by conveying the laws and inspiring righteous hearts toward righteousness. These were manifestations of guidance for them and through them.

* * *

**[p. 234]**

﴿The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp. The lamp is within glass. The glass is as if it were a pearly star lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light.﴾

It appears that this clause is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing [the truth]﴾ [al-Nur: 34], since the word "verses" (ayat), and its description as "clearly showing" (mubayyinat), contain what the listener wishes to know: what the verses are and what their clarification is. So the clause is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani). The clause ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ came as a parenthetical clause between this clause and the preceding one, as a preparation for the greatness of this light which is illustrated by the niche.

Much of what the exegetes said indicates that it is an explanation of the clause ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. In that case, its position is that of an appositive ('atf al-bayan), and for this reason it was separated without a conjunction.

The pronoun in His saying "His light" (nurihi) refers to the Name of Majesty, Allah, meaning "the example of the light of Allah." By "His light" is meant either His Book or the religion He chose, meaning its example in illuminating the minds of those who are guided.

So the discourse is an illustration of the manner of Allah's guidance of the believers, in the form of a lamp surrounded by the means of strong radiance. It is therefore certainly the light of Allah. The reason the comparison was chosen with a lamp described with what accompanies it of attributes, rather than comparing His light to the rising of the sun after the darkness of night, is to complete the resemblance of the appearance being likened: that it is the state of a light appearing within darkness, which dispels that darkness within an area that is to be illuminated. Nor was it compared to the appearance of the moon rising within the darkness of the horizon, in order to complete the resemblance, because the moon appears and sets during part of the night, unlike the described lamp. Furthermore, the intent is to mention what surrounds the lamp of implements, so that the complete illustration can be accomplished by accepting the distribution of comparisons, as will come, and that is not possible with the moon.

The "example" (mathal) is the comparison of one state with another, and it was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. So the meaning of ﴿The example of His light﴾ is: the likeness of His guidance is the state of a niche... to its end. There is therefore no need to estimate "like the light of a niche," because the thing compared is the niche and what follows it.

His saying ﴿like a niche within which is a lamp﴾ means: like a lamp in a niche. He placed the niche first in mention because the thing being compared is the whole configuration. So the expression that refers to the thing compared is the entire compound beginning with "like a niche" and ending with ﴿and even if no fire touched it﴾. For this reason, the attaching of the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) to the word "niche" rather than to the word "lamp" does not imply that the word "niche" is primary in the configuration being compared, over the word "lamp." Rather, the purpose of this order is to follow the mental order in imagining this configuration for the imaginer, when the observer glimpses the emission of light, then looks at its source, sees a niche, and then a lamp appears to him within glass.

The niche, as known from the statements of the lexicographers, is a recess in a wall, like an alcove (kuwwa), but not open through; if it were open through, it would be a kuwwa. No reliable Arabic authority has any other meaning of it, and al-Raghib, the author of al-Qamus, and al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) confined themselves to this meaning. They agreed that it is an Abyssinian word which the Arabs adopted into their speech, and so it is counted among the words in the Qur'an that are not in the language of the Arabs. This occurs in Sahih al-Bukhari in what he explained of the vocabulary of Surat al-Nur.

It is reported in the tafsir of al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya from Mujahid that the niche is the pillar on whose top is the lamp-stand. In al-Tabari, also from Mujahid: the niche is the brass, i.e., a piece of it resembling the reed that is inside the lamp. In a similar sense is what he (al-Tabari) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the niche is the place of the wick. In a similar sense also is what Ibn 'Atiyya reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: the niche is the iron and lead piece in which the wick is placed inside the glass. And al-Azhari's statement: he meant the reed of the glass by which one lights the lamp, which is the place of the wick.

Al-Azhari also interpreted it this way: the reed of the glass was likened to the niche, which is the alcove, and so the name niche was applied to it.

The lamp (al-misbah): it is the name of the vessel in which oil is burned for illumination. It is one of the patterns of instrument nouns, like al-miftah (key). It is derived from the word for morning (al-subh), meaning the beginning of daylight. So the lamp is the instrument of "becoming morning" (al-isbah), i.e., illumination. When the niche is the name of the reed placed inside the lamp-stand, then the lamp is intended to mean the wick placed inside that reed.

Ibn 'Ashur's repetition of the word (al-misbah, "the lamp") instead of saying "in it is a lamp in a glass" as in His words ﴿like a niche in which is a lamp﴾ is a making-apparent (izhar) in a place where a pronoun would be expected, to draw attention to the lamp, since it is the greatest pillar of this parable. Likewise is the repetition of the word (al-zujajah, "the glass") in His words ﴿the glass, as if it were a glittering star﴾, since it is among the greatest pillars of the parable. Such repetition is called tashabuh al-atraf ("resemblance of the extremities") in the science of badi' (rhetorical embellishment), and they recited on it the verse of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah in praise of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf:

When al-Hajjaj descends upon a sick land,
he traces its deepest disease and heals it.
He heals it from the lethal illness that is in it
a youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink.
He gives it drink and quenches it with the draught of his buckets,
the blood of men who milk its udders.

Among the things in which the verse excels is that this repetition does not occur more than twice.

Al-zujajah (glass) is the name of a vessel made of glass. It is called zujajah because it is a piece made of glass (al-zujaj), with the zay vowelled with a damma and the two jims lightened, with the ta' marbutah attached to the end of the word; this ha' is the sign of the singular of a collective noun (ism jam'). It is as though they treated glass in the manner of collective nouns, like tamr ("dates"), naml ("ants") and nakhl ("palms"). They used to make vessels of glass for wine, and lamp-holders for lighting with oil lamps, because glass is transparent: it does not block the light of the lamp, nor does it hide the colour and clarity of the wine from the drinker, so that he may see it.

[Page 237]

Glass (al-zujaj) is a kind of fired clay made from a specific paste of sand that is found in the earth's strata, and it is not beach sand (raml al-shuttut). This paste is called in the terminology of chemistry silica (silika). It is mixed with parts of the ash of a plant called in chemistry soda (sudah), and called by the Arabs al-ghasul, which is what they use to make soap. To these two is added a part of lime (al-kils al-jir) and of potash (al-butas) or lead oxide, and that clay becomes fluid. It is put into the fire and melted in a special furnace of very great heat until it liquefies and its parts mix together. Then it is taken out of the furnace in pieces according to what the craftsman wants to make from it. At that point it is soft, resembling sweets, and so it is then capable of stretching and of swelling when blown into with an iron tube which the craftsman places in his mouth, connected to the piece of melted clay. He blows into it, and when the air of the breath enters it, it expands and takes on a shape as it happens; the craftsman then manipulates it, shaping it into the form he desires. From it he makes vessels of various shapes: cups, bottles, large and small flasks, wine decanters, and lamp-oil containers, which surpass all others in that they do not block the lamp's light and increase its radiance.

Glass was already known to the ancient Phoenicians and to the Copts from about the thirtieth century BC; then the Arabs came to know it, calling it al-zujaj and al-qawarir.

Bashshar said:

Be gentle with 'Amr when you move his lineage,
for he is an Arab, of the qawarir (glass).

The Israelites knew it in the time of Solomon, and Solomon made from it a floor in the courtyard of his palace, as occurs in His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "It is a palace paved with glass"﴾ [al-Naml: 44]. The Greeks also knew it in antiquity. Among the sayings of the sage Diogenes the Greek: "The crowns of kings are like glass; ruin rushes toward them." The Arabs called glass billawr, on the pattern of sinnawr and of tannur. Its craft was famous among the people of al-Sham (Syria). Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "(in a glass)" means a lamp of bright white Syrian glass.

In the third Christian century, the people of Venice (al-Bunduqiyyah) became famous for the fineness of its manufacture; they coloured it and decorated it with gold, and Venice has remained to this day the source of fine glasswork of various shapes and colours, which connoisseurs vie to acquire. Likewise the lands of Bohemia in the land of Hungary, for the quality of the sand used in their country.

[Page 238]

Among the most useful applications of glass is making panes to place over the windows and casements, to keep winds, winter cold and rain away from the inhabitants of houses, while not blocking light from them. The invention of using these panes occurred in the third century of the Christian era, but its benefit was delayed for a long time despite the need for it, because of the difficulty of using it, its quick breakage in transport and the abundance of its cost. For this reason it was first used in windows only in the lands where it was made, and it remained for a long time specific to the houses of kings and the wealthy.

Al-kawkab means "the star". Al-durri, with a damma on the dal and a shadda on the ya' (taḥtiyyah), is in the reading of the majority, and is the singular of al-darari, which are the bright shining stars such as Venus and Jupiter, attributed to the pearl (al-durr) in clarity and whiteness of colour. The ya' in it is the ya' of nisbah (relative attribution), and it is the nisbah of resemblance, as in the words of Tarafah describing his mount:

A camel-like, strong-necked (she-camel) ... (the line)

meaning: like a camel in the greatness of its body and in strength. And their proverb: "He spent a night of Nabighan sleeplessness", meaning like the sleeplessness of al-Nabighah in his verse:

So I spent the night as though a small (serpent) had attacked me
... (the verses)

Al-Hariri said: "So I spent a night of Nabighan (sleeplessness) and Ya'qubi sorrows." (al-Maqamah 27).

From this is their saying: "wardi in colour", meaning like the colour of the rose. And the pearl is struck as a proverb for brilliance and purity. Labid said:

And she shines in the face of darkness, illuminating,
like a pearl of the sea whose string has been drawn out.

It was said: al-kawkab al-durri is a proper name by predominance for the planet Venus.

[Page 239]

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (dirri'un) with a kasra on the dal and a long vowel on the ra', on the pattern of shirrib, from al-dar' which is repelling, because it repels darkness with its light; or because some of its rays repel others in what the observer imagines.

Hamzah, Abu Bakr from 'Asim read with a damma on the dal and a long vowel on the ra', also from al-dar', on the basis that its form is fa'il, which is a rare pattern in Arabic speech, but according to Sibawayh it is among the patterns of their speech; and from it are 'ulliyyah, surriyyah and dhurriyyah, all three with a damma on the first letter.

He took the path of comparison (tashbih) in expressing the extreme clarity of the glass, because it is more concise in wording and clearer in description. This is a single comparison within the parable, and it has no share in the parable itself.

The clause ﴿it is kindled from a blessed tree, an olive﴾ and so on is in the position of a description (sifah) of (misbah, "lamp").

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read (yuqadu, "is kindled") with a ya' (taḥtiyyah) at its beginning, vowelled with a damma, followed by a sukun on the waw, and with a fatha on the qaf, in the passive, meaning it is kindled by a kindler; so the clause is a circumstantial (hal) relating to (misbah).

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim and Khalaf read (tawaqqadu) with a ta' (fawqiyyah) at its beginning, vowelled with a fatha, a fatha on the waw, a shadda on the qaf vowelled with a fatha, and a damma on the dal, as the present tense of tawaqqada, from which one of the two ta's has been dropped; its original form is tatawaqqadu. It is either a description or a circumstantial clause relating to (mishkah), or to (zujajah), or to the mentioned items, which are the niche, the lamp and the glass, meaning it shines. Attributing the kindling to it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli).

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it like the reading of Hamzah and those with him, but with a fatha on the dal, as a past-tense verb, a circumstantial clause or a description of (misbah).

Al-iqad is the placing of fuel (waqud), which is what is added to a burning fire so that its flame grows strong; and what is meant here is what the lamp is supplied with of oil.

In the form of the present tense, according to the reading of the majority, there is the indication that its kindling is continuous, that is, it is never extinguished or put out. According to the reading of Ibn Kathir and those with him, in the past tense, it indicates that its fuel is established and assured.

[Page 240]

The tree is mentioned by the name of its genus, and then (zaytunah, "olive") is substituted for it, which is the name of its species, because of the vagueness that is followed by detail, in concern that this should be firmly fixed in the mind. The olive is described as blessed (mubarakah) because of its abundant benefit: its fruit is eaten, and its oil likewise; its oil is used for light, enters into medicines and the remedying of many matters; and its wood is used, and it is the best wood, since it contains oily substance. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. And benefit is derived from the good air of its groves.

It has been said that its blessing is because it is one of the trees of the land of al-Sham, and al-Sham is a blessed land from the time of Abraham, peace be upon him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 71], meaning the land of al-Sham.

The description of the olive as "blessed" on this view is an explanatory description (wasf kashif). It may also be a restrictive description (wasf mukhassis) for (zaytunah), meaning a tree possessing blessing, that is, growth and abundance of fruit among the olive trees; so the mention of this attribute serves to beautify the object of comparison (al-mushabbah bihi), so that from it there results an embellishment of the thing compared (al-mushabbah), as in the words of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

It was split, with water of a spring (?) ... clear, in a valley that dawned and was dyed (?)
The winds clear away its impurities, and he has poured it out
from a cloud, white and fine-lined.

For his saying "wa-afrathahu" ("and he has poured it out") and what follows does not add to the water's clarity, but it is a state that beautifies it in the listener's estimation.

His words: ﴿neither eastern nor western﴾ are a description of (zaytunah). The negating particle (la) enters into both descriptions, so that it becomes like a letter of spelling belonging to the word that follows it. For this reason it has no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab), unlike the definite article (al-) which al-Damamini posed as a riddle in his words:

I challenged you that you should tell what two names are,
whose first (letter) is inflected in the second.
It is always indeclinable in every state;
there it is, plain to the observer as to the eye.

It serves to express the quality of being characterized by the negation of each description and the conjunction over each description of its opposite, because the intended meaning is a quality intermediate between the two negated descriptions, since the two descriptions are opposites, following the manner of the saying: "The pomegranate is sweet-sour." The conjunction here is of descriptions

[Page 241]

like His words: ﴿neither to these nor to those﴾ [al-Nisa': 143], and the saying of the fourth woman in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihamah: neither hot nor cold," meaning intermediate between heat and cold; and the saying of al-'Ajjaj describing a wild ass:

He gurgled quietly in his throat and gasped,
until one says he brays, yet he did not bray.

The meaning is: it is an olive tree whose direction is between the direction of the east and the direction of the west, so it is denied that it is eastern and denied that it is western. This usage is of the type of kinayah (allusion), because the intended meaning is a necessary consequence of the meaning, not its explicit sense. But when the two negated matters are not opposites, their negation does not imply more than the negation of their occurrence, as in His words: ﴿and a shade of black smoke, neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43], and the saying of the first woman among the women in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is the meat of a camel on the top of a mountain: neither easy to climb nor fat enough to be carried away."

Know that this usage occurs only in the conjunction of negated nouns. As for the conjunction of negated verbs, it is a conjunction of clauses, as in ﴿so he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31], and his saying (ﷺ): "She neither fed it nor left it to eat from the creeping things of the earth."

Know also that this has occurred only with the negation by la. For this reason al-Hariri was able to give the olive tree the epithet "la wa-la" ("neither-nor") in his words in the forty-sixth maqamah: "Blessed are you, O one of ṭalā' (fresh dates)..." Hmm, as blessed is "la wa-la"; that is, the tree of which God said concerning it: ﴿neither eastern nor western﴾.

Then it is possible that the meaning of ﴿neither eastern nor western﴾ is that it grows in a place between the east and the west of the lands of the Arabs, and that is the Syrian lands; and it has been said that the original home of the olive tree is the land of al-Sham. It is also possible that the meaning is that the side of that tree, among the olive trees surrounding it, is a position other than the rising and the setting of the sun, namely that it faces the south; that is, nothing blocks it from the southern direction, and that is more beneficial for the life of the tree and the goodness of its fruit. Thus its oil is the finest oil, and when it is finer it burns more brightly; therefore there follows the clause ﴿its oil would almost shine forth﴾, which is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

[Page 242]

The clause ﴿even if no fire had touched it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to (zaytiha, "its oil").

Zayt (oil): the extract of olive seeds and whatever resembles it of every oily extract, such as sesame oil and sesame-seed (julјulan) oil. It is a foodstuff. For this reason, zakat is obligatory on olive oil when its olive yield reaches the nisab of five awsuq, and likewise the zakat on sesame and julјulan oil.

Law (lau) here is wasliyyah (the "even if" particle). The implied meaning is: it almost glows in every state, even in a state in which no fire has touched it.

This is a comparison that reaches the utmost clarity. Although it is a comparison of one state (hay'ah) with another state, it is also one in which the individual comparisons of the parts of the compound image are matched with the individual parts of the compound image compared to it. That is the highest degree of the figurative comparison (al-tashbih al-tamthili) in the art of eloquence (balaghah).

Since the intended purpose is to compare a state with a state, and a compound with a compound, it is fitting for the particle of comparison to enter upon some of what indicates a part of the compound, so that it serves as an indicator that the intended comparison is the compound one. Had the intended comparison been only the guidance, he would have said: "His light is like a lamp in a niche..." and so on to the end.

The light is the knowledge of the truth as it is, acquired from the revelation of Allah, which is the Qur'an. It is compared to the lamp enclosed by everything that increases its light in spreading and shining.

The clause "light upon light" is a resumptive (mustanʾafah) clause, indicating that the purpose of the totality of the parts of the figurative compound here is to reach the clarification that the state compared to it has reached the limit of multiplication of the means of illumination; for the niche, the lamp, the pure glass, and the clear oil all cooperate in it. When the lamp is in a niche, its ray is confined within it and does not spread, so it is brighter for it than if it were in a house. When it is placed in a clear glass, its light is multiplied, and when its oil is pure and clear, it gives more brightness. Thus there is represented the condition of the religion or the revealed Book from Allah, in its clarity and the speed of its spreading among people, by the condition of the bursting forth of the lamp's light and its spreading in what surrounds it of causes of the strength of its ray and its spreading in the direction illuminated by it.

So his saying "light" (nur) is the predicate of a deleted subject, indicated by his saying: "The likeness of His light is like a niche..." to the end; that is, this which has been mentioned, by which the truth has been likened, is "light upon light."

"Upon" ('ala) is for figurative elevation, which is support and cooperation. The meaning: it is light repeated and multiplied. I have already pointed out that this figurative comparison is capable of distributing the comparison over all the parts of both sides of the image, such that each part of the compared state resembles a part of the state compared to it, and that is the highest form of figurative comparison.

The niche resembles in it what is in the divine guidance of the firmness of certainty and the encompassing of indication over what is indicated without doubt or break, and the protection of the lamp from extinguishing, along with what surrounds the Qur'an of its preservation by Allah in His saying: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian" [al-Hijr: 9].

The meanings of the guidance of Islamic direction resemble the lamp in giving insight and clarification, and the explanation of realities from that guidance.

Its safety from doubt and confusion reaching it resembles the glass in making clear the condition of what it contains, as He said: "And We have certainly sent down to you verses that make things clear" [al-Nur: 34].

The revelation by which Allah conveyed the realities of the religion, from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, resembles the blessed tree that yields fruit from which the indications of guidance are extracted.

The tolerance of Islam and the absence of hardship from it resemble the tree's position between the two extremes of the horizon: it is a middle course between harsh severity that causes distress and excessive leniency.

The continuity and renewal of that guidance resemble the kindling (al-iqad).

The Prophet's ﷺ teaching of his community by explaining the Qur'an and legislating rulings resembles the pure oil by which insight is attained, and it is, along with that, clear and easy to take, almost not needing the insistence of a teacher.

The Prophet's ﷺ standing up for teaching, peace be upon him, resembles the touch of fire to the lamp, and this hints at the continuity of this guidance.

Just as His saying "from a tree" hints at the need for the scholars of religion to exert effort (ijtihad) in extracting its guidance over the passage of times; for extracting oil from the fruit of the tree depends on pressing the fruit, and that is deduction (istinbat).

* * *

"Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah presents parables for the people, and Allah is Knowing of all things."

These three clauses are parenthetical (mu'taridah) or a concluding remark (tadhil) to the figurative comparison. The meaning: to dispel amazement at the failure of many people to be guided by the light that Allah sent down, which is the Qur'an and Islam; for if Allah does not will the guidance of someone, He creates him and fashions him upon stubbornness and disbelief.

And that Allah presents parables to people, hoping they will be reminded by them: among them are those who take heed from them and are guided, and among them are those who turn away and persist in their misguidance. But the nature of those parables is that whoever has a seal upon his heart will not be guided by them.

The clause "and Allah is Knowing of all things" is a concluding remark (tadhil) for the content of the two clauses before it; that is, nothing escapes His knowledge. Among that is His knowledge of who is receptive to guidance and who is insistent upon his error. This is an allusion (ta'rid) to promise for the first and warning for the second.

[Page 245]

The exegetes differed over what the prepositional phrase in his saying, "in houses" (fi buyutin), is connected to. It was said: his saying "in houses" is part of the parable (tamthil), meaning that "in houses" is connected to something that precedes it. It was said that it is connected to his saying "it is kindled" (yuqadu), meaning: the lamp is kindled in houses. It was also said that it is an attribute of "a niche" (mishkat), meaning: a niche in houses, and what comes between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraud). The plural "houses" (buyut) is used although "niche" (mishkat) and "lamp" (misbah) are singular, because what is meant by them is the category (jins), so singular and plural become equivalent.

Then it was said: "houses" is meant as mosques. This does not hold, since there were no lamps in the mosques of the Muslims at that time. Lamps were introduced into Islamic mosques during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and 'Ali said to him: "May God illuminate your resting place, O son of al-Khattab, as you have illuminated our mosque." It is also narrated that Tamim al-Dari lit the Prophet's Mosque with lamps that he brought from Syria, but Tamim embraced Islam in the ninth year, that is, after the revelation of this verse. It was also said: the houses are the mosques of Bayt al-Maqdis, which at that time were churches (biya') of the Christians. This is because what is mentioned of the description of the houses and what happens in them, which gives them beauty in the souls of the believers.

*"Upon a path with no landmarks by which one can be guided."*

*"It illuminates the darkness in the evening, as if it were the beacon of a devoted monk at dusk."*

[Page 246]

He also said:

*"Its brightness shines, or the lamps of a monk, [burning] olive oil in a twisted wick."*

Al-Salit is oil, meaning pouring oil onto the wick. In that state it gives more light. They would be guided by these at night on their journeys. Imru' al-Qays also said:

*"I ascended toward it while the stars were like lamps of monks kindled for returning travellers."*

Al-qufal is the plural of qafil, meaning those returning from their journeys.

It was also said that what is meant by "raising" is a spiritual elevation, which is honour and exemption from defects. Then "permission" would mean "command."

Furthermore, this is far from the aims of the Qur'an, especially the Medinan part of it, because the praise of these men is extensive, and it is followed by His saying: ﴿that God may reward them for the best of what they did﴾.

This abstraction is then a return to the true structure indicating the figure compared, like the saying of Tarafa:

*"Among the tribe is a dark-skinned man who shakes off the lotion from his hair, with the glimmer of two strands of pearls and emerald."*

Along with this, the verse includes an explanation of what was summarized in the phrase "the parable of His light." For this reason the verse is more eloquent than Tarafa's line, because the verse combines abstraction and explanation, while Tarafa's line has only abstraction.

The implied sense is: men glorify God in houses. His saying "therein" is an emphasis of "in houses" to increase concern for them. In this there is an honouring of the mosques and the performance of prayer and remembrance in them, as in the hadith: "The prayer of one of you in the mosque, that is, in congregation, exceeds his prayer in his house by twenty-seven degrees."

What is meant by "the morning" (al-ghuduww) is the time of morning, which is dawn, because it is the time when people go out to attend to their affairs.

"Asal" is the plural of asil, which is the end of the day. It was discussed at the end of al-A'raf and in Surat al-Ra'd.

What is meant by "men" are the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and those who were like them in attachment to the mosques.

The specification of glorification to men on this view is because they were the predominant ones in the mosques, as in the hadith: "...and a man whose heart is attached to the mosques..."

In my view it is also permissible that "in houses" is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), with "men" as the subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), arising from His saying: ﴿God guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. [Page 247]

Trade (tijara) is bringing goods for profit in selling them, while sale (bay') is more general, being that one sells what one needs the price of.

*"Let Yazid be wept for, the one humbled by quarrel, and the one entangled in what the calamities bring down."*

The turning of hearts and eyes is their agitation from their places out of fear and dread, as a person turns in his place. It has been discussed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes﴾ [al-An'am: 110] in Surat al-An'am. [Page 248]
