Al-Salit is oil, meaning pouring oil onto the wick. In that state it gives more light. They would be guided by these at night on their journeys. Imru' al-Qays also said:

*"I ascended toward it while the stars were like lamps of monks kindled for returning travellers."*

Al-qufal is the plural of qafil, meaning those returning from their journeys.

It was also said that what is meant by "raising" is a spiritual elevation, which is honour and exemption from defects. Then "permission" would mean "command."

Furthermore, this is far from the aims of the Qur'an, especially the Medinan part of it, because the praise of these men is extensive, and it is followed by His saying: ﴿that God may reward them for the best of what they did﴾.

In my view, the more apparent reading is that His saying "in houses" is a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr), which is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "His light" in His saying: ﴿The parable of His light is like a niche﴾ [al-Nur: 35], etc., indicating that "light" (nur) in the saying "the parable of His light" refers to the Qur'an. This circumstantial clause is then an abstraction (tajrid) of the allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya) by mentioning what is suitable to the figure compared, namely the figure of receiving the Qur'an, reciting it, and reflecting upon it among the Muslims, which is indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No people gather in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, except that tranquillity descends upon them, mercy covers them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him." This abstraction is then a return to the true structure indicating the figure compared, like the saying of Tarafa:

*"Among the tribe is a dark-skinned man who shakes off the lotion from his hair, with the glimmer of two strands of pearls and emerald."*

Along with this, the verse includes an explanation of what was summarized in the phrase "the parable of His light." For this reason the verse is more eloquent than Tarafa's line, because the verse combines abstraction and explanation, while Tarafa's line has only abstraction.

It is also possible that "in houses" is not connected to what precedes it, and that it is the beginning of a new independent sentence, and that the prepositional phrase is connected to his saying "glorifies Him therein." Placing the prepositional phrase first serves to emphasise those houses and to create suspense about what the prepositional phrase depends on, which is the glorification and those who perform it. The implied sense is: men glorify God in houses. His saying "therein" is an emphasis of "in houses" to increase concern for them. In this there is an honouring of the mosques and the performance of prayer and remembrance in them, as in the hadith: "The prayer of one of you in the mosque, that is, in congregation, exceeds his prayer in his house by twenty-seven degrees."

What is meant by "the morning" (al-ghuduww) is the time of morning, which is dawn, because it is the time when people go out to attend to their affairs.

"Asal" is the plural of asil, which is the end of the day. It was discussed at the end of al-A'raf and in Surat al-Ra'd.

What is meant by "men" are the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and those who were like them in attachment to the mosques.

The specification of glorification to men on this view is because they were the predominant ones in the mosques, as in the hadith: "...and a man whose heart is attached to the mosques..."

In my view it is also permissible that "in houses" is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), with "men" as the subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), arising from His saying: ﴿God guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. So the questioner asks himself about specifying some of those whom God has guided to His light, and it is said: "men in houses." The men are the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the houses are the mosques of the Muslims and other houses of prayer in the land of Islam, including the Prophet's Mosque and the Mosque of Quba' in Medina, and the Mosque of Juwathā in Bahrain.

The meaning of ﴿neither trade nor sale distracts them﴾ is that trade and sale do not preoccupy them from the prayers and their times in the mosques. There is therefore nothing in the statement that they do not trade or sell at all.

[Page 247]

Trade (tijara) is bringing goods for profit in selling them, while sale (bay') is more general, being that one sells what one needs the price of.

Al-Jumhur read "yusabbihu" with a kasra on the ba' and the verb in the active voice, with "rijal" as its subject. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read with a fatha on the ba', in the passive voice. Then the deputy subject (na'ib al-fa'il) is one of the three prepositional phrases, namely ﴿for Him therein in the morning﴾, and "rijal" is the subject of a verb omitted from a resumptive sentence. What indicates the omitted verb is the word "yusabbihu," as if it were said: "Who glorifies Him?" So it is said: "Men glorify Him." This is like the saying of Nahshal ibn Hari, lamenting his brother Yazid:

*"Let Yazid be wept for, the one humbled by quarrel, and the one entangled in what the calamities bring down."*

The clauses ﴿neither trade nor sale distracts them﴾ and ﴿they fear﴾ are two attributes of "rijal," meaning: these things do not preoccupy them from performing what was obligatory upon them of fear of God, and ﴿the establishment of prayer﴾, etc. This is an allusion to the hypocrites.

"Iqam" (establishing) is a verbal noun of the form if'al. It is a defective-middle root (mu'talla al-'ayn), so the vowel of its middle was transferred to the preceding sound consonant, and the weak letter was changed to an alif. However, most of its counterparts are accompanied at the end by the feminine ta' marbuta, such as idama and istiqama. The verbal noun of iqam came without the ta' in some places, as here. The meaning of the establishment of prayer was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara.

"Yawman" in His saying "they fear a day" is in the accusative as a direct object, not as an adverb of time by implying a noun, meaning: they fear its terrors.

The turning of hearts and eyes is their agitation from their places out of fear and dread, as a person turns in his place. It has been discussed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes﴾ [al-An'am: 110] in Surat al-An'am. The purpose of their fear is acting for what brings success on that day, as His saying indicates: ﴿that God may reward them for the best of what they did﴾.

[Page 248]

His saying ﴿that God may reward them for the best of what they did﴾ is connected to "they fear," meaning their fear was the cause for reward for their deeds that arose from that fear.

"The increase from His bounty" is the increase in the reward of the monks if they believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) when his call reaches them, in accordance with the authentic hadith that they will have two rewards. Or it is the increase in the virtue of prayer in mosques if the houses are meant as the mosques of Islam.

His saying "God provides for whom He wills without reckoning" is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for "that God may reward them." The concluding effect has been achieved by the generality contained in "whom He wills," meaning: they are among those for whom God wills the increase.

"Hisab" (reckoning) here means specification (tahdid), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37] in Surat Al 'Imran. As for His saying: ﴿a reward from your Lord, a sufficient gift﴾ [al-Naba': 36], it means determination and preparation, for the sake of showing concern for them.

**[Page 251]**

When the discussion of the deeds of the God-conscious believers and their recompense had come, through His words, exalted is He, ﴿There glorify Him therein, in the mornings and the evenings, men﴾ [al-Nur: 36], up to His words, ﴿that God may recompense them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty; and God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [al-Nur: 38], He followed that with its opposite, the condition of the deeds of the disbelievers, which they reckon to be acts of devotion before God, though they are of no benefit to them whatsoever. This follows the Qur'an's usual practice of coupling glad tidings with warning, and the reverse of this, as in His words, ﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting-place. But those who feared their Lord, for them are gardens﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197], and so on. Thus the introduction of the condition of the deeds of the disbelievers is like the introduction of one narrative after another. Perhaps the polytheists, when they heard what God had promised the believers of reward for righteous deeds,

**[Page 252]**

would say: "We too maintain the Sacred Mosque, circumambulate, feed the poor, give drink to the pilgrims and host the guest," as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿Have you made the providing of water to the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in God and the Last Day?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19]. They were counting these as deeds of goodness. These verses therefore nullified their reckoning. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. We have already informed you that most of this surah was revealed after the Hijrah, at the time when the polytheists were tracking the news of the Muslims in their migrations and spying on what of the Qur'an was revealed.

The sentence is a fresh, independent beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i, "a resumptive opening"). (And those who disbelieved) is the subject, and its predicate is the sentence (their deeds are like a mirage) and so on. The subject was made to be something indicating the persons of the disbelievers, and then a second subject, namely (their deeds), was built upon it. The deeds of those who disbelieved were not made the subject at the outset, because opening with mention of "those who disbelieved" carries an element of arousing curiosity to know what will be mentioned of their affairs, so that it becomes firmly fixed in the soul, and so that it becomes apparent that those who disbelieved have a share in the simile, such that the likened thing is not solely their deeds.

In the use of the relative pronoun with its relative clause there is an indication of the reason for the predicate's construction, namely that it is a consequence of their disbelief in God. Moreover, the designation "those who disbelieved" may have come to be applied predominantly to the polytheists of Makkah, so that opening the speech with this description is an indication that it nullifies something the disbelievers believed in. Accordingly, the comparison of the disbelievers and their deeds is a figurative simile (tamthil, "an extended image-based comparison"): the state of their exertion in deeds and their eagerness to multiply them, together with their supposition that these bring them closer to God's pleasure, is likened, and then it becomes clear that these deeds do not benefit them, but rather that they meet punishment at the very time they supposed themselves to be winning. This is likened to the state of a thirsty man who sees a mirage and supposes it to be water, so he goes toward it; but when he reaches the distance he imagined to be the place of water, he finds no water, and finds there a creditor who seizes him and holds him to account for the evil deeds he had committed earlier.

Know that the likened state is composed of the sensible and the rational, whereas the state used as the comparison is a sensible state, that is, one that falls within the perception of the senses.

**[Page 253]**

The mirage (al-sarab) is a dense moisture that rises over the ground and does not ascend into the air. It arises from between the moisture of the earth and the heat of the air in hot sandy regions, so that it appears from afar as though it were water. The cause of the mirage's occurrence is the intensification of the heat of sand on level ground: the layer of air adjacent to the sand becomes intensely hot, and the air layer above it becomes less hot than the layer adjacent to it. Thus the heat decreases in each layer of air relative to the layer beneath it, and by this the density of the air increases with height above the surface of the earth. By the heat of the lowest layer, which lies next to the earth, undulating movements occur within it, so that a part of it rises to the layers above, and so on, with the result that each layer is denser than the one beneath it. When the light of the atmosphere is reflected upon those rays from near sunrise until the rest of the day, those rays take on the colour of water. So at the first appearance of light the mirage appears as though it were still water or a sea, and whenever the brightness intensifies, a shimmering appears in the mirage as though it were flowing water.

Then the term "sarab" may be applied to this undulating air throughout the day, from the morning until the afternoon. It may also be specifically designated, for the period between the beginning of the day and forenoon, by the name "al-ali" (the shimmer), and then "sarab." According to this, the view of most lexicographers and Arabs is that they are lenient in applying either of the two terms in place of the other. I have observed it in the month of November between dawn and sunrise, near a place called Umm al-'Ara'is in the regions of Tozeur, while I was on the railway train, and at first glance I thought we had come to the edge of a sea.

His words (bi-qay'ah): the bā' here is in the sense of fī ("in"), and qay'ah means "a land." The prepositional phrase is a descriptive qualifier of "sarab," and it is a clarifying (kāshif) qualifier, because the mirage only forms in a qay'ah. This is like their proverb for the humiliated person: "he is a fiqa' in a qarqar," for the fiqa' (a kind of mushroom) grows only in a qarqar. The qay'ah is level ground with no elevations, and its synonym is al-qā'ah. It has been said that qay'ah is the plural of qā'in, like jirah being the plural of jār; and perhaps the plural form has come to predominate in it until it equals the singular.

**[Page 254]**

His words, ﴿the thirsty man supposes it to be water﴾, specify the aspect of resemblance (wajh al-shabah) and contain one of the pillars of the simile, namely the thirsty man, who resembles the disbeliever who performed the deed.

(Ḥattā) here is a beginning particle (ibtida'iyyah), so it has the sense of the particle of consequence fa-. The arrival of the thirsty man at the mirage occurs by his reaching a distance that the origin of the water was estimated to be, according to what his imagination showed him, such as when he delimits it by a tree or a rock. When he reached the place where he imagined the existence of water, he did not find water, and so he realised that what had appeared to him was a mirage. This is the meaning of His words ﴿until, when he comes to it﴾, that is, when he comes to the place where he imagined that, if he reached it, he would find water. Otherwise the mirage keeps appearing to him afterwards whenever the traveller proceeds on his journey. Thus this is a parable for the nearness of the time when the disbeliever arrives at his deed, at the time of his death when he sees his place (in the Hereafter), or at the time of the Gathering.

His words (﴿he finds it to be nothing﴾) mean: he does not find what was made to appear to his eye as water; he does not find it to be anything.

The "thing" (shay') is that which exists in a manner known to people, and the mirage exists and is visible; so His words (nothing) mean nothing of water, by the indication of the context. This simile is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23].

(Idhā) here is a pure adverb of time, free of the conditional sense. The meaning is: the time of his coming to the mirage, that is, his arrival at the place.

His words ﴿and he finds God with him﴾ are part of the completion of the simile: that is, he did not find water, but he found, in the place where water is expected to be of benefit, one who, if he seized his forelock, would not let him go. That is, at the moment he supposed he had won what he sought, there came upon him one who takes him to punishment. This is the meaning of His words ﴿so He pays him his account in full﴾: that is, He gave him the recompense of his disbelief in full. The meaning of (fa-waffāhu) is that there is no lightening of it; he has laboured and exerted himself in the deed, yet finds no recompense but punishment, like one who comes to water to drink and finds someone who holds a blood-debt against him, and seizes him.

**[Page 255]**

The sentence ﴿and God is swift at reckoning﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl). "Swift" (al-sarī') is the opposite of "slow." The meaning is that He does not delay the reckoning or postpone it when its time for falling due arrives; it is general with respect to the reckoning of good and evil, and that is why it is a concluding statement.

Know that this marvellous simile is suitable for having its parts separated in the comparison, such that it resolves into similes and metaphors. The deeds of the disbelievers resemble the mirage in that they have the appearance of water but are not water. The disbeliever resembles the thirsty man in his need to benefit from his deed. So in His words ﴿the thirsty man supposes it﴾ there is an explicit metaphor (isti'ārah musarriḥah); and the disbeliever's disappointment at the reckoning resembles the thirsty man's disappointment upon coming to the mirage, so there is in it an explicit metaphor. The disbeliever's surprise at being seized and dragged away, by the soldiers of God or by God's ordaining, resembles the surprise of one who supposed he would reach water to drink, but arrived at a place where he realised there was no water, and found at the place he had reached someone lying in wait to seize or capture him. Here there is an implicit metaphor (isti'ārah makniyyah), in that he likened God's command or His angels to an enemy, and he alluded to the enemy by His words ﴿so He pays him his account in full﴾. The transitive use of the verb (wajada, "found") with the Divine Name as its object, with an elided genitive-governing noun, is the transference of a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 40:

﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is a wave, above which is a cloud: darknesses, one above another. When he holds out his hand, he can hardly see it. And whomever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light.﴾

The usage of (aw, "or") when it comes in a series of similes is that it indicates the listener's option to liken the matter to what precedes it or to what follows it. This was discussed earlier at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19] in Surat al-Baqarah, meaning with the unity of the aspect of resemblance. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Its brightness shines, or the lamps of a monk

and the saying of Labid:

Is that one, or a wild cow hunted by beasts, ∗∗∗ abandoned, its leader of the herd guiding it, its stance...

If the speech here follows that usage, the meaning is the depiction of those who disbelieved in their deeds, which they think they draw near to Allah by, with the state of the darkness of a night that covers a navigator in a deep sea of intense waves, who has plunged into that sea to reach a sought goal. Their state in their deeds resembles the state of a swimmer in the darkness of a night, in a deep sea covered by a wave that rides one upon another because of the intensity of its succession. This happens only when the winds are violent, to the extent that he can hardly see his hand, which is the nearest thing to him and the clearest in his sight; so how could he hope for salvation?

If the speech is following the option of likening with a difference in the aspect of resemblance, the meaning is the depiction of the state of those who disbelieved in their deeds which they perform while they are not believers, and the state of one who boards the sea hoping to reach a goal, and then he is in darkness by which he cannot find a path. So the aspect of resemblance is the misguidance of disbelief surrounding their deeds, which prevents them from attaining what they seek.

What favors this aspect is the appending of the simile with the words: ﴿And whomever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light﴾.

On both views, his saying "(like darknesses)" is coordinated with "(like a mirage)", and the implied meaning is: "and those who disbelieved, their deeds are like darknesses."

This simile is of the kind of likening an intellectual state to a sensible state, as one says: "I have witnessed the blackness of disbelief in the face of so-and-so."

Al-zulumat: intense darkness. The plural is used to denote what necessarily accompanies multiplicity, which is intensity; so the plural is a metonymy, because the intensity of darkness arises from the combination of several darknesses. Do you not see that the darkness between the two night prayers ('isha'ayn) is more intense than the darkness right after sunset, and the darkness of 'isha' is more intense than what precedes it?

We have mentioned earlier that the singular form zulmah does not occur in the Qur'an; see the beginning of Surat al-An'am. The meaning of their being "(in a sea)" is that their blackness is impressed upon the water of a sea,

so it becomes as if they were in the sea, like His saying: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. This was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah, where He placed the darknesses in the rainstorm.

Al-lujji is attributed to al-lujjah, and al-lujj is the deepest part of the sea, i.e., in a deep sea. The attributive form here is used to express the full possession of the quality, as in the line of Abu al-Najm:

And time with man is dawwari (turning),

meaning dawwar (constantly turning), and as in the expression: "a man who is mushrikiyy (intensely polytheistic)" and "a man who is ghilabiyy (very overpowering)," meaning strong in polytheism and abundant in overpowering.

Al-mawj: a collective noun (ism jam') for mawjah. Al-mawjah: a quantity that rises from the water of a sea or river above the surface of its water due to the agitation of its surface by a wind blowing from one side, pushing it toward the shore. Its origin is the verbal noun of: maja al-bahr, i.e., the sea was agitated, and what arises from it was named by it.

The meaning of ﴿from above it is a wave﴾ is that the wave does not break until another wave reaches it from above, and that is more lasting for its darkness.

Al-sahab was discussed in Surat al-Ra'd. Clouds increase the darkness in obscuring, because they veil the light of the stars and the crescent moon.

His saying: ﴿darknesses, one above another﴾ is a resumptive clause. The implied meaning is: "they are darknesses." The darknesses mentioned here are not the same as those meant in "(or like darknesses)," because the plural here is a plural of types, whereas there it is a plural of individuals of one single type.

The majority read (sahabun zulumatun) with tanwin in both. Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read (min fawqihi sahabu zulumatin) without tanwin on (sahab) and with its idafah to (zulumat). Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read it with the raising of (sahabun) with tanwin and the lowering of (zulumatin) as a substitution (badal) for his saying: "(or like darknesses)."

His saying: ﴿he can hardly see it (lam yakad yaraha)﴾ is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they hardly were about to do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]. The aspect of this usage was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah, along with the story of the verse of Dhu al-Rummah.

The sentence ﴿And whomever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light﴾ is a concluding appendage to the simile, i.e., they have returned with failure in what they sought from what they did, and misguidance surrounded them intensely in what they did, until they lost its benefit; because Allah did not create guidance in their hearts when He did not grant them faith. That is, Allah created them unable to accept guidance, so He did not place its acceptance in their hearts, and nothing of guidance settles in them.

In it is an alert that Allah, the Exalted, disposes of giving and withholding according to His will and wisdom and the order of His governance that preceded.

This simile is suitable for considering differentiation in likening the parts of the likened image to the parts of the image likened to it. Thus the misguidances resemble the darknesses, and the deeds into which the disbeliever plunged seeking to draw near through them resemble the sea, and the vain deeds mixed with his good deeds, such as the bahirah and the sa'ibah, resemble the wave in its mixing with the good deed and its intrusion into it; this is the first wave. What comes upon that of deeds of disbelief, such as slaughtering for idols, resembles the overwhelming wave that comes over all of that by intrusion and corruption; this is the second wave. And what surrounds his belief of bewilderment in distinguishing the good from the frivolous and from the ugly resembles the cloud that covers what remains in the sky of the faint gleam of the starlight; and his seeking benefit from his deed resembles the navigator's extending his hand to repair the matter of his ship or to take what he needs, so he cannot see his hand, let alone the thing he wants to take.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 41:

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah glorify all those who are in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight? Each one has known its prayer and its glorification. And Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

Having followed the illustration of the misguidance of the people of misguidance, and how Allah deprived them of guidance, in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur: 39] up to His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light﴾ [al-Nur: 40].

Page 258
By seeking reflection and consideration, [the verse shows] how Allah, exalted is He, guided many of those in the heavens and the earth to the glorification of Allah, which necessitates believing in Him alone, and [it shows] what He inspired in the birds, to sounds that express their joy at the blessing of their existence and their provision, which arise from Allah's sustaining them with these two. So their sounds are indications of a state pointing to Allah's glorification and His being exalted above partners; their sounds are glorification through the tongue of state (lisan al-hal).
The sentence is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and its connection is what you have known.

The sentence ﴿each one has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ is a second resumptive sentence, and it is part of the completion of the lesson, since Allah deposited in all of those what binds them to what they were created upon of magnifying Allah and glorifying Him.

The glorification of rational beings is literal (haqiqah). The glorification of the birds is a figurative (majaz mursal) in indicating glorification. In it is the use of the word "tasbih" in both its literal and figurative senses, and for this reason the two were differentiated in the second sentence, expressing it as "salah" (prayer) and "tasbih" in consideration of the difference in the state of the two groups: the group of rational beings and the group of birds, even though the word "kull" (each) encompasses both. So the glorification of rational beings is called by the name "salah," because it is literal glorification. Thus what is meant by "salah" is supplication (du'a'), which is among the characteristics of rational beings, and the name "tasbih" is not applied to the states of birds, because it is used figuratively for indicating by sound, by the relation of generality, and this is by distribution; had that not been intended, it would have said: "each one has known its tasbih," or "each one has known its salah."

The address in His saying (Have you not seen) is to the Prophet (ﷺ). What is meant is whoever reaches him, or the address is to an unspecified addressee, so it includes every addressee, as is the case in similar expressions.

The interrogative is used as a metaphor (kinayah) for expressing wonder at the state of the group of polytheists, who are among the possessors of intellect, and yet they have been deprived of guidance because Allah did not place it in them. Guidance has been placed in the dumb creatures, since He created them with the capacity to perceive the trace of the blessing of existence and provision. This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44].

Page 259
The word "al-saffat" is among the attributes of birds: what is meant by it is their spreading their wings in the air at the time of flight. The specification of birds by mention among creatures is for the sake of contrast between the creatures of the earth and the heaven by mentioning creatures in the atmosphere between the heaven and the earth, and for this reason it was restricted by "saffat" (spreading their wings).
The verb "'alima" (knew) is meant as knowledge (ma'rifah), because of the evident difference between the knowledge of rational beings of their prayers and the knowledge of birds of their glorification, for the latter is merely awareness and a purpose toward action.

The pronouns in ﴿knew its prayer and its glorification﴾ refer necessarily to "kull" (each).

If the intended meaning of them were distribution over those in the heavens and the earth and the birds on one side, and over the Name of Majesty (Allah) on the other side, then a separating pronoun (damir fasl) would have occurred after "'alima," and it would have referred to Allah, exalted is He.

The seeing here is visual (basariyyah), because the glorification of rational beings is witnessed by everyone with sight, and the glorification of birds is witnessed in consideration of its named reality; so the observer needs only to know that this thing is worthy of the name of glorification.

On this consideration the rhetorical interrogation has a firm effect.

If you wish, you may say: the phrase "Have you not seen" operates as a proverbial expression in the speech of eloquent speakers, so there is no attention in it to the meaning of seeing.

It was said: the seeing here is intellectual (qalbiyyah), and the verbal noun (masdar) sufficed in place of the two objects.

The sentence ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyil), and it is an informing of the vastness of Allah's knowledge, exalted is He, which encompasses glorification and other states.

The use of the plural pronoun for rational beings is by prevalence (taghlib). It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who went out from their homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them﴾ [al-An'am: 6] in Surat al-An'am.

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return.﴾

صفحة ٢٦٠ [Page 260]

A confirmation of what the preceding discourse indicated, namely His giving guidance to the dumb creatures in their affairs and His depriving a group of the rational beings of it. For if that were happening according to what is deserved, these people would be better guided in their affair than the birds.

The fronting of the two objects (al-ma'mulayn, the two complements of the verb, placed before it) indicates exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: the disposal of the worlds belongs to Allah and not to anyone else.

In this there is a transition to indicating, through the states of the existing things, that Allah the Exalted alone is the Creator. For this reason it is followed by His saying:

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 43:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds gently, then joins them together, then makes them a heap, and you see the rain coming out from within them? And He sends down from the sky, from mountains [of clouds] within which is hail, so He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾

It follows the indication of guidance given in the laws of inspiration among the dumb creatures with an indication of the creation of properties in inanimate matter, such that they move along the course which Allah has determined for them, a course that does not change. Thus they are more rightly guided than the group of disbelievers who have intellects and senses, yet do not use them to be guided to the knowledge of Allah the Exalted and to reflect upon His proofs. In this there is an indication of the greatness of power, the breadth of knowledge, and the oneness of governance. This is an argument from the regular order of some events of the atmosphere, until it reaches His saying: ﴿So He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills﴾.

From this there has resulted a fine transition (husn al-takhallus) to the move to the argument for the greatness of power, the sublimity of wisdom, and the breadth of divine knowledge.

And (yuzjī): yasūqu (he drives). It is said: azjā al-ibila izjā'an (he drove the camels).

The term izjā' is applied to the drawing near of some clouds to others, by the decree of Allah the Exalted, resembling driving, until it becomes a dense cloud. The joining of some clouds to others is expressed by the joining together of their parts in His saying the Exalted: ﴿then joins them together﴾, etc.

Page 261
The discussion of clouds has already occurred in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿and the clouds subjected [between the sky and the earth]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], and at the beginning of Surat al-Ra'd.

(Bayna) has entered upon the pronoun of the cloud, because the cloud has parts, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Between al-Dakhūl and Ḥawmal"

That is: He joins the clouds together from it.

Al-rukām (heaped cloud) is derived from al-rakm. Al-rakm means gathering and compressing. The pattern fu'āl and fu'āla indicate the sense of the passive participle. So al-rukām means al-marku̇m (the heaped). As in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And if they see a piece of the sky falling, they say, "A heaped-up cloud"﴾ [al-Tur: 44], in Surat al-Tur.

When the clouds pile up upon one another, there occurs in them what is called in the science of atmospheric phenomena the electrical discharge, and it is lightning (al-barq). Some exegetes said: it is al-wadq. Most exegetes hold that al-wadq is the rain, and this is what the dictionaries have confined it to, and rain comes out from within the clouds.

Al-khilāl: the openings, plural of khalal, like jabal and jibāl. Khilāl al-diyār has already occurred in Surat al-Isrā'.

The meaning of (yunazzilu min al-sama') is: it drops from a height to a lower place, i.e., it sends down from the atmosphere of the sky to the earth. Al-sama' is the atmosphere which is above the direction of the earth.

His saying "min jibāl" is a substitute (badal) for "min al-sama'", with the repetition of the preposition that governs the replaced noun, and it is a partial substitute (badal ba'd), because what is meant by "jibāl" is clouds like mountains.

The use of mountains as an image for abundance is well known: one says, "So-and-so is a mountain of knowledge" and "a towering mass of knowledge." In the Hadith of al-Bukhari, through the route of Abu Hurayra, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If I had gold as much as Uhud, it would not please me that three nights pass over me while I have any of it left, except something I set aside for a debt." That is: it would not please me. So the statement carries the sense of negation, meaning: it would not have pleased me, or it would not have pleased me, etc.

Page 262
The first (min) is for the beginning, the second (min) likewise, and (min) in His saying (min barad) is redundant in affirmative speech according to the view of those who permitted the redundancy of (min) in affirmative speech. Or (min) may be a noun meaning "some (ba'd)."

The object of (yunazzilu) is omitted, indicated by His saying: ﴿therein is hail﴾. The implied sense is: He sends down hail.

The use of (min) as redundant is for the purpose of matching His saying: (﴿min jibāl﴾).

His saying: ﴿so He strikes with it whom He wills﴾ made the descent of hail a striking (iṣāba), because when iṣāba is used in their speech it indicates the arrival of something disagreeable. From this, the calamity that befalls and is disliked is called muṣība. As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50]; here "ḥasana" (good) is an indicator that iṣāba is applied to mere occurrence, either as a metaphorical extension (majāz mursal), or as a lexical homonym (mushtarak lafẓī), or as a semantic homonym (mushtarak ma'nawī). For (aṣāba) is derived from ṣawb, which is descent, and from it comes ṣawb al-maṭar (the downpour of rain). So he made the descent of hail a striking, because it spoils the crop and the fruit. The pronoun in (bihi) refers to the hail.

The clause ﴿The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ is a description of (saḥāban). The pronoun in (barqihi) refers to (saḥāban). The benefit of this description is to alert minds to reflect on these changes, since people's awareness of the occurrence of lightning is clearer and greater than their awareness of the formation of clouds, their piling up, and the descent of rain and hail, for people may neglect those because of how frequently they occur and their familiarity with them, unlike the intensity of lightning, for no one is free from having encountered it several times. Those whose eyesight was stirred by the flashing of lightning remember that strange state, which indicates power. For this subtle point this condition of lightning was singled out for mention.

Al-sanā, with a short vowel (maqṣūr), is the light of lightning and the light of fire. As for al-sanā'  with a long vowel (mamdūd), it means elevation. Ibn Duraid said in some verses of his on the homographs of the short and long forms:

"The brightness departed from his two eyes, and departed from the nobility of elevation."

Page 263
The definite article in (al-abṣār) is the article of the genus (lām al-ḥaqīqa). His saying: ﴿The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ is like His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], except that in this verse the word sanā has been added, because this verse comes in a context of reflection upon the formation of clouds and the sending down of rain, so the context required emphasis on this lightning and the intensity of its brightness, so that the reflection would be on two matters: the formation of lightning in the clouds, and the strength of its brightness, such that it nearly takes away the sight. The verse of al-Baqarah comes in a context of threat and depicting their condition when they displayed Islam while concealing disbelief and denial, so their state was like the state of rain containing thunderbolts, thunder and lightning: its outward appearance is benefit, but within it are calamities and misfortunes.

Because of the difference of the two contexts, the expression here is (﴿takes away the sight﴾) and there (﴿snatches their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]), since snatching (khaṭf) carries a sense of harming them and overpowering them which (dhahaba) does not have, for it is merely taking away.

As for the expression here with (al-abṣār) defined by the article, it is because the intention is that the lightning is close to removing a portion of the kind of sight; for the article here is the article of the genus, as in His saying: ﴿that the wolf may eat him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], and the saying: "Enter the market," because the judgment concerns the state of intense lightning as such. Unlike the verse of al-Baqarah, which is in a context of rebuke to them, that what is meant to benefit people has come close to harming them; therefore it mentioned the word abṣār (sights) in the plural, attached to their pronoun, along with what this variation contains of expressing one utterance in varied styles, so that the speech is not repetitive, even if the meaning is one, and you will find that the precision of brevity is not lost, for these two utterances are equal in letters and pronunciation. Thus we see the eloquence of the Qur'an, its inimitability, and the sweetness of its composition.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read (yadhhabu) with a fatḥa on the initial yā' and a fatḥa on the hā', so the bā' is for transitivity, i.e., "yudhhibu al-abṣār" (takes away the sights). Abu Ja'far alone read it with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the hā', so the bā' is then redundant for emphasis of adhesion, like His saying: ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 44:

﴿Allah turns the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have insight.﴾

Page 264
At-taqlib (turning over) is changing a state into its opposite. From it is the verse ﴿So he began to turn over his palms over what he had spent on it﴾ [al-Kahf: 42], meaning he turns his palms from their back side to their front side. Thus the turning of the night and the day is the change of the horizon from the state of night to the state of brightness, and from the state of day to the state of darkness. So what is turned (al-muqallab) is the atmosphere together with what varies upon it of accidents. But since the state of the darkness of the atmosphere is called "night" and the state of its light is called "day," he expressed the atmosphere in its two states by these two, and the turning was transferred to them on this basis.
Among what enters into the meaning of turning is the change in the form of night and day by their lengthening and shortening. And in consideration of the repeated recurrence of turning in both its senses, he expressed it with the present tense (al-mudari'), which requires repetition and renewal.

The sentence is a resumption (isti'naf). It was brought as a resumed sentence, not conjoined (ma'tufan) to the signs of consideration mentioned before it, because the intention was to move from reasoning by what may be hidden from some eyes to reasoning by what every person of sight witnesses every day and every month, so it is hardly hidden from anyone with sight. This is a gradation in the placement of this sentence after the sentence ﴿The brightness of its lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ [al-Nur: 43], as we indicated just above. Therefore the purpose of the speech is the sentence ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have insight﴾, but the arrangement of the speech was built on placing the verbal sentence first, because of what it requires of conveying renewal, unlike saying: "Indeed in the turning of the night and the day is a lesson."

The demonstrative in the phrase "Indeed in that" (inna fi dhalika) refers to the verbal noun contained in the verb (yuqallibu). That is: indeed in the turning. What supports this intention is the mention of "lesson" in the indefinite singular form.

The emphasis by "indeed" (inna) is either merely for the sake of giving attention to the news, or for placing the polytheists, in their neglect of taking this as a lesson, in the position of one who denies that there is a lesson in that.

Page 265
It has been said: the demonstrative in the phrase "Indeed in that" refers to everything mentioned just before, beginning from the words ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. Then the singular form in the phrase "a lesson" (la'ibratan) looks to the fact that the whole of that conveys the genus of lesson, which encompasses certainty that Allah is the one who disposes of the cosmos.
The word "lesson" (al-'ibrah) does not occur in the Qur'an either with the definite article of the genus (al-jins) or in the plural form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 45:

﴿And Allah has created every moving creature from water; so of them are those that walk on their bellies, and of them are those that walk on two legs, and of them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾

Since the lesson lies in the equality of the kinds of animals in their origin of creation from the water of procreation, despite the difference in the initial states of those kinds in the marks of their creation, which is the state of walking, the continuation of that order without exception is what is meant. And since this was established, the expression of this meaning by placing the subject (al-musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate (al-khabar al-fi'li) served two purposes: affirmation (al-tahaqquq) through placing it before the verbal predicate, and renewal (al-tajaddud) through the predicate being verbal.

The use of the proper name Allah instead of a pronoun is to draw attention to this wondrous creation.

The past tense verb was chosen to indicate the affirmation of the matter, that this is an established affair since antiquity, while the sense of repetition is not lost, since the speech is followed by His words: ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾.

The Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَ كُلَّ دَابَّةٍ﴾ with the past tense form and the accusative of (kull). Al-Kisa'i read it (﴿وَاللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ دَابَّةٍ﴾) with the active participle form and the genitive of (kull), by the annexation of the active participle to its object.

Page 266
The dabba (moving creature) is whatever crawls upon the surface of the earth, i.e., walks. Here the human being is given precedence, so the pronoun for rational beings is used, meaning by it both the human being and others, twice.

The indefiniteness of (ma') (water) is for the intention of kinds, to draw attention to the difference in the attributes of water for each kind of moving creature, since the aim is to alert people to the difference of the sperm drops for the sake of increasing the lesson.

This is unlike His words: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 30], where He intended there that all kinds of animals are created from the kind of water, which is one kind whose types differ. Thus the definiteness of the genus there is an indication of what people know generally and are accustomed to, that every animal is created from the sperm drops of its origins. This is the basis of the distinction between indefiniteness, as here, and the definiteness of the genus, as in the verse ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 30].

And (min) is initial (ibtida'iyya), related to (khalaqa) "created".

The mention of the kinds in the state of walking is ordered according to the strength of their indication of the greatness of power, because the one that walks without a fully functioning walking apparatus is more wondrous than the one that walks on two legs, and this walking is by crawling. The walking was applied to crawling on the belly for harmony with the rest of the kinds. There is nothing in the verse that requires restricting walking to these three states, because the aim is the lesson from what is commonly observed.

The clause ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾ is an addition to the lesson; i.e., the creation of Allah of what He wills to create renews, of what you know and what you do not know, so it is a resumptive clause (jumla mustani'fa).

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ is a causal explanation and a concluding summation (ta'lil wa tadhyil). In it the proper name Allah is expressed in the place of a pronoun, so that it is complete and independent in itself, because the nature of a concluding summation is to be like a proverb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 46:

﴿We have certainly sent down clear verses, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

Page 267

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the proofs and lessons mentioned earlier, and it is the outcome of the argument (natijat al-istidlal). For this reason it is concluded with His words ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, meaning: if the people of misguidance do not become guided by those verses, then that is because Allah has not guided them, for He guides whom He wills. The intended meaning of "the verses" here is the verses of the Qur'an, as the verb (anzalna, "We sent down") requires. For this reason this sentence is not joined by a conjunction to what precedes it, unlike his earlier statement: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses﴾ [al-Nur: 34].

Since the purpose of this is to establish the proof rather than to bestow favour, He did not restrict the sending down of the verses to being addressed to the Muslims, as He restricted it in His earlier words: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses﴾ [al-Nur: 34], as has already been explained.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (mubayyanat) with a fatha on the ya', in the form of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), meaning that Allah has made them clear and manifest through their eloquence and the strength of their proof. The rest read it with a kasra on the ya', in the form of the active participle (ism al-fa'il). In this reading, attributing the act of making clear (al-tabyin) to the verses is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), since they are the cause of the clarification.

The meaning is that the indications of the truth are manifest, but Allah decrees guidance to the truth for whomever He wills to guide.

[Page 268]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 24, verses 47–50 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They say, "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey," then a faction of them turn away after that. Those are not believers.﴾ ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a faction of them are turning away.﴾ ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him in submission.﴾ ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾

[Page 268, continued]

The clause "They say" (wa-yaqulun) is conjoined to the clause ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [al-Nur: 46], because the clause "He guides whom He wills" implies the guidance of some people and the deprivation of others from guidance, as is required by "whom He wills." This is a transition (takhallus) to mention some of those whom Allah did not will to guide, namely those who concealed disbelief and displayed Islam, who are the people of hypocrisy (ahl al-nifaq). After the proofs of Allah's sole divinity had been mentioned, and after the open disbelievers who were not guided by them had been mentioned in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur: 39] and the verses that follow, the context became ready for mentioning another category of disbelievers, who were not guided by the signs of Allah yet displayed that they had been guided by them.

The plural pronoun refers to persons known to the listeners, namely the hypocrites, because what is mentioned after it concerns their conditions. The return of a pronoun to something not previously mentioned is common in the Qur'an. Moreover, something that alludes to them by way of indirect reference (ta'rid) has already preceded in His saying ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat﴾ [al-Nur: 37].

The verse refers to the hypocrites in general, and then to a faction among them who displayed their dissatisfaction with the judgment of the Messenger (ﷺ). Both groups are marked by hypocrisy, but one of them persisted in hypocrisy and equivocation, while the other soon displayed their return to disbelief openly by disobeying the Messenger.

In His saying "They say" there is an indication that their share of faith is merely the utterance without belief, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

He expressed it in the present tense (al-mudari') to convey the renewal of this from them and their continuance in it, because it involves the repetition of lying and similar traits of hypocrisy, which I explained in Surah al-Baqarah. The object of "we obey" (atana) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "we obey Allah and the Messenger."

The demonstrative in His saying "Those are not" refers to the subject of "They say," meaning: they say "we believe" while they are liars in their statement. Their disbelief becomes apparent only when calamities and disputes befall them, so they do not feel at ease with the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is not permissible to take it as referring to "a faction" in His saying ﴿when a faction of them are turning away﴾, because their turning away is sufficient evidence of the absence of faith.

[Page 269]

Accordingly, the pronoun in His saying "And when they are called" refers back to the antecedent of the pronoun in "They say." The attribution of the verb "they were called" to all of them, even though only a faction of them turned away and not all of them, is to indicate that they are equal in their readiness to turn away, but they do not display it except when calamities befall them. Those who turn away are the ones upon whom disputes have fallen.

The verse included a group of hypocrites upon whom disputes had fallen, who refused the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ) either before he had judged against them or after he had judged against them and his judgment did not satisfy them. The exegetes narrated that "Bishr, one of the Aws or the Khazraj, had a dispute with a Jew before the Prophet (ﷺ). When the Prophet judged in favor of the Jew, Bishr was not content with his judgment and invited him to judge at the court of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the Jew. The Jew refused, and they both went to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and recounted the matter to him. When 'Umar learned that Bishr was not content with the judgment of the Prophet, he said to them both: 'Stay where you are until I come to you.' He entered his house, took out his sword, struck Bishr with it, and killed him. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave 'Umar on that day the title al-Faruq, because he distinguished between truth and falsehood." That is, he distinguished between them by direct witnessing.

It was also said: "One of the hypocrites, named al-Mughirah ibn Wa'il, from the Aws, from the Banu Umayyah ibn Zayd al-Awsi, had a dispute with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib over land they had divided. Then Umayyah disliked the share he had taken and sought to annul the division, but 'Ali refused to annul it, and invited him to judgment before the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Mughirah said: 'As for Muhammad, I will not go to him, because he bears enmity toward me, and I fear that he will be unjust to me.' So this verse was revealed." This has been mentioned previously in the commentary on His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 60] in Surah al-Nisa'.

Among the absurdities of reports is what al-Tabrisi the Shi'i transmitted in his tafsir entitled Majma' al-Bayan: "From al-Balkhi: there was a dispute between 'Ali and 'Uthman over land that 'Uthman had bought from 'Ali. Stones emerged from it, and he wanted to return it on the ground of a defect, but 'Ali did not accept it, and said: 'Between me and you is the Messenger of Allah.' Al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As said to him: 'If you go to judgment with him before his cousin, he will rule in his favor, so do not bring him to judgment before him.' Then the verses were revealed."

[Page 270]

No reliable exegete has narrated this, and I have no doubt that it is among the things that have been habitually attributed to the Banu Umayyah by those who distort their state, seeking to stir up discord. As for al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As, he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest and settled in Madinah. Could one suppose that he would say such a statement among Muslims?

The reason that calling to Allah and His Messenger is mentioned together, although they were called to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, is that the judgment of the Messenger is the judgment of Allah, because he does not judge except through revelation. For this reason, the pronoun in His saying "that he may judge" is singular, referring to the nearest antecedent, and He did not say "that they may judge."

His saying ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him﴾ means: they come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The meaning of ﴿if the right is theirs﴾ is that it is so in the assumption and certainty of the one who holds the right, that he is in the right. Its implication is that whoever among them has no right, and knows that he is in the wrong, does not come when called to the Messenger (upon him be prayers). Thus it is understood that the group who turn away are the wrongdoers. This is also the case with everyone who is in the right: he does not refuse just judgment, whereas it is the nature of the wrongdoer to refuse justice, because justice does not suit his love of transgressing upon the rights of people. Therefore, the reason for the turning away of those who turn away is their knowledge that falsehood is on their side, and they are certain that the Messenger judges only by manifest truth.

This is the explanation of the position of the clause ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts﴾ to its end.

The particle of sudden occurrence (idha al-mufaja'ah) came in the response of the conditional "idha" to indicate that they hasten to turn away without delay, because they had previously been certain of the justice of the Messenger, and they were certain that falsehood was on their side, so they did not hesitate in turning away.

Al-idh'an (إذعان) means submission and obedience.

Since this is a strange matter, a clause containing interrogatives was introduced after it,

[Page 271]

used to draw attention to their characters and to direct minds to what they concealed. The reason for this is that these are hidden conditions, because they used to display the opposite.

Some of the interrogatives were followed by others with the particle "am" (أم) used disjunctively (al-munqati'ah), which here serves as a transitional idrab (إضراب انتقالي, transitional shift). It functions this way as it does when it conjoins interrogative clauses. When it conjoins clauses, it is not used to request specification as it is when conjoining single words, because what is conjoined by it in that case is not something that requires specifying one part over another. As for the meaning of interrogation, it is necessarily attached to it, since it is understood after "am."

The transition here is a gradual enumeration of their characters. The meaning is that a questioner asked about their being characterized by one of these mentioned traits, and the one questioned knew that they were characterized by it, so the interrogation repeated three times was used to call attention as a figurative usage (majaz mursal). An example is His saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk, or do they have hands with which they strike, or do they have eyes with which they see, or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195] in Surah al-A'raf.

The hearts (al-qulub) means the intellects. The disease (al-maradh) is used metaphorically for corruption or for disbelief, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased their disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], or for hypocrisy.

On the side of this interrogation the nominal sentence was used, to indicate the permanence of the disease in their hearts and its rootedness in them, to the extent that faith has not entered their hearts.

Al-irtiyab (الارتياب) means doubt. The intended meaning is that they came to doubt the truth of Islam, meaning that doubt arose in them after they had believed with an unsteady faith.

On its side the verbal sentence was used, which indicates occurrence and renewal, meaning that doubt arose in them after they had believed with a shaken conviction. This indicates that they are two groups: a group that never believed but displayed faith and concealed their disbelief, and a group that believed with a weak faith and then their disbelief became apparent through their turning away.

Al-haif (الحيف) means injustice and oppression in judgment. On its side the two verbs were used in the present tense to indicate that they feared, in the present, injustice in the future, as the entry of "an" (أن), the particle of the future, upon the verb "yahif" requires. They feared the occurrence of injustice after the dispute had been raised, and therefore they turned away from seeking judgment from the Messenger (ﷺ).

Injustice was attributed to Allah and His Messenger in the sense that what Islam legislated would be injustice that does not reveal rights. The exegetes narrated that "Bishr, one of the Aws or the Khazraj, had a dispute with a Jew before the Prophet (ﷺ). When the Prophet judged in favor of the Jew, Bishr was not content with his judgment and invited him to judge at the court of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the Jew. The Jew refused, and they both went to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and recounted the matter to him. When 'Umar learned that Bishr was not content with the judgment of the Prophet, he said to them both: 'Stay where you are until I come to you.' He entered his house, took out his sword, struck Bishr with it, and killed him. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave 'Umar on that day the title al-Faruq, because he distinguished between truth and falsehood." That is, he distinguished between them by direct witnessing.

It was also said: "One of the hypocrites, named al-Mughirah ibn Wa'il, from the Aws, from the Banu Umayyah ibn Zayd al-Awsi, had a dispute with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib over land they had divided. [Page 270]
