The restriction (qasr) resulting from the definiteness of both parts and from the separating pronoun (dhamir al-fasl, ضمير الفصل) is an emphatic restriction, meaning: they are the wrongdoers, not the law of Allah nor the judgment of His Messenger.

He added the demonstrative to emphasize the predicate, so four emphases occurred in it: two from the form of restriction, since restriction and specification are nothing but emphasis upon emphasis; the third is the separating pronoun; and the fourth is the demonstrative.

The demonstrative pronoun, which is set for distinction, is used here figuratively to establish their attribute of wrongdoing. They judge people by the measure they apply to themselves, so because they were people of injustice, they assumed that the one who is characterized by fairness is unjust, as Abu al-Tayyib (al-Mutanabbi) said:

When a man's conduct is bad, his suspicions become bad,
and he confirms what his habit of imagining has accustomed him to.

There is no connection between this verse and the ruling concerning one who is summoned to the judge for a dispute and refuses; this is because the blame and rebuke in it were directed at a refusal arising from their disbelief and hypocrisy.

[Page 268]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 24, verses 47–50 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They say, "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey," then a faction of them turn away after that. Those are not believers.﴾ ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a faction of them are turning away.﴾ ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him in submission.﴾ ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾

[Page 268, continued]

The clause "They say" (wa-yaqulun) is conjoined to the clause ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [al-Nur: 46], because the clause "He guides whom He wills" implies the guidance of some people and the deprivation of others from guidance, as is required by "whom He wills." This is a transition (takhallus) to mention some of those whom Allah did not will to guide, namely those who concealed disbelief and displayed Islam, who are the people of hypocrisy (ahl al-nifaq). After the proofs of Allah's sole divinity had been mentioned, and after the open disbelievers who were not guided by them had been mentioned in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur: 39] and the verses that follow, the context became ready for mentioning another category of disbelievers, who were not guided by the signs of Allah yet displayed that they had been guided by them.

The plural pronoun refers to persons known to the listeners, namely the hypocrites, because what is mentioned after it concerns their conditions. The return of a pronoun to something not previously mentioned is common in the Qur'an. Moreover, something that alludes to them by way of indirect reference (ta'rid) has already preceded in His saying ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat﴾ [al-Nur: 37].

The verse refers to the hypocrites in general, and then to a faction among them who displayed their dissatisfaction with the judgment of the Messenger (ﷺ). Both groups are marked by hypocrisy, but one of them persisted in hypocrisy and equivocation, while the other soon displayed their return to disbelief openly by disobeying the Messenger.

In His saying "They say" there is an indication that their share of faith is merely the utterance without belief, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

He expressed it in the present tense (al-mudari') to convey the renewal of this from them and their continuance in it, because it involves the repetition of lying and similar traits of hypocrisy, which I explained in Surah al-Baqarah. The object of "we obey" (atana) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "we obey Allah and the Messenger."

The demonstrative in His saying "Those are not" refers to the subject of "They say," meaning: they say "we believe" while they are liars in their statement. Their disbelief becomes apparent only when calamities and disputes befall them, so they do not feel at ease with the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is not permissible to take it as referring to "a faction" in His saying ﴿when a faction of them are turning away﴾, because their turning away is sufficient evidence of the absence of faith.

[Page 269]

Accordingly, the pronoun in His saying "And when they are called" refers back to the antecedent of the pronoun in "They say." The attribution of the verb "they were called" to all of them, even though only a faction of them turned away and not all of them, is to indicate that they are equal in their readiness to turn away, but they do not display it except when calamities befall them. Those who turn away are the ones upon whom disputes have fallen.

The verse included a group of hypocrites upon whom disputes had fallen, who refused the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ) either before he had judged against them or after he had judged against them and his judgment did not satisfy them. The exegetes narrated that "Bishr, one of the Aws or the Khazraj, had a dispute with a Jew before the Prophet (ﷺ). When the Prophet judged in favor of the Jew, Bishr was not content with his judgment and invited him to judge at the court of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the Jew. The Jew refused, and they both went to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and recounted the matter to him. When 'Umar learned that Bishr was not content with the judgment of the Prophet, he said to them both: 'Stay where you are until I come to you.' He entered his house, took out his sword, struck Bishr with it, and killed him. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave 'Umar on that day the title al-Faruq, because he distinguished between truth and falsehood." That is, he distinguished between them by direct witnessing.

It was also said: "One of the hypocrites, named al-Mughirah ibn Wa'il, from the Aws, from the Banu Umayyah ibn Zayd al-Awsi, had a dispute with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib over land they had divided. Then Umayyah disliked the share he had taken and sought to annul the division, but 'Ali refused to annul it, and invited him to judgment before the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Mughirah said: 'As for Muhammad, I will not go to him, because he bears enmity toward me, and I fear that he will be unjust to me.' So this verse was revealed." This has been mentioned previously in the commentary on His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 60] in Surah al-Nisa'.

Among the absurdities of reports is what al-Tabrisi the Shi'i transmitted in his tafsir entitled Majma' al-Bayan: "From al-Balkhi: there was a dispute between 'Ali and 'Uthman over land that 'Uthman had bought from 'Ali. Stones emerged from it, and he wanted to return it on the ground of a defect, but 'Ali did not accept it, and said: 'Between me and you is the Messenger of Allah.' Al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As said to him: 'If you go to judgment with him before his cousin, he will rule in his favor, so do not bring him to judgment before him.' Then the verses were revealed."

[Page 270]

No reliable exegete has narrated this, and I have no doubt that it is among the things that have been habitually attributed to the Banu Umayyah by those who distort their state, seeking to stir up discord. As for al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As, he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest and settled in Madinah. Could one suppose that he would say such a statement among Muslims?

The reason that calling to Allah and His Messenger is mentioned together, although they were called to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, is that the judgment of the Messenger is the judgment of Allah, because he does not judge except through revelation. For this reason, the pronoun in His saying "that he may judge" is singular, referring to the nearest antecedent, and He did not say "that they may judge."

His saying ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him﴾ means: they come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The meaning of ﴿if the right is theirs﴾ is that it is so in the assumption and certainty of the one who holds the right, that he is in the right. Its implication is that whoever among them has no right, and knows that he is in the wrong, does not come when called to the Messenger (upon him be prayers). Thus it is understood that the group who turn away are the wrongdoers. This is also the case with everyone who is in the right: he does not refuse just judgment, whereas it is the nature of the wrongdoer to refuse justice, because justice does not suit his love of transgressing upon the rights of people. Therefore, the reason for the turning away of those who turn away is their knowledge that falsehood is on their side, and they are certain that the Messenger judges only by manifest truth.

This is the explanation of the position of the clause ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts﴾ to its end.

The particle of sudden occurrence (idha al-mufaja'ah) came in the response of the conditional "idha" to indicate that they hasten to turn away without delay, because they had previously been certain of the justice of the Messenger, and they were certain that falsehood was on their side, so they did not hesitate in turning away.

Al-idh'an (إذعان) means submission and obedience.

Since this is a strange matter, a clause containing interrogatives was introduced after it,

[Page 271]

used to draw attention to their characters and to direct minds to what they concealed. The reason for this is that these are hidden conditions, because they used to display the opposite.

Some of the interrogatives were followed by others with the particle "am" (أم) used disjunctively (al-munqati'ah), which here serves as a transitional idrab (إضراب انتقالي, transitional shift). It functions this way as it does when it conjoins interrogative clauses. When it conjoins clauses, it is not used to request specification as it is when conjoining single words, because what is conjoined by it in that case is not something that requires specifying one part over another. As for the meaning of interrogation, it is necessarily attached to it, since it is understood after "am."

The transition here is a gradual enumeration of their characters. The meaning is that a questioner asked about their being characterized by one of these mentioned traits, and the one questioned knew that they were characterized by it, so the interrogation repeated three times was used to call attention as a figurative usage (majaz mursal). An example is His saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk, or do they have hands with which they strike, or do they have eyes with which they see, or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195] in Surah al-A'raf.

The hearts (al-qulub) means the intellects. The disease (al-maradh) is used metaphorically for corruption or for disbelief, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased their disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], or for hypocrisy.

On the side of this interrogation the nominal sentence was used, to indicate the permanence of the disease in their hearts and its rootedness in them, to the extent that faith has not entered their hearts.

Al-irtiyab (الارتياب) means doubt. The intended meaning is that they came to doubt the truth of Islam, meaning that doubt arose in them after they had believed with an unsteady faith.

On its side the verbal sentence was used, which indicates occurrence and renewal, meaning that doubt arose in them after they had believed with a shaken conviction. This indicates that they are two groups: a group that never believed but displayed faith and concealed their disbelief, and a group that believed with a weak faith and then their disbelief became apparent through their turning away.

Al-haif (الحيف) means injustice and oppression in judgment. On its side the two verbs were used in the present tense to indicate that they feared, in the present, injustice in the future, as the entry of "an" (أن), the particle of the future, upon the verb "yahif" requires. They feared the occurrence of injustice after the dispute had been raised, and therefore they turned away from seeking judgment from the Messenger (ﷺ).

Injustice was attributed to Allah and His Messenger in the sense that what Islam legislated would be injustice that does not reveal rights. This is a kinaya (كناية, metonymy) for their believing that it is not sent down from Allah, and that the Messenger's judgment is other than what Allah commanded. They thus cast doubt on the judgment and on the judge. This is only because they do not believe that the law of Islam was sent down from Allah, nor do they believe that Muhammad (upon him be prayers and peace) was sent by Allah. So the statement is a kinaya for their denial that the law is divine, and that the one who brought it is truthful in what he brought.

Know that the hypocrites were characterized by these three matters, and all of them arise from their not affirming the Messenger, whether for one to whom a case befell or for one to whom no case befell.

What we have explained regarding His saying ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts﴾ contains that which delights the heart of the one who reflects and removes the silence of the silent and the bewilderment of the bewildered.

[Page 272]

"Bal" (بل) is a transitional idrab from the interrogation used for calling attention to another statement. The idrab here does not use "am," because "am" must always carry the meaning of interrogation, and the intention is not to conjoin their being wrongdoers to the interrogation used for calling attention. Rather, the intention is to convey that they are characterized by wrongdoing exclusively, since their condition has become clear, so there is no need to present it in the form of an interrogation for calling attention. "Bal" here is not for nullification (al-ibtal), because it is not right to nullify all the preceding categories, for among them is the disease of their hearts, which is established. There is no evidence that it intends to nullify the last category alone, nor to nullify the other two categories.

The clause ﴿Those are the wrongdoers﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani), because the listener, after those three interrogations had struck his ear and were followed by the particle of transition, awaits what the verification of their condition will rest upon. So His saying "Those are the wrongdoers" came as an explanation of what the listener was awaiting.

The meaning is that they fear the Messenger would be unjust toward them and wrong them. But the Messenger is not one who wrongs; rather, they are the wrongdoers. The restriction (qasr) resulting from the definiteness of both parts and from the separating pronoun (dhamir al-fasl, ضمير الفصل) is an emphatic restriction, meaning: they are the wrongdoers, not the law of Allah nor the judgment of His Messenger.

He added the demonstrative to emphasize the predicate, so four emphases occurred in it: two from the form of restriction, since restriction and specification are nothing but emphasis upon emphasis; the third is the separating pronoun; and the fourth is the demonstrative.

The demonstrative pronoun, which is set for distinction, is used here figuratively to establish their attribute of wrongdoing. They judge people by the measure they apply to themselves, so because they were people of injustice, they assumed that the one who is characterized by fairness is unjust, as Abu al-Tayyib (al-Mutanabbi) said:

When a man's conduct is bad, his suspicions become bad,
and he confirms what his habit of imagining has accustomed him to.

There is no connection between this verse and the ruling concerning one who is summoned to the judge for a dispute and refuses; this is because the blame and rebuke in it were directed at a refusal arising from their disbelief and hypocrisy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 51:

﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is only that they say: "We hear and we obey." And those are the successful.﴾

It is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because the report about those who turn away when they are called to adjudication, that they are not believers while they display faith, raises the question of a questioner about the distinction that separates the true believer from the one who makes a show of his faith. When one is called to adjudication before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it requires that the difference between the two states be clarified for the questioner, lest faith that is feigned be confused in his mind with sincere faith. The hypocrites used to give the impression that the turning away of those among them from submitting to the Messenger of Allah's judgment was not due to any doubt in the truthfulness of the Messenger, but was rather a turning away out of regard for some worldly ties, like the saying of Bishr: "The Messenger hates me." So Allah made clear the falsehood of that by showing that the believer does not doubt the justice of the Messenger nor his freedom from partiality.

This resumption also conveys praise of the deserving believers, the opposite of the censure of the hypocrites. This is among the purposes of this resumption, in keeping with the Qur'an's practice of following rebuke with encouragement, threat with promise, warning with good news, and blame with praise.

The restrictive form with "innama" (only) is used to exclude the possibility that one who differs from this state in some respect could be counted as a believer even if he claims with his tongue that he is a believer. Thus this restriction is relative (qasr idafi): that is, this is the saying of the believers who are truthful in their faith, not like the saying of those who turned away from the Messenger's judgment when they said: ﴿We believe in Allah and the Messenger and we obey﴾ [al-Nur: 47]; then when they were called to the Messenger's judgment, they disobeyed his command, for their turning away is the opposite of obedience, and its explanation will come shortly. It is not a true restriction, because the sayings of the believers when they are called to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he may judge between them are not confined to the saying "We hear and we obey," nor to its synonym, for perhaps some of them add to that.

In the Muwatta' from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani: "Two men disputed before the Messenger of Allah. One of them said: O Messenger of Allah, judge between us by the Book of Allah," meaning that he wanted the Messenger of Allah to rule in his favour. As has been stated explicitly in the narration of al-Layth ibn Sa'd in al-Bukhari: "A man from the Bedouins came to the Messenger of Allah and said: I adjure you by Allah, judge for me only by the Book of Allah. The other said, and he was the more learned of the two: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, judge between us by the Book of Allah, and permit me to speak. He meant: do not rule in his favour against me; so permit me to explain. The Messenger of Allah said: Speak." ... etc.

The intended meaning of the saying "We hear and we obey" is not these two particular words specifically, but rather their wording or their synonyms, since in the object of the verb "to say" there is latitude that it need not be quoted in its exact wording, as is well known. These two words were singled out for mention here because they are a well-known expression said in such a situation, and they have become like a proverb, just as one says "sam'un wa ta'atun" (with nominative case) and "sam'an wa ta'atan" (with accusative case). The discussion of this has already passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they had said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Nisa': 46] in Surat al-Nisa'. And in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet said to the Ansar: You will spare us the burden and we will share the fruit with you. The Ansar said: We hear and we obey."

﴿The saying of the believers﴾ is the predicate of "kana" (was), and "an yaqulu" (that they say) is the subject of "kana." The predicate of kana was placed before its subject in conformity with Arabic usage, because when they come after "kana" with "an" and the verb, they only bring the predicate before the subject, considering that the verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb is more definite than a plain verbal noun, and they only put the predicate first out of dislike for two particles following each other, namely "kana" and "an." Similar instances of this usage are numerous in the Qur'an. It was previously discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their saying was only that they said: Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147] in Surat Al 'Imran.

In describing the believers with success, the same construction is used as was used to describe the hypocrites with wrongdoing, in the form of emphatic restriction, so that the praise of the believers may be the complete opposite of the blame of the hypocrites.

Know that the restriction conveyed by "innama" here is a restriction of exclusion (qasr ifrad) to one of the two types of saying. Its aim is praise of the believers for the firmness of their faith and the steadfastness of their obedience in ease and hardship. It also contains an allusion (ta'ridh) against the hypocrites, who utter the word of obedience and then undo it with its opposite of words of turning away and doubt. A parallel to this verse in the form of restriction with "illa" (except) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their saying was only that they said: Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147] in Surat Al 'Imran.

The conjunction (wa) is either parenthetical (i'tiradiyya) or coordinating (ʿatifa) over the sentence "﴿And those are the successful ones﴾ [al-Nur: 51]". The implied sense is: "and they are the ones who prosper." This wording, with this expansiveness (itnab), was adopted so that the ruling and the one it applies to become general.

صفحة ٢٧٦
The position of this sentence is that of a concluding statement (tadhyil), because it encompasses what was mentioned before it, namely the words of the believers: ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Nur: 51], and it includes other acts of obedience, whether by speech or by deed.

"Man" (min) is a general conditional particle, and the sentence "﴿fa-ulaʾika﴾" ("then those") is the response (jawab) of the condition. Al-fawz is attaining the sought-after good by success (al-zafar bi'l-matlub al-salih). Ta'a (obedience) is carrying out commands and avoiding prohibitions.

Khashya (fear, khashya) is fear. It relates specifically to whatever shortcoming one may have committed in the obligations, though it also encompasses all shortfall.

Taqwa (God-consciousness, taqwa) is caution against violating the obligations in the future.

Thus the verse gathers the causes of success in the Hereafter and also in this world.

The form of restriction (sigha al-hasr) is an allusion to those who turn away when they are called to God and His Messenger, and it is patterned on the form of restriction (sigha al-qasr) that preceded it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 53:

﴿They swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if you ordered them, they would surely go forth. Say: "Do not swear; obedience is known. Indeed, God is Aware of what you do."﴾

It is coordinated with the sentence ﴿And they say, "We believe in God and in the Messenger"﴾ [al-Nur: 47]. The narration of their saying that was followed by the narration of an oath they swore by God, in order to clear themselves of the stigma that their turning away from judgment before the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, had caused. They came to him and swore that they do not conceal disobedience to him in what he decides, for if the Messenger ordered them to do the most difficult thing, which is going forth to fight, they would obey him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is about the hypocrites who turned away when they were called to God and His Messenger. Al-Qurtubi said: When he [God] made clear their aversion to the Prophet's judgment, they came to him and said: "By God, if you ordered us to leave our homes and our wealth, we would leave, and if you ordered us to strive (jihad), we would strive." Then this verse was revealed.

The speech of al-Qurtubi implies that they mentioned two kinds of going forth. Accordingly, there is in the verse a concision (ijaz) in omitting the object of the going forth, so that it includes whatever the word "going forth" is applied to, both literally and figuratively, by the indication of what is known from the story of the occasion of revelation that day, for it was on account of a dispute over property; thus the meaning of going forth from property was more immediate in intention. The majority of exegetes restricted the meaning of (they would surely go forth) to going forth from their wealth and their homes. Al-Tabari restricted it to going forth to jihad, according to the difference of opinion about the occasion of revelation.

The word al-iqsam means uttering an oath, that is, a vow.

The pronoun in (they swore) refers to the same antecedent as the pronoun in (they say). The past tense is used here because that is something that occurred and ended.

Al-jahd, with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the ha', means the utmost limit of one's capacity. For this reason it is applied to hardship, as in the hadith of the beginning of revelation: "He pressed me until I reached the limit of exertion (al-jahd)," because a difficult matter is not performed except with the utmost capacity. It is the verbal noun of (jahada), like (manaa), when transitive, meaning to make another exhausted.

The accusative of (jahda aymanihim) may be a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in (they swore), with the verbal noun interpreted as an active participle, as in His saying: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], that is, striving. The implied meaning is: striving themselves, that is, reaching with them the utmost capacity. This is in the manner of tajrid (abstraction). The meaning of that is: they repeated the oaths and multiplied their formulations until they exhausted themselves, in order to give the impression that they were sincere in their oaths. The idafa of (jahda) to (aymanihim) on this aspect is an idafa in the sense of (min), that is, an exertion arising from their oaths.

It is also permissible that (jahda) be accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) that stands in place of its verb. The implied meaning is: they exerted their oaths with an exertion, and the implied verb is in the position of a circumstantial state from the pronoun in (they swore). The implied meaning: they swore while exerting their oaths with exertion. The idafa of (jahda) to (aymanihim) on this aspect is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object; it made the oaths like a person who has an exertion, so there is in it a metaphor by implication (isti'ara makniyya), and an allusion to the comparandum by what belongs to its attributes, namely that someone exerts him, that is, extracts his capacity from him, since every repetition of the oath is like imposing upon the oath a repeated action that exhausts it, so this too is a metaphor.

The discussion of some of this has preceded at His saying: ﴿Are these the ones who swore by God with their most emphatic oaths?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 53] in Surat al-'Uqud, and His saying: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them﴾ [al-An'am: 109] in Surat al-An'am.

The clause (﴿if you ordered them﴾) etc. is an explanation of the clause (they swore). The object of (﴿you ordered them﴾) is omitted, indicated by His saying (they would surely go forth). The implied meaning: if you ordered them to go forth, they would surely go forth.

So God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to say to them these words rich in meanings: ﴿Do not swear; obedience is known﴾. This is a directed speech, because their being forbidden to swear after the oath had been uttered may be a prohibition against repeating it, since they were on the verge of repeating it, meaning: there is no need for you to emphasize the oath, for emphasis is in the status of what is emphasized in being a lie.

It is also possible that the prohibition is used in the sense of not requiring an oath, that is, it was not for you to swear, since there is no need for an oath when there is no doubt about your affair.

It is also possible that the prohibition is used in the sense of equalization, like ﴿Be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you﴾ [al-Tur: 16].

It is also possible that the prohibition is used in its literal sense, with the object of the oath omitted, that is: do not swear to go forth from your homes and your wealth, for God does not impose that on you. The situation of confronting their hypocrisy requires that these possibilities be intended.

His saying (﴿obedience is known﴾) is a statement sent forth as a proverb, and beneath it are many meanings, which differ according to the possibilities mentioned above in His saying (﴿Do not swear﴾).

The indefiniteness of (obedience) is because what is intended is the kind of obedience, not a specific obedience; so it is of the type: a date is better than a locust. And (﴿known﴾) is its predicate.

According to the possibility that the prohibition against swearing is used to forbid repeating it, the meaning is of the kind of mockery: there is no sanctity for the oath, so do not repeat it, for your obedience is known, that is, its weakness and its non-existence are known.

According to the possibility that the prohibition is used to mean not demanding an oath, the meaning is: why do you swear? Do I doubt your state? For your obedience is known to me, that is, I know that it does not occur; and the statement is also mockery.

According to the possibility that the prohibition is used for equalization, the meaning is: your oath and its negation are equal, because your oaths are wicked and your obedience is known.

Or (obedience) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, that is: a known obedience is better than oaths; and the attribute (known) is derived from knowledge (ma'rifa) in the sense of knowing, that is: an obedience that is known and realized is better than oaths upon an obedience that does not occur; and it is like the recognition in their saying: "I will not recognize you doing such-and-such."

If the prohibition is used in its literal sense, the meaning is: do not swear this oath, that is, to go forth from your homes and your wealth; because God does not impose obedience upon you except in what is known, so the attribute (known) is derived from recognition (irfan), that is, the absence of denial, as in His saying: ﴿and they will not disobey you in what is known﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 12].

The clause ﴿Indeed, God is Aware of what you do﴾ is suitable as a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the possibilities mentioned above, and it is a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it.

[Page 280]

This is another instruction to the Messenger, peace be upon him, by which he may repel their falsehood. He should show little concern for their false promises, and they should confine their obedience to obedience to God and His Messenger in what He imposed on them, rather than in what they volunteered falsely. The meaning of ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger﴾ varies between a command to bring about the obedience that is lacking, and the implication of a demand that they persist in obedience, according to their own claim.

The command to speak is repeated to draw attention to this statement, so it comes as an independent sentence, not joined to what precedes it by a conjunction.

His saying, ﴿But if they turn away﴾, may be a derivation (tafri') from the verb "obey" (ati'u), so that the verb "turn away" (tawallaw) is part of what the Prophet, peace be upon him, was commanded to say to them. It would then be a present-tense verb with the second-person "ta" prefix. Its original form is "tatawallaw" with two "ta"s, and the second-person "ta" has been dropped from it for lightness, which is a common elision in usage. The statement is a communication from God Most High to them, so the pronouns in ﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with﴾ refer to the Messenger, peace be upon him.

It may also be a derivation from the verb "say" (qul), meaning: when you say that, and they turn away and do not obey, and so on. In that case the verb "turn away" is a past-tense verb with a single "ta", addressed to the Prophet, peace be upon him. That is: if they turn away and do not obey, then upon you is what you have been charged with of conveyance, and upon them is what they have been charged with of the consequence of the obligation. This is like the meaning of God Most High's saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance﴾ [al-Nahl: 82] in Surat al-Nahl. In that case, there is a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person within a sentence) in the pronouns of ﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾. The original form of the speech would be: then upon you is what you have been charged with, and upon them is what they have been charged with. The iltifat is an embellishment and needs no special purpose.

By these two possibilities, the verse conveys two meanings: one from the bearing of God Most High's address to them, which is an allusive threat and warning, and one from the Prophet's, peace be upon him, admonition to them and his bidding them farewell. All of this is a rebuke to them, so that they know that by turning away they harm none but themselves. A parallel to this is His saying in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 23], meaning the Jews, ﴿who are called to the Book of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 23], down to His saying: ﴿Say: Obey God and the Messenger. But if they turn away, then God does not love the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 32].

[Page 281]

Know that these two considerations do not apply in the places where a present verb beginning with two "ta"s occurs in a context of prohibition, such as His saying: ﴿And do not exchange the bad for the good﴾ [al-Nisa': 2], and His saying: ﴿And do not aim at the bad, from which you spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267], and His saying in Surat al-Anfal: ﴿And do not turn away from it while you hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 20]. As for His saying in Surat Muhammad: ﴿But if you turn away, He will replace you with a people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38], there both "ta"s remain, because the address there is directed to the believers, so there was nothing requiring the composition to be arranged in a way suitable for conveying the two meanings mentioned in Surat al-Nur and Surat Al 'Imran.

"Al-balagh" (conveyance) is a verbal noun (ism masdar, a noun functioning as the verbal noun) meaning the act of conveying, like "al-ada'" (fulfilment) meaning the act of fulfilling. Its being "clear" (mubin) means that it is eloquent and plain.

The clause ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾ is a follow-up (irdaf) to the intimidation contained in His saying ﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, by means of encouragement to obedience, in thoroughness in calling to right guidance.

The clause ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ explains the ambiguity in His saying ﴿what he has been charged with﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 55 (part 1 of 2):

﴿God has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors (istikhlaf) in the earth, as He made successors those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely replace their fear with security. They worship Me, not associating anything with Me. And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

It is more likely that this statement is a fresh, independent beginning (istinaf ibtida'i, a new sentence not grammatically tied to what precedes it), which moved to this point because of its connection (munasabah) with the mention of the conditions of the hypocrites. Their hesitation about the outcome of the Muslims' affair kept them in hypocrisy, and they feared that the Muslims would not remain settled in Medina, that the polytheists would attack them, or that the hypocrites would drive them out when they found the opportunity for that. This is as God the Exalted related from the words of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy: ﴿If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. So they would show Islam out of caution about the full success of Islam's affair, and conceal disbelief in collusion with the people of association (shirk). Then, when they prevailed over the Muslims, they would not blame the hypocrites for having changed their religion. There is also a connection between this statement and His words: (﴿If you obey him, you will be guided﴾ [al-Nur: 54]). So the meaning is: if you obey him, you will be guided, supported, and secured. Together with what has been transmitted of incidents that frightened the Muslims about their weakness before their enemies, so that they were anxious about an attack by the people of association and about the schemes of the hypocrites and their guiding the polytheists to the weak points of the Muslims, it was said that those incidents were the cause of the revelation of this verse.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "The Messenger of God remained in Mecca for ten years after revelation came to him, fearful, he and his companions. Then he was commanded to emigrate to Medina, and they were there in fear, morning and evening carrying weapons. A man said: 'O Messenger of God, will there not come a day upon us when we are secure and lay down our weapons?' The Messenger of God said: 'You will not wait long (lā taghburūn), meaning you will not remain except a little while, until one of you sits in the great assembly, reclining, with no iron upon him.'" And this verse was revealed.

So the convergence of these occasions was the cause of the revelation of this verse in this its place, with what it included of the promise, which was not limited to replacing their fear with security, as the report of Abu al-'Aliyah implies. Rather, that was among the things promised, just as its cause was among the causes.

The Muslims were confident of security, but God placed before His promise of security a promise of istikhlaf (succession) in the earth and the establishment of the religion and the law among them. This is a reminder to them that it is God's way (sunnah) that no nation is secure from the might of another until it is strong, firmly established, and dominant over its lands. In the promise of succession, establishment, and the replacement of fear with security, there is an indication of the readiness to acquire its causes, together with the assurance of success and triumph for them if they take up that course. The foundation of this is obedience to God and to the Messenger ﷺ (﴿If you obey him, you will be guided﴾ [al-Nur: 54]). When guidance settles in the souls, righteous deeds arise, and then their effects (musabbabat) pour down upon the community. Thus the causes are faith and the doing of righteous deeds.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is general and is not restricted to a specific group, and its generality is customary ('urfi), meaning that it is predominant. So it is not contradicted by the fact that some in the community fall short in doing righteous deeds, since those benefits return to the community as a whole.

The address in (minkum, "of you") is to the community of the call, including its polytheists and hypocrites: the group in which faith and the doing of righteous deeds are realized is the one promised by this promise.

The definite article in (al-salihat, "the righteous deeds") is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), meaning they did all righteous deeds, and these are the deeds that the Law (shar') described as righteous, and they abandoned the deeds that the Law described as corruption, because nullifying corruption is itself righteousness.

Thus al-salihat is the plural of salihah, which is the trait or act possessing righteousness, that is, what the Law has attested to be righteous. This was discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

The comprehensiveness of (al-salihat) is customary comprehensiveness, meaning they performed most of the righteous deeds, their important matters, and their principal duties, those things which return to the realization of the universal objectives (kulliyyat) of the Law and the community's conduct following the path of uprightness. This is achieved by uprightness in one's private life and by good conduct in the civil relations among the community, in accordance with what religion commands of the individuals of the community, each in what belongs to the work of his like, from the caliph down to the lowest. This applies in the majority of their conduct, and no attention is paid to the lapses that contradict it, for these are pardoned if one does not persist in them and if effort is made to correct them.

Uprightness in private life is what necessitates this promise, and it is faith and the foundations of Islam. Uprightness in dealings is what facilitates the cause of what is promised.

God the Exalted has made clear the principles of the orderly conduct of the community's affairs within His Book and through the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ, such as His words: ﴿God commands justice and excellence and giving to close relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression﴾ [al-Nahl: 90]. And His words:
﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except through trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29].
And His words in the context of blame: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the earth to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and lineage, and God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205]. And His words: ﴿So would you, if you were given authority, cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad: 22]. The Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, explained the conduct of rulers toward their subjects, toward the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah), and toward enemies in war, in truce, in armistice, and in treaty, and explained the principles of dealings among people.

Therefore, whenever the rulers and the general community are concerned with following what the Law has made clear to them, the promise of God to them with this great promise is realized.

These obligations which God made for the good of the community's affairs, and promised for them the granting of the caliphate, establishment, and security, became, by the arrangement of that promise upon them, causes for it. The promise was like the effect (musabbab) resulting from them. Thus they resembled in this respect the discourse of causation (khitab al-wad', the legal discourse establishing causes and conditions). Faith was made the pillar of these and a condition for being free of the obligation to fulfill them, and a guarantee for the attainment of their effects, by making it the means of attracting His pleasure and care. Through it, the community finds it easy to take up the causes of success, and through it the divine kindness surrounds the community throughout its stages of practice and pursuit, so that it repels from them obstacles and hindrances. Perhaps kindness and care surround them even when they fall short in carrying out these obligations, and when they mix righteousness with corruption, He shows them gentleness, does not hasten evil upon them, and delays the punishment for them. This is indicated by His words: ﴿And We had already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants. Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship. And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. He intends by all of that the Muslims. This matter was discussed in the commentary on surah al-Anbiya', and in His words: ﴿Indeed, God defends those who believe﴾ [al-Hajj: 38] in surah al-Hajj.

So if a people who are not Muslims were to conduct their lives and the affairs of their subjects by the same righteous deeds God commanded the Muslims to do, to the extent that they lacked nothing except faith in God and His Messenger, they would gather from their conduct forms resembling the realities that the Muslims gather, because those deeds become causes and sunnahs (established patterns) whose effects follow from them, which God made into laws and civilizational norms. Except that, because of their poor dealings with their Lord, by denying Him, or by associating others with Him, or by not affirming His Messenger, they will be far removed from His protection and support, and from His defense of them and His repelling of enemies from them. Rather, He leaves them to their own works and efforts according to the customary way. Do you not see that the European leaders, after they borrowed from Islam its laws and its system through what they observed of the affairs of Muslims during the Crusades, and then through what they acquired from studying books of Islamic history, Islamic jurisprudence, and the Prophetic biography, organized their realms on the principles of justice, excellence, mutual aid, and aversion to oppression and aggression, so their states grew great and their affairs became stable. This is no wonder, for God gave power to the Assyrians, who were polytheists, over the Children of Israel because of their corruption, and He said: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you would cause corruption in the earth twice and would become excessively arrogant. So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they ransacked the homes, and it was a promise fulfilled﴾ [al-Isra': 4]. This was discussed in surah al-Isra'.

Al-istikhlaf: making them successors (khulafa'), meaning successors of God in managing the affairs of His servants, as He said: ﴿Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successor﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], which was discussed in surah al-Baqarah. The sin and ta' (in istakhlafa) are for emphasis. Its origin is: layukhlifannahum fi al-ard (He will surely make them succeed in the earth).

The attachment of the act of istikhlaf to the whole group of those who believe and do righteous deeds, even though the management of the community's affairs is entrusted to its rulers and not to the whole community, is because the whole community benefits from it and assists in it, each according to his position in society, as God the Exalted related the words of Moses to the Children of Israel: (﴿And He made you kings﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20]), as was discussed in surah al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah).

For this reason, the correct view is that the intended meaning of "the earth" is all of it, and that the indication of place conveyed by the particle (fi, "in") is apparent for a part of the earth, namely the seat of the community's government and the place where its rulings reach its inhabitants. The default in the indication of place is that the contained does not encompass the container, as in His words: ﴿and He settled you in it﴾ [Hud: 61].

The discourse was phrased in this composition and was not limited to His words (﴿He will surely make them successors﴾) without restriction by His words (in the earth) for (﴿He will surely make them successors﴾), to indicate that the istikhlaf will occur over most of the earth. This admits of expansion and contraction, as was the case on the day the lands of al-Andalus went out of the rule of Islam. But the sanctity of the community and the protection of its might spread throughout the inhabited world, so that those other nations in the lands not under their rule fear them and strive greatly to win their approval and their peace. This is complete istikhlaf. For this reason, the verse is oriented by comparing it with the istikhlaf of those before them, meaning the nations that ruled most of the world and frightened all of it, such as the Assyrians, the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, the Jews in the time of Solomon, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans.

It is reported from Malik that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and 'Umar, so the plural relative pronoun is used with the meaning of the dual. It is reported from al-Dahhak: this verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, and 'Ali. Perhaps this is what Malik intended. On this view, the intended meaning of "those before them" is the righteous kings, such as Yusuf, Dawud, Sulayman, Anushirvan, Ashama al-Najashi, Melchizedek (Malik Sadiq) who was in the time of Ibrahim and is called Hammurabi, Dhu al-Qarnayn, Alexander the Macedonian, and some of those who governed the Greek republic.

In the verse there is clear evidence that the caliphs of the community, such as Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, al-Hasan, and Mu'awiyah, were in a station of God's good pleasure, because He made them successors with a complete istikhlaf, as He made successors those before them, and He opened the lands for them from the East to the West, and made the Chosroes and the Caesars fear them.

The clause (﴿He will surely make them successors﴾) explains the clause (He promised), because it is the very thing promised. And since it is a clause of oath, and an oath is a kind of speech, one of the two clauses is an explanation of the other.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read (﴿as He made [them] successors﴾) with the active voice, meaning as God made successors those before them. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it in the passive voice, so that (al-ladhina, "those") is the deputy subject.

[Page 288 of the original]

*Tamkin al-din* (the establishing of the religion): its spread among tribes and nations and the abundance of its followers. The word *tamkin*, whose literal meaning is firm establishment and rooting, is used metaphorically (*isti'arah*) for the meaning of widespread diffusion. This is because when a thing spreads, it is no longer feared to vanish, so it is like a thing firmly fixed and rooted. When its followers are few, it is like a thing unsettled and unstable. This promise is what the Prophet ﷺ pointed to in many hadiths, including the hadith of al-Hudaybiyah, in which he said: "If they refuse, that is, except for fighting, then by Him in whose hand is my soul, I will fight them for this matter of mine until my neck is severed," that is, until the front part of the neck separates from the body, "and God will surely make His command prevail."

His words "for them" (*lahum*): the apparent requirement is that it should come after "their religion" (*dinahum*), because a prepositional phrase (*al-majrur bi'l-harf*) is weaker in its connection than the object of a verb. He placed "for them" before it to indicate concern for them, that is, that the establishment is for their sake, similar to placing the prepositional phrase before the two objects in His words: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast, and remove from you your burden?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1].

The attribution of the religion to their pronoun (*dinahum*, "their religion") honors them with it, because it is God's religion, as indicated by His following words: ﴿which He has approved for them﴾, that is, which He chose to be their religion. This implies that He also chose them to be the followers of this religion. There is in this an indication that those described by this relation are the ones who spread this religion among the nations, since it is their religion, so its establishment among people comes through them.

He said ﴿and He will surely change [their state] after their fear into security﴾ and did not say "and He will grant them security," as He said regarding those before them, because they did not aspire at that time to security, as is related in the hadith of Abu al-'Aliyah mentioned just above. They were in a state that was the opposite of security. Had they been given security without being in a state of fear, security would have been a single favor. The attribution of the fear to their pronoun indicates that it was a known and established fear.

The indefiniteness of *amnan* (security) is for magnification, as shown by the context that it is substituted for "after their fear," which was known for its severity. The intended meaning is security from their enemies, the polytheists and the hypocrites. In this there is good news that God will remove polytheism and hypocrisy from the community. This promise does not require that no events of fear occur in the community in some regions, such as the fear that befell the people of Medina from the uprising of the people of Egypt, who were led by the misguided Malik al-Ashtar al-Nakha'i, and like the fear that occurred in Medina on the day of al-Harrah, and other such events. Those were consequences of human causes, and to God is their return and upon God is their reckoning.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *wa-layubaddilannahum* with a fatha on the *ba'* and a shadda on the *dal*. Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *dal*. The meaning is one.

The clause *ya'budunani* ("they worship Me") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the preceding third-person pronouns, meaning: this promise occurred while they were worshipping Me. In this circumstance there is notice that this promise is a reward for them, that is, I promised them this promise, which encompasses them and extends to their successors, because they worship Me with worship sincere of any association.

He used the imperfect tense (*al-mudari'*) to convey the continuation of their state in this, as an allusion to the hypocrites, who used to believe and then turn back.

The clause ﴿they do not associate anything with Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun in ﴿they worship Me﴾, restricting the worship to this state, because polytheists may worship God but also associate others with Him. In these two clauses there is something that supports what we mentioned above, that faith is the condition for God's guarantee to the community of this promise.

The clause ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (*al-fasiqun*)﴾ is a warning after the good news, following the Qur'anic custom of following good news with warning and vice versa, to prevent complacency.

The reference in His words "after that" is to the faith expressed here by ﴿they worship Me, not associating anything with Me﴾, and expressed at the beginning of the verses by His words ﴿God has promised those who believe﴾. That is: whoever disbelieves after faith and after what he obtained of good news upon it, those are the defiantly disobedient from the truth.

The form of restriction (*sigha al-hasr*) derived from defining the predicate with the definite article of genus is used for emphasis, to indicate that this is complete defiance.

The description of them as *al-fasiqun* has a graceful placement, because the root *f-s-q* indicates going out of a place through a narrow exit.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 56:

﴿And establish the prayer, and give the zakat, and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭafa) upon the clause ﴿They worship Me, not associating anything with Me﴾ [al-Nur: 55], because it contains the sense of a command to abandon shirk. It is as if it were said: "Worship Me, do not associate others with Me, and establish the prayer," for when a statement contains the meaning of a command, it has the force of an imperative verb, to the point that its response may be put in the jussive, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Saff: 11], up to His saying: ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾ [al-Saff: 12], where (yaghfir) is in the jussive, because His saying "you believe" (tu'minun) has the force of saying "Believe in Allah!"

The address is directed specifically to those who believe, after it had been directed to the community of the call in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. Therefore the obedience commanded here is other than the obedience in His saying: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger; but if they turn away﴾ [al-Nur: 54] etc., because that is a call to those who turn away, and this is an increase for the believers.

This verse has gathered all the righteous deeds: the most important of them are mentioned explicitly, and the rest are covered by a general omission of the object in His saying: ﴿and obey the Messenger﴾ [al-Nur: 54], meaning in everything he commands you and forbids you.

Upon this is ordered the hope that mercy may be attained by them: in this world, through the fulfilment of the promise, of which security is part of His mercy, and in the Hereafter, through the high ranks. The discussion of (laʿalla) has preceded in more than one place in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 57:

﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape [Allah] upon the earth. Their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the destination.﴾

Page 290

This is an independent resumptive sentence (istitnaf ibtida'i) to confirm what was implied by His words: ﴿And He will surely replace them, after their fear, with security﴾ [al-Nur: 55]. The polytheists at that time still possessed power and numbers, and the Muslims were still fearing their violence. Thus the promise of security from their violence may have been received with wonder and with a delay resembling hesitation, so His words came as reassurance and consolation: ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape [Allah] upon the earth﴾.

The address is to one in whom wonder and delay may stir, without specifying a particular person.

The purpose of the prohibition against this supposing is to draw attention to the certainty of the report.

The reading of the majority is (تَحْسَبَنَّ) with the feminine-second-person prefix (the ta' of address). Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah alone read it with the ya' of the third person, so that (الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا) becomes the subject of (يَحْسَبَنَّ), leaving (مُعْجِزِينَ) as its single object. Abu Hatim, al-Nahhas and al-Farra' said: this is an error or weak, because the verb of supposing (fi'l al-husban) requires two objects. This view is a presumption against a mutawatir reading. Al-Zajjaj said: the first object is omitted, its estimated form being (أنْفُسَهم, "themselves"), and this is well-aimed, since omission is not rare in speech. In al-Kashshaf, it is stated that (في الأرْضِ, "upon the earth") is the second object, meaning: do not suppose that people are escapers upon the earth (i.e., there is nothing on earth that is not within the reach of Allah's power; if He wills, He seizes it; thus there is no refuge for them anywhere on earth). He said: "This is a strong and good meaning."

(Mu'jiz), the one who renders another incapable: that is, makes him unable to overcome him. This was discussed previously at His words: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape [it]﴾ [al-An'am: 134] in Surat al-An'am. Likewise, (mu'ajiz), in the sense of one who attempts to make the other incapable, was discussed at His words: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate [them]﴾ [al-Hajj: 51] in Surat al-Hajj.

(Al-ard), "the earth," is the earth of this world; that is, they are not dominant in this world, as they supposed that there is no other realm. (Upon the earth) is connected to (mu'jizin) according to the reading of the majority, and according to some interpretations of the reading of Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir; or it is the second object according to some interpretations, as you have known.

Page 291

His words: (﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾), that is, in the Hereafter it is known that their refuge is the Fire, so they have lost both worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verses 58–59:

﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not reached puberty ask permission of you at three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you put off your clothing at midday, and after the night prayer. These are three times of privacy for you. There is no blame on you or on them beyond these, as they circulate among you, some of you attending to others. Thus does Allah make the verses clear to you, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make His verses clear to you, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

This is a transitional resumption (istinaf) to a topic from the rules of mixing and association. It returns to the theme with which the surah began, which was interrupted at His words: ﴿and an admonition for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Nur: 34], as has been mentioned previously.

In this verse is mentioned the legislation of seeking permission for the followers of the household and for those who are very much in contact with the household when they wish to enter a house. It is thus one of the complements of what was mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. In terms of its time-reference, it requires the specification of the generality of His words: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own﴾ [al-Nur: 27] and what follows, because that is general in respect of places and times. So His words ﴿those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not reached puberty﴾

[Page 292 continues]

up to His words ﴿and after the night prayer﴾ are legislation for their seeking permission at these times. This implies that they do not need to seek permission at other times than these three times. Thus the implicit meaning (mafhum) becomes a specifier of the generality of the prohibition in His words: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. Furthermore, this command is also specified by the generality of "those whom their right hands possess" and by the generality of ﴿the male attendants who have no sexual desire, or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private aspects of women﴾ [al-Nur: 31], from His words, exalted is He: ﴿and not to reveal their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31] etc., mentioned just above.

It has been reported that Asma' bint Marthad: "An elderly male servant of hers entered upon her at a time when she disliked his entering. This was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private aspects of women﴾ [al-Nur: 31].

What comes after the night prayer is the whole night until the time of rising from sleep before dawn. The phrase ("three times") is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of ("let them ask permission of you"), because ("times") carries the force of ("permissions").

The command was not explicitly directed to the addressees to seek permission from those whom their right hands possess, because it is rare for masters to enter upon their slaves or their young servants, since the normal situation is that when they need them, they call them. As for when the need arises for entering upon them, the ruling regarding them is the same. The reason has been indicated by His words: ﴿They circulate among you, some of you attending to others﴾.

His words ("﴿They circulate among you﴾") are the predicate of a deleted subject, whose estimate is: "They are those who circulate," referring to ﴿those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not reached puberty﴾.

The discourse is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), i.e., "The reason why blame is lifted from them and from you in entering without permission after those three times is that they circulate among you; so if they had to seek permission, that would be a hardship for them and for you."

("some of you attending to others") is also a new independent sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah). ("some of you") may be considered the subject (mubtada'), and ("upon others") is connected to a deleted predicate, whose estimate is: "a circulator upon others". The predicate was deleted and what is connected to it remained; that is a specific sense (kawn khass) that was deleted because ("circulate") indicates it. The estimate is: "some of you is a circulator upon others." It is not good for someone who makes ("some of you upon others") a substitute (badal) for the waw in ("circulate among you") to do so, because it refers back to ﴿those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not reached puberty﴾. So it is not good for some of the addressees to be substituted for it, since they are not from either group, except with an estimate.

His clarification reaches the utmost degree of perfection, such that if one wished to liken it to something, it would be likened only to itself. It has been mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verses are attributed here to the Divine Name (Allah) for the sake of firmness and to strengthen the emphasis on the meaning of complete clarification that arises from His words ("thus").
