Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 60:

﴿And as for women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments, without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾

This verse specifies His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And not to display their adornment except what appears thereof; and to draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾ [al-Nur: 31], up to His saying: ﴿...or the private parts of women﴾ [al-Nur: 31].

The occasion for this specification here is that it came after the obligation of seeking permission (istidhan) at the times when men and women take off their garments from their bodies. So the discourse turned to a kind of removing of garments from the one wearing them, namely the putting aside by elderly women of some of their garments. Thus, from the general category of women, those who have advanced in age, to the point that they have reached the time of menopause (al-iyas min al-mahid), are exempted. He granted them leave not to draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not to draw their outer cloaks (jalabib) down over themselves. From Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas: "al-thiyab" means "al-jilbab", i.e., the outer wrap and the veil that is over the khimar. And al-Suddi said: it is also permissible for them to remove the khimar.

صفحة ٢٩٧
"Al-qawa'id" is the plural of qa'id without the feminine ta' (ha' al-ta'nith), like hamil and ha'id; because it is a descriptive term that was transferred to a meaning specific to women, namely sitting (qu'ud) from childbearing and from menstruation. The term "sitting" was borrowed for lack of ability, because sitting prevents reaching what is desired; and a woman's desire is for children, and menstruation is among the causes of childbirth. When it was borrowed for that and became common in usage, the descriptive "qa'id" in this sense became specific to the feminine, so the ta' of feminization was not attached to it, since there is no need for the ta' to distinguish masculine from feminine. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾, and that is due to old age.

His saying ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾ is a descriptive clause clarifying "al-qawa'id", not a restrictive condition.

The conjunction of the predicate with the fa' in His saying ﴿then there is no blame upon them﴾ is because the speech carries the sense of causation and conditionality, since this subject (mubtada') implies anticipation of what follows it, so it resembles the conditional, as was previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. There is no need to claim that the "al" in it is a relative (mawsulah), since the meaning of the relative does not appear from the definite article, even though this is common in the speech of the grammarians. And "an yada'na" is connected to "junah" with the implied "fi" (in).

By "the garments" is meant some of them, namely that which the woman is commanded to draw down over herself, by the indication of the context of specification.

Wad' (putting down) is attaching one thing upon another; its original construction is with the preposition "'ala", and it may be constructed with the preposition "'an" when it is intended that it was removed from a place and placed upon another, and this is what is meant here, like the verb "targhabun" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] in Surat al-Nisa', i.e., that they remove their garments from themselves so that they place them on the ground or on a clothes-rack. The reason for this concession is that men's desire for such elderly women is generally absent or diminished due to advanced age. Since the command to draw the khimar over the chests or to draw down the jalabib imposed hardship on the women commanded, which was required by the closing of the means (sadd al-dhari'ah), when that means ceased to exist, that ruling was lifted out of Allah's mercy. Indeed, the Sharia does not impose hardship in a ruling because of necessity except that it lifts that hardship when the necessity ceases, and this is the meaning of rukhsah (concession).

Therefore this concession is followed by His saying: ﴿But to refrain is better for them﴾.

صفحة ٢٩٨
Al-istif'af means ta'affuf (restraint), so the sin and ta' in it are for emphasis, like "istajaba". That is, their restraint from removing their garments is better for them. For this reason this permission is qualified by the condition: ﴿without displaying adornment﴾, i.e., a removal not accompanied by displaying adornment.

Al-tabarruj means takashshuf (uncovering). The ba' in "bi-zinah" is for accompaniment, so the meaning returns to the removal of garments not being an exposure of adornment that was previously concealed. What is meant is the display of what believing women are accustomed to concealing. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not display yourselves as the displaying of the former Jahiliyyah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], for when a woman displays herself with adornment that it is her custom to conceal except from her husband, it is as if she is alluding to attracting men's admiration and arousing their desire for her. Even if she is among the elderly, her alluding to this contradicts good manners and removes the dignity of her age, and some people of desire may still be drawn to her, because the display of adornment may cover her defects or distract from them by focusing on the beauty of her adornment.

Thus tabarruj with adornment is adorning oneself with what is not customary to display outwardly, such as reddening and whitening, and likewise rare colours. Bashshar said:

And when you go out, veil yourself with red [veils], for beauty is red.

'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, was asked about dyeing, colouring, and amulets, i.e., silver cases in which amulets and charms are placed which a woman hangs, and earrings, anklets, gold rings, and thin garments. She said: "God has permitted you adornment, not displaying yourselves to those for whom it is not lawful for you to be seen by them as unlawful." She referred the matter to what is customary and well known. So tabarruj is the appearance of what the garment cast over her used to conceal, such as a tattoo on the hand or chest, or black engraving on the neck or chest called in Tunisia "al-hurquss" (a non-Arabic word). In the Muwatta': Hafsah bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr entered upon 'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, and Hafsah had on a thin khimar, so 'A'ishah tore it and clothed her with a thick khimar, i.e., she tore it so that she would not cover herself with it afterwards.

It was said: what is meant by His saying ﴿without displaying adornment﴾ is without uncovering themselves by going out from their homes into the road; that is, they may put aside their garments in their houses. So if she goes out, it is not permissible for her to leave off her outer cloak. The meaning thus returns to their putting aside their garments in their houses, and this is a reinforcement of what was previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and not to strike their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31]; that is, their being of the elderly does not warrant leave except in putting aside their garments in a manner free of any intention of attracting desire towards them.

The clause ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾ is placed as a concluding statement (tadhyil) warning against extending the concession or making it a pretext for what is not praiseworthy in the Sharia. The attribute "Hearing" is a reminder that He hears what their souls whisper to them of intentions, and the attribute "Knowing" is a reminder that He knows the circumstances of their putting aside garments, their displaying themselves, and the like.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 24, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, [any] blame.﴾

Scholars have differed over whether His statement, ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ and so on, is separate from His statement ﴿nor upon yourselves﴾, and whether it serves a purpose other than eating in homes. In that case it would be part of the verse on seeking permission (al-isti'dhan). Alternatively, it is connected to what follows and serves one purpose.

Al-Hasan and Jabir ibn Zayd held the first view. It is also the view preferred by al-Jubba'i, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-'Arabi and Abu Hayyan. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is the apparent meaning of the verse." This is the view we choose, to avoid the artificial reasoning that their opponents used to explain its connection to what follows, namely the justification for the concession to these three categories regarding eating in the mentioned houses. Also, in His statement ﴿that you eat from your houses﴾ through to the end of the listed items, its connection to the blind, the lame and the sick is not clearly apparent. Therefore this verse is a negation of blame for these three from the hardships that their infirmities bring upon them in their actions. Blame is lifted from them in everything their infirmities compel them to do. Their intention requires them to perform it completely, and their excuse requires that it be done by them. Thus blame is negated for the blind in duties that require sight, for the lame in duties that require walking and riding, and for the sick in duties that illness causes to be dropped, such as fasting, the conditions of prayer, and military expedition (al-ghazw).

Page 300

However, the appropriateness of mentioning this concession directly after the seeking of permission is that the purpose is to permit the blind man that seeking permission is not obligatory upon him, since the cause that requires it is absent. Then he mentioned the lame and the sick by way of incorporation (al-idmaj) and to complete the ruling of concession for them, because of the relation between them and the blind man.

The second view was held by the majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin). They strained greatly to explain why these three categories are counted among those who eat from the food in the houses of those mentioned in the following verse.

In both views, the sentence is a fresh, independent beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i).

* * *

﴿Nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or what you possess the keys to, or your friend. There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately.﴾

The connection of these concessions to the concession for the blind man, on the assumption that the verse is separate from it as mentioned above, which is the view preferred by the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun), is that both are related to seeking permission and entering houses, whether the purpose is eating in them or visiting and the like, since all share in the lifting of blame. On the assumption that it is connected to what precedes, according to the view of the majority, the grouping of all of them in one ruling is the concession for all of them to eat. God therefore permitted the blind, the lame and the sick to enter to eat, because they are needy and cannot earn a living, and earning a living at that time was by physical labour. So He granted these people permission to enter the houses of the Muslims to fill their stomachs.

Page 301

This is the most apparent of the explanations for counting these three together with those who are joined to them. The exegetes have mentioned other explanations, which Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi in his Ahkam al-Qur'an reduced to eight, none of which satisfies the heart, so we will not go into them at length.

The particle (la) was repeated with the conjoined item following the earlier negated item, to emphasize the meaning of negation. This is a very common usage.

What is meant by eating here is eating without an invitation. This applies when the food is present, not when it is stored.

What is meant by "yourselves" (al-anfus) is the persons of the addressees, marked by the signs of address. It is as if it were said: "And there is no blame upon you that you eat," through to the end. Thus the address is to the community.

What is meant by a person eating from his own house is unusual eating, that is, eating in a manner in which the rest of his household does not share, such as when a man eats while his wife is absent, or when she eats while her husband is absent. This is a permitted particularity (athara murakhkhasa).

He joined the houses of their fathers to the houses of "yourselves", but did not mention the houses of their children, even though children are closer to the one who eats than fathers are, and so they are more entitled to eat from their houses. It has been said that this is because children live with their fathers in their houses. This is not valid, for a son who married would build a house for himself, as in the report about 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. The correct view is that the ruling on the houses of children is known by a fortiori reasoning (bi-al-awla) from the rest, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You and your wealth belong to your father."

Among those enumerated in the verse there is a kinship, guardianship or friendship that normally produces leniency among them in attending to eat without an invitation. Generally, none of them feels embarrassed about this.

The (ma) in His statement, ﴿or what you possess the keys to﴾, is a relative pronoun referring to a place or food. It is joined to ﴿the houses of your maternal aunts﴾, not to ﴿your maternal uncles﴾. For this reason (ma) is used, since it is most commonly used for non-rational beings.

Page 302

The possession of keys is meant in the sense of guarding them, as indicated by its being attributed to the keys rather than to the houses or walls. The word (mafatih) is the plural of (maftah), which is the name of an instrument for opening. It is also said (miftah), and its plural is (mafatih).

This is a concession for the agent (wakil) and the keeper of food, and the guardian of a fruit orchard, that each of them may eat from what is under his control without permission, and not exceed the fill of his stomach. This is because custom makes it like a permission. For this reason the jurists have said: if one of these people has a wage for his work, it is not lawful for him to eat from what is under his hand.

(Sadiq, friend), here, is meant generically, as a collective noun that applies to a group, as indicated by its being attributed to the plural pronoun of the addressees. It is a word in which agreement with the one it describes or predicates, whether singular, dual, plural, masculine or feminine, is permissible, and this is the original usage. In eloquent usage, however, it most commonly keeps one invariable form. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any devoted friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100]. Similar is (khalit) and (qatin).

The (sadiq) is of the form (fa'il) in the sense of (fa'il) in the active sense, meaning one who is sincere in affection. It has been placed in the rank of kinship, because of what is held in high regard in souls concerning love for maintaining ties with friends. One of the wise men was asked: "Which of the two men is more beloved to you, your brother or your friend?" He said: "I only love my brother when he is my friend."

The sentence ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ is repeated as emphasis for the first in His statement ﴿nor upon yourselves﴾, since blame (junah) and hardship (haraj) are almost synonymous. This emphasis is good after the condition and its bearer have been specified, namely the plural waw in His statement ﴿that you eat from your houses﴾. Because it serves as emphasis, it is separated without a conjunction.

(Jami') means those gathered on a matter.

(Ashtat) means those dispersed in a matter in which their normal state is to be gathered. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are divided﴾ [al-Hashr: 14].

(Ashtat) is the plural of (shatt), which is the verbal noun of (shatta), meaning to be scattered. (Shatta) is the plural of (shatit).

Page 303

The meaning is: There is no blame upon you that one of you eats together with a group who came to eat in the same way, or that he eats alone, separate from a partner, lest one of them think that if he finds someone who came to eat before him, he must refrain from eating until the one who came first leaves. Or that one of you eats with the household of the house, or that he eats alone.

The reading of (buyut) with a kasra on the (ba') is the reading of the majority. It is read with a damma by Warsh and by Hafs from 'Asim. This was mentioned earlier at His statement, ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses﴾ [al-Nur: 27] in this surah.

* * *

﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses that you might understand.﴾

This is a consequence of the permission granted to them to eat from these houses, reminding them of the etiquette of entering that was mentioned earlier in His statement: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. This is so that they do not treat kinship, friendship and familiarity as something that permits abandoning manners. A person's duty is to observe good manners with relatives and strangers alike, and he should not be deceived by the people's saying: "When love is equal, manners fall away."

The meaning of ﴿greet one another﴾ is: let some of you greet others, as in His statement: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29].

Some people have clung to the apparent wording and neglected its subtle meaning, thinking that the one entering greets himself if he finds no one. This is far removed from the aims of the duties and manners. As for what is reported in the tashahhud, His statement "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God", this is peace in the sense of invoking safety. The Prophet (ﷺ) made it their substitute for what they used to say: "Peace be upon God; peace be upon the Prophet; peace be upon Gabriel and Michael; peace be upon so-and-so and so-and-so."

Page 304

The Messenger of God said to them: "God is Peace (al-Salam)", refuting their saying "Peace be upon God." Then he said to them: "Say: Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God, for when you say it, it reaches every righteous servant of God in heaven and on earth."

As for peace in this verse, it means greeting, as He explained it with His statement: ﴿a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾. No one is commanded to greet himself.

(Tahiyya), its origin is the verbal noun of (hayyahu tahiyya), then the two yas were assimilated for lightness, and it is the saying: "May God give you life (hayyaka Allah)." This was discussed earlier at His statement, ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, respond with one better than it﴾ [al-Nisa': 86] in Surat al-Nisa'.

So (tahiyya) is a verbal noun of a verb derived from the sentence containing the verb (hayya), like the saying (jazahu), when one says to him: "May God reward you with good", as was mentioned earlier in the verb (wa tusallimu 'ala ahliha) just above. This word was the greeting of the Arabs before Islam, the common greeting. Al-Nabigha said:

"May my Lord give you life, for it is not lawful for us to indulge in the pleasures of women, and religion has indeed resolved."

The greeting of kings was "Be well in the morning (i'm sabahan)". Islam made the greeting the phrase "Peace be upon you (al-salamu 'alaykum)", which is one of the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim). This is because the purpose of the greeting is to make the one entering feel at ease, by granting him security if he is unknown to them, and by showing kindness to him if he is known.

The word (al-salam) combines both meanings, because it is derived from safety (al-salama). It is therefore a supplication for safety and a grant of security by peace. Because when he prays for safety for him, he is surrendering (muslim) to him, so the statement became a metaphor for granting security. When both matters are realized, great good is achieved, since safety does not coexist with any evil in the person who is safe, and security does not coexist with any evil coming from an aggressor. Thus it is a supplication whose answer is hoped for, and a pledge of security that must be fulfilled. In the phrase "upon you" (alaykum) there is the sense of firm establishment, that is, safety is settled upon you.

Because the phrase "peace" (al-salam) comprises this meaning, God bestowed a favour upon the Muslims with it, by making it from God, since He is the one who taught it to His Messenger through revelation.

Page 305

(Tahiyyatan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the greeting (al-taslim) implied by (fa-sallimu), like the return of the pronoun to the verbal noun in His statement: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8].

(Mubaraka) means one in which blessing (baraka) has been placed. Blessing is the abundance of good. This greeting is blessed because of the intention of peace it contains, the goodness of meeting and familiarity, and this secures the good of Islamic brotherhood.

(Tayyiba) means possessing goodness, and this is a metaphorical goodness, in the sense of purity and acceptance in people's souls. The reason the greeting is good is that it is a supplication for safety, and an announcement of peace and friendly relations. The pattern of (tayyiba) is (fay'ila), an intensive form for description, like (al-faysal). It was discussed earlier at His statement: ﴿He said, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 38] in Al 'Imran, and at His statement: ﴿and they sailed with them in a favourable wind﴾ [Yunus: 22] in Surat Yunus.

The meaning is that the phrase "Peace be upon you" is a greeting of goodness, better than the greeting of the people of the pre-Islamic age (jahiliyya). This is like His statement: ﴿and their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10], that is, their greeting is this phrase.

The sentence ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾ repeats the two sentences that came before it in the verse of seeking permission (al-isti'dhan); for in everything that came before this sentence there is an explanation of the verses of the Qur'an, by which the rulings they contain have become clear. This is an explanation with which it is hoped that you will attain understanding and knowledge of what it contains, which is the perfection of your affairs.

**Verse 62 of Surah 24:**

﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So when they ask your permission for some matter of their own, give permission to whomever you wish among them, and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

[Page 306]

When the preceding discussion concerned seeking permission to enter, it was followed by the ruling on seeking permission to leave and to depart from gatherings. Among these rulings, the one given the most attention is the obligatory one: seeking the permission of the Messenger (ﷺ) to leave his assembly, or to leave a gathering that was convened by his permission for an important matter, such as consultation (shura), fighting (qital), gathering for admonition (wa'z), and the like.

It was among the practices of the hypocrites (munafiqun) to attend these gatherings and then slip away from them, either to avoid a burdensome task or out of weariness at hearing speech they did not value. Allah censured this conduct, informed that it contradicts faith, and that it is the mark of hypocrisy. He did this by turning away from describing the hypocrites' hypocrisy and instead giving attention to the true believers' possession of the opposite quality. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And whenever a surah is sent down, some of them look at others, [asking], "Does anyone see you?" Then they turn away. Allah has turned their hearts away, because they are a people who do not comprehend.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 127]. For this reason, at the end of these verses comes His saying: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, clinging to one another.﴾ [An-Nur: 63].

Thus the restriction (qasr) conveyed by "innama" (only) is a restriction of the subject to a particular attribute (qasr mawsuf 'ala sifah). The definiteness in "al-mu'minun" (the believers) is either the definiteness of genus (ta'rif al-jins), meaning the genus of believers, or the definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), meaning that those known by the attribute of faith are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger and do not depart until they ask his permission. The predicate is the combination of the three matters, and this is a restriction relative to a particular situation (qasr idafi), specifically a restriction of singling out (qasr ifrad). That is, only those possessing this attribute among those who display faith do not leave when the Messenger wishes to depart, without asking his permission. This attribute was therefore made a distinctive mark of the true believers as opposed to the hypocrites of that time, since none of the true believers at that time would leave the Prophet's gathering without his permission. The aim, then, is to display the mark of the believers and to distinguish them from the mark of the hypocrites.

The context of the verse is not to define the reality of faith, because faith has a known reality, and seeking the Prophet's permission when wishing to leave is not among its pillars. Therefore, it is clear that the purpose of this restriction is not to deny faith from one who leaves without permission, when this is done by one of the true believers without intent to forsake or harm the Prophet (ﷺ). For if one of the believers did this, it would amount to nothing more than a lapse in etiquette that deserves reprimand and a warning to avoid it, because it is a trait of hypocrisy, as warnings against the traits of hypocrisy have been reported in many hadiths.

[Page 307]

You should also know that the definiteness in "al-mu'minun" does not intend the meaning of perfection (kamal), for if it did, the purpose of exposing the hypocrisy of the hypocrites would not be achieved.

"Al-amr" means the matter or the state of importance. It was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿And those in authority among you﴾ [An-Nisa: 59], in Surah An-Nisa.

"Al-jami'" is that which, by its nature, people gather for, either for consultation or for learning. What is meant here is that which the Muslims gather for around the Messenger (peace be upon him), in his assembly or in congregational prayer. This is what the particles "ma'a" (with) and "'ala" (on) in His saying ﴿on a matter of common concern⁠ (ma'ahu 'ala amrin jami')⁠﴾ indicate: "ma'a" conveys the sense of participation, and "'ala" conveys the sense of being engaged in it.

Describing the matter as "jami'" (gathering) is a metaphor of attribution (majaz 'aqli), since the matter is the cause of the gathering. A similar usage appeared earlier in His saying: ﴿So resolve upon your plan⁠﴾ [Yunus: 71], in Surah Yunus.

It is related from Malik that this verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq), and that was in the fifth year after the Hijrah. The hypocrites would slip away from the army at the Trench and offer false excuses.

The clause ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission⁠﴾ through to its end is a confirmation (ta'kid) of the clause ﴿The believers are only those⁠﴾, because the meaning of this clause is the same as the meaning of the clause ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger⁠﴾, and so on. The author has varied the wording of the second clause by changing the structure of the first: what was the predicate in the first becomes the subject in the second, and what was the subject in the first becomes the predicate in the second. Both structures ultimately amount to the same thing, since the end result is an assertion that "this is that," in the manner of "my poetry is my poetry," to highlight the importance of seeking permission. Upon this is built the following consequence: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some matter of their own⁠﴾, in order to teach the believers the excuses that justify seeking permission. That is, they are not permitted to ask leave to depart except for a matter of importance among their affairs.

There is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab) in His saying "yasta'dhinunaka" (they ask your permission), honoring the Messenger (ﷺ) by addressing him directly.

Allah gave His Messenger the choice to grant permission to whomever among the believers asked him, because he knows best the matter whose resolution outweighs the presence at the common gathering. The Prophet's choice is never based on whim, but rather on a valid excuse and a benefit.

[Page 308]

His saying ﴿and ask Allah's forgiveness for them⁠﴾ indicates that such departure is contrary to what is proper, because it prioritizes their own need over assisting the need of the community.

This verse is a foundation of the organization of communal gatherings for the welfare of the community, because it is part of the Sunnah that every gathering should have an imam and a leader who manages its affairs. The legislation of the imamate (imamah) points to this system. It is also part of the Sunnah that when any group gathers, they appoint a leader over themselves. Thus, the one who presides over the gathering stands in the place of the ruler of the Muslims, and so he stands in the place of the Prophet (ﷺ). No one should depart from his gathering except after seeking his permission, because if the matter of slipping away were left to the desire of each attendee, it would become a pretext for the dispersal of gatherings before the benefit for which they were convened is achieved. Likewise, it is proper etiquette to not be absent from a gathering when one is summoned to it, such as parliamentary, judicial, or religious assemblies, or to not be absent from an agreed-upon time for gathering, except for a valid excuse and after seeking permission.

[Page 309]

Since gathering around the Messenger for matters occurs after he calls the people to gather, and Allah had commanded them not to leave the Messenger's assemblies ﷺ without a valid excuse and his permission, He informed them with this verse of the obligation to respond when the Messenger calls them. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], has already been mentioned in Surat al-Anfal. The meaning is: ﴿Do not make the Messenger's calling you to attend him something you may choose to answer, as you choose in answering one another's call.﴾ So the point of comparison being denied between the two calls is choice in responding. The purpose of this sentence is that they should not suppose that what is required is to remain at the Messenger's assemblies once they have attended, and that when they are called to them they have a choice. On this interpretation, *al-du'a'* (calling) is the verbal noun of *da'aahu*, meaning he called him or sent for him to come.

The annexation of *du'a'* to *al-Rasul* is an annexation of the verbal noun to its agent. It is also permissible that the annexation of *du'a'* is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object, with the implied agent being the addressees. The meaning would then be: ﴿Do not make your calling of the Messenger...﴾, so the meaning is a prohibition addressed to them.

There is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person to address to the believers, to urge them to receive the sentence with lively understanding. The address is to the believers, about whom He spoke with His saying, ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nur: 62], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission﴾ [al-Nur: 62], and so on. They were forbidden to call the Messenger at his summons as some of them call others, either in words or in manner. As for words, this means they should not say, "O Muhammad," or "O son of 'Abd Allah," or "O son of 'Abd al-Muttalib," but rather "O Messenger of Allah," or "O Prophet of Allah," or use the kunya, "O Abu al-Qasim." As for manner, this means they should not call him from behind the apartments, and they should not insist in calling him when he does not come out to them, as came in Surat al-Hujurat, because all of this is from rudeness, which is not fitting for the greatness of the Messenger ﷺ. This is a discipline for the Muslims and a closing of the doors of harm from the hypocrites. Since the verse's wording may bear this meaning, it is valid for the reflective reader to derive this meaning from it, for it suffices that whoever sees a meaning in it takes what has become apparent to him.

*Baynakum* (among you) is an adverbial phrase, either *laghw* (superfluous) related to *tajʿalu* (make), or *mustaqirr* (settled) as a qualifier of *du'a'*, that is, his calling in your speech. The benefit of mentioning it on both readings is an allusion to the hypocrites who colluded among themselves to stay behind from the Messenger of Allah whenever he called them, whenever they found a way to do so, as indicated by His saying, ﴿It was not fitting for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to stay behind from the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 120]. So the meaning is: ﴿Do not make the Messenger's calling among you like what the hypocrites made among themselves, colluding over it.﴾

[Page 310]

This sentence is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*) between the sentence ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nur: 62] and what follows it, and between the sentence ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away covertly﴾.

The sentence ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away covertly﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) of threat, addressed to those who were the cause of the revelation of the verse ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nur: 62] and so on. That is: those believers, and their opposites who are alluded to, are not believers. Allah knows them and is aware of their slipping away.

*Qad* here confirms the report, because they think that if they slip away concealed, the Prophet will not notice them. So Allah informs them that He knows them, that is, that He informed His Messenger of it.

The entry of *qad* upon the present tense often comes to indicate multiplicity, because *qad* with the present tense functions like *rubba* (many a), which is used for multiplicity. Among its examples is His saying, ﴿Allah already knows those among you who hinder others﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18], and the saying of Zuhayr:

"A man of trust, wine does not ruin his wealth, but his giving can indeed ruin wealth."

*Alladhina yatasallaluna* (those who slip away) are the hypocrites. *Tasallul* is slipping out of a gathering, that is, leaving it secretly, leaving as if something were drawn out of something. One says *tasallala*, meaning he undertook to slip away, just as one says *tadakhkhala* when he undertook to enter himself.

*Liwadh* is the verbal noun of *lawadhahu*, when the other takes refuge with him. The concealment of some of them behind others, by agreement and conspiracy when departing secretly, is compared to the taking of refuge of some of them in others, because the one who shields the departing person until he leaves is in the position of one who takes refuge with him as well, so the occurrence of his act together with the act of the one taking refuge is treated as if it were a reciprocal action from *lawdh*.

*Liwadhan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), because it is in the sense of an active participle.

*Minkum* is related to *yatasallaluna*. The pronoun in *minkum* is addressed to the believers, that is: Allah already knows those who leave your congregation, slipping away and taking refuge with one another. Derived from what the sentence ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away covertly﴾ contains, after drawing attention to the fact that He, Exalted is He, is aware of their slipping away, comes a warning against opposing what Allah forbade in His saying, ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you...﴾, and so on.

[Page 311]

*Mukhalafa* means being different in the path one walks, by one walking on a path other than the one the other walked on. So its verb is transitive. Its object is omitted here because it is evident that what is meant is those who oppose Allah. The verb *mukhalif* is transitive with the particle *'an*, because it is treated as containing the sense of turning away, just as it is transitive with *ila* in His saying, ﴿I do not want to oppose you by doing what I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88], since it contains the sense of going. One says *khalafahu ila al-ma'* when he went to the water without him. Had its transitivity been left without a preposition, it would have indicated the basic sense of opposition in the purpose for which the speech is directed.

The pronoun in *'an amrihi* refers back to Allah, Exalted is He. *Amr* (command) is what His saying ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾ contains, for the prohibition of a thing implies the command to its opposite, so it is as if He said: "Make the Messenger's call an obedience both in public and in private." This is like the saying of Ibn Abi Rabi'a:

"So they said to her in secret, 'We ransom you, let him not depart sound; and if you do not kill him, then come close to doing so.'"

He made their saying "let him not depart sound" a prohibition meaning "kill him," then built on it his saying "and if you do not kill him, then come close."

*Al-hadhar* is avoiding a frightening thing. *Al-fitna* is the disturbance of people's condition, and it has already been mentioned at His saying, ﴿Fitna is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqara: 191] in al-Baqara. *Al-'adhab al-alim* here is the punishment of this world, which is the punishment of killing.

[p. 312]

**Commentary on verse 24:64**

﴿Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He knows your condition, and on the Day they are returned to Him He will inform them of what they did. And Allah is Knower of all things.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding appendage) to everything that preceded in this entire surah. Its opening with the particle of alerting (*harf al-tanbih*), *ala* ("Surely"), signals the end of the discourse and calls people's attention so that they attend to what follows the particle: that Allah owns what is in the heavens and the earth, so He will recompense His servants according to what they deserve, and He is aware of what they do.

The meaning of ﴿ma antum ʿalayhi﴾ ("what you are upon") is the states that they are associated with, whether good or bad. The preposition *ʿalā* (on, upon), which denotes elevation, is used metaphorically to express being firmly established in something.

He reminded them of the return (*al-maʿad*, the Resurrection) because the polytheists and the hypocrites were denying it.

His words ﴿fa-yunabbiʾuhum bi-ma ʿamilu﴾ ("then He will inform them of what they did") are a *kināya* (metonymy) for recompense, because informing them of their deeds would have no purpose if it were not a metonymy for recompense.

His words ﴿wa-Allahu bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalim﴾ ("and Allah is Knower of all things") are a *tadhyil* to the clause ﴿qad yaʿlamu ma antum ʿalayhi﴾ ("He knows your condition"), because it is more general than it.

In this verse there is a subtle point about His being aware of their states, because they used to conceal their hypocrisy.

[p. 313]

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**Surat al-Furqan**

This surah was named *Surat al-Furqan* during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and in his presence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I heard Hisham ibn Hakim ibn Hizam reciting Surat al-Furqan during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, so I listened to his recitation, and behold, he was reciting it in many different readings (*ḥurūf*) which the Messenger of Allah had not taught me. I almost pounced upon him during the prayer, but I restrained myself until he finished. Then I seized him by his cloak and led him to the Messenger of Allah, and I said: 'I heard this man reciting Surat al-Furqan in readings which you did not teach me.'" ... the hadith.

No other name is known for this surah besides this one. The teachers (*al-muʾaddibūn*) among the people of Tunis call it "Tabarak al-Furqan," just as they call Surat al-Mulk "Tabarak," and "Tabarak al-Malik."

The reason it is named "Surat al-Furqan" is the occurrence of the word *al-Furqan* in it three times: at its beginning, its middle, and its end.

It is Meccan according to the majority. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he excepted from it three verses which were revealed in Medina, namely the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ (Al-Furqan: 68) up to His words: ﴿And Allah has ever been Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (Al-Furqan: 70). The authentic report from him is that these three verses are Meccan, as in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the commentary on Surat al-Furqan: It is related from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah that he asked Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Is there repentance for one who kills a believer intentionally?" I recited to him ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ (Al-Furqan: 68). Saʿid said: "Did you recite it to Ibn ʿAbbas as you recited it to me?" He said: "This is Meccan; it was abrogated (*nasakhat*) by a Medinan verse, the one in Surat al-Nisaʾ," meaning His words: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ (Al-Nisaʾ: 93), and so on. It is also reported from al-Dahhak that the surah is Medinan except for the first three verses, from its beginning up to His words: ﴿nor resurrection﴾ (Al-Furqan: 3).

[p. 314]

The style and the aims of the surah bear witness that it is Meccan.

It is the forty-second surah in the chronological order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat Ya-Sin and before Surat Fatir. The number of its verses is seventy-seven, by agreement of those who counted the verses.

* * *

**The aims of this surah**

This surah includes beginning with the praise of Allah, exalted is He, and expressing commendation of Him, and describing Him with the attributes of divinity and oneness.

Included within this is the highlighting of the Qur'an, the greatness of its station, and the guidance it contains, along with an allusion to the favour Allah bestowed upon people through its guidance and its direction toward avoiding ruin, and the exaltation of the status of the Prophet (ﷺ).

This surah is established upon three pillars:

The first: affirming that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, and the exaltation of the Messenger upon whom it was sent down (ﷺ), the proofs of his truthfulness, and the loftiness of his station, above having the worldly interests (*ḥuẓūẓ*) that others have, and that he follows the same path as other messengers. Among this is the reception by his people of his call with denial.

The second pillar: affirming the resurrection and the recompense, warning of the recompense in the Hereafter, giving glad tidings of reward there for the righteous, and warning the polytheists of the evil of their fate on that Day, when they will feel remorse for their denial of the Messenger and for their associating partners with Allah and following the leaders of their disbelief.

The third pillar: the argument for the oneness of Allah and His being the sole Creator, His transcendence above having a son or a partner, the refutation of the divinity of idols, and the refutation of what they claimed about the angels being daughters of Allah, exalted is He.

In the verses of each of these three pillars the surah opens with the phrase ﴿Blessed is He who...﴾ (*tabāraka alladhī*), and so on.

Al-Tibi said: The focus of this surah is that he (ﷺ) was sent to all people, to warn them of what is before them and what is behind them. For this reason its opening, the excellence of its beginning, was:

[p. 315]

﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ (Al-Furqan: 1).

It mentions wondrous aspects of His creation, combining argument and reminder.

It follows this with strengthening the Messenger (ﷺ) in his call and in his resistance to the disbelievers.

It sets forth examples of both situations through the sending of earlier messengers and what they encountered from their peoples, such as the people of Moses, the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the People of the Well (*Aṣḥāb al-Rass*), and the people of Lot.

It also includes trust in Allah, praise of the believers in Him, commendation of their qualities and noble characters, and an indication of a near punishment that will befall the deniers.
